hero.eyebrow: Stage 2 of 3 · exploratory data analysis · complete
hero.title: What Australia's IP data show so far, and how we know
hero.lead: This research asks how Australia's intellectual property system creates public value, and where IP Australia could add the most. Before answering, the data have been examined in two stages: every measure on its own, then every pair of measures together. These pages set out what both stages found, in plain English, and let you follow any finding back to the public data it came from.

site.banner: **Stage 1 describes; Stage 2 relates; neither explains.** Stage 1's observations say what the data show: how much, how often, for whom, since when. Stage 2's say which measures go together, how strongly, and whether the link holds in a second period or sample. None says why, none is a cause, and none answers a research question yet. Stage 3 tests whether the links survive other factors; anything causal needs designs that come after it.
site.journey_intro: The analysis has three stages, each looking at the same data in a new way. Only after the third, and with the research owner's agreement, are the five questions answered.

stages.name: Each variable on its own
stages.short: What each measure looks like, how complete it is, and its quirks. 124 observations (U0 to U123).

stages.name: Pairs of variables
stages.short: Which measures move together, how strongly, and for whom. 62 observations (B1 to B62).

stages.name: Many variables together
stages.short: Whether the signals survive once other factors are allowed for.

stages.name: Answering the questions
stages.short: The five questions, with evidence proportionate to each claim.

featured.intro: Every observation can be followed from the published data to the finding. This one, from Stage 2, shows how.
featured.title: Patents filed without an attorney are rarely granted
featured.text: Of Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone, 4.9% were granted, against 40.8% with an attorney: a gap of about 36 percentage points in both decades. Open it to see where the data came from, the reasoning, and why this is an association and not a cause.

stage2.title: What Stage 2 found
stage2.intro: Stage 2 measured every pair of measures in each lens and kept only those that are at least small, survive the correction for the number of pairs tested, and hold in a second period or sample. Most such pairs are how the IP system works, or one broad gradient of development running through places and countries. These are the signals left once those are set aside: associations to test in Stage 3, not explanations.

items.title: Filing without an attorney goes with poorer outcomes
items.text: Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone are granted about 36 percentage points less often, in both decades and among examined applications too; lone filers' trade marks and designs are renewed far less. The arrow may run backwards: an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney.

items.title: Value made here is often owned or used elsewhere
items.text: One patent in seven made in Australia is filed from overseas; the Australian patents that move overseas are the wide, granted ones and young firms'; only 3% to 5% of the US patents citing Australian research have Australian links.

items.title: Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries but are kept longer
items.text: Within fields too. Their lower citations go mostly with their narrower reach. Older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete in the records, so these are read from FY2010.

items.title: Filing follows advantage and remoteness, not one firm
items.text: Each step of area advantage goes with 1.7 to 1.9 times the standard patent rate, and the gradient holds with remoteness allowed for and with each area's largest filer removed. It is a standing difference: areas that gained graduates or income over a decade did not gain filing.

items.title: Among firms, filing goes with company form, age, cities, size and industry
items.text: R&D spend goes with patenting only weakly, even within size bands; about half of R&D claimants have never filed IP, mostly young private companies. Among large employers, industry sorts patenting far more than size.

items.title: Across countries, IP follows R&D and income
items.text: Australia's business R&D fell from 13th to 20th in the OECD and its patenting sits near what that predicts; within a decade, changes in R&D barely move patenting. Few of Australia's researchers work in business.

items.title: Policy changes leave clean breaks; fee changes rarely do
items.text: Two rushes, three steps and the 1995 pauses are far outside anything seen at placebo dates, the starting points for natural experiments. Fee changes rarely moved filing or lapsing, except patent cessations after the 2002 renewal rise.

items.title: Women's share among inventors varies by field more than by filer
items.text: From 4.2% in civil engineering to 26.9% in biotechnology, an order that holds across decades. On provisionals, organisations' inventors include more women than individuals'.

items.title: Across industries, patents follow R&D once services are counted
items.text: Through the crosswalk with services, patents per business follow business R&D per business; innovation as the business survey asks it does not go with patenting in three surveys.

items.title: Institutions whose research inventors use also patent and license more
items.text: Larger, more cited universities file more patents per work; across institutions, disclosures go with patents and patents with licence income. Industry-partnered grants do not go with joint filing.

site.ten_intro: Read together, Stage 1's observations point to a handful of patterns. Each is descriptive: a shape in the data worth testing, not an explanation. The numbers link to the observations behind them.

ten.title: Patents are mostly filed from overseas; trade marks mostly from home
ten.text: About nine in ten standard patents filed in Australia come from overseas (the United States alone 43.5%), against 59.0% of trade marks filed by Australians. China now files as many patent applications here as Australians do, and three-quarters of Australians' own applications are made abroad.

ten.title: Almost everything is concentrated
ten.text: The top 1% of filing firms filed 55.3% of firms' standard patents; the tenth of postal areas with the most patents filed 72.5% of them with 29.2% of the people; five attorney firms handle 63.96% of standard patents; the Group of Eight hold two-thirds of ARC and NHMRC funding.

ten.title: Places differ far more than chance would make them
ten.text: 68.2% to 72.5% of areas file below what chance allows around the national rate, and 6.7% to 15.5% above it, in small areas and pooled ones alike. Later stages must model this spread rather than assume it away.

ten.title: Australians, above all individuals, often file without an attorney
ten.text: Overseas filers use an attorney for 99.0% of standard patents, Australian filers for 85.4%, and Australian individuals file 62.4% of their trade marks alone.

ten.title: Provisional applications doubled in FY2026
ten.text: 10,069 against 4,143 to 5,047 a year before, driven by individuals without business numbers, both broadly and through a few heavy filers. It is real, not a recording artefact. Why is a question for IP Australia.

ten.title: Policy changes leave clear marks
ten.text: Rushes to file before a rule changed (Raising the Bar, 4.39 times Australians' usual month; the innovation patent's closure, 4.31 times), steps, and pauses when new Acts began. These are the raw material for the natural experiments the later questions need.

ten.title: Patents are kept longer than they were; about half of trade marks are renewed at ten years
ten.text: Standard patents' median years in force rose from 10.7 (1980s) to 13.5 (2000s and 2010s). The research owner has adopted years in force as a working measure for Stage 2, alongside other signals.

ten.title: Australia's research is used, but mostly abroad
ten.text: 93.6% of US patent citations to Australian research institutions' work come from inventions with no Australian applicant or inventor. Research intensity peaked in 2008 and has fallen below the OECD median.

ten.title: The register's history shapes what it can say
ten.text: Early years hold only the rights that survived until records were computerised; some events were dated in batches; patent ownership history starts in FY2003. Each is handled, but each limits comparisons over time.

ten.title: Links between datasets are the weakest point
ten.text: Firms' IP counts are lower bounds; fewer recent filers are linked to a business number; no firm has an industry; half the universities' patents carry a postcode that is not a place where people live.

reading.intro: Every observation page has the same parts, and each part looks different, so that a finding is never confused with the reasoning, assumptions or limits around it.

parts.title: The observation
parts.text: The finding itself, in a green box with its number (U0 to U123 in Stage 1, B1 to B62 in Stage 2). Only this is a finding.

parts.title: Reasoning steps
parts.text: How the data lead to the finding, one step at a time, in dashed grey. Steps are not findings.

parts.title: Assumptions
parts.text: Where the analysis takes something as given. Marked in amber, so you can judge them.

parts.title: Limits
parts.text: What the observation cannot tell you, in rose.

parts.title: Explainers
parts.text: Statistical or technical terms, explained in blue beside the text, and on any dotted word.

reading.strength_intro: The research goal asks every claim to say how strong its evidence is. There are four levels. Everything in Stage 1 is the first; most of Stage 2 is the second.

strengths.name: Descriptive
strengths.text: What the data show. How much, how often, for whom. No claim about why.

strengths.name: Observational
strengths.text: Two things go together. There may be other explanations. Stages 2 and 3 produce these.

strengths.name: Causal
strengths.text: One thing causes another. Needs a design, such as a natural experiment, that this exploration does not have.

strengths.name: Projected
strengths.text: An estimate of the future, with its assumptions stated. Belongs to Question 5.

site.observations_intro: Every observation from Stages 1 and 2, grouped by lens. Filter by lens, by research question, by stage, or by whether it describes the IP system or the data themselves. Stage 1's (U numbers) describe one measure at a time, and many are about the data: what is complete, what was repaired, what can safely be compared. Stage 2's (B numbers) relate two measures and say whether the link held in a second period or sample.
site.storage_text:
**Kept as published.** Each publisher's file is downloaded and kept exactly as released (the "raw" copy), so any number can be traced back to the original.

**Tidied, not changed.** Each raw file is converted into tidy tables in a standard format (Parquet), one row per record, with the publisher's values kept. Where a source had to be repaired, the repair is written into code and recorded in a decision record, and the raw file still holds the original.

**Fingerprinted.** Every file gets a fingerprint (a SHA-256 hash: a code that changes if a single character of the file changes), its size, rows and location, in the project's manifest. Tests check the files against the fingerprints.

**Stored in two places.** Small tables are kept in the GitHub repository itself. Large ones (IP RAPID's events, the business register and others) are kept in a private cloud storage bucket (Cloudflare R2), because they are too big for GitHub; the manifest records them in the same way.

lenses_page.intro: A lens is an analysis-ready table with one row per thing being described: an IP right, a firm, a place, a country in a year, a month, an industry in a year, or a research institution in a year. Every source in the corpus is attached to at least one lens.
lenses_page.why: Two measures can only be compared if they describe the same thing. A patent count and a population cannot be set side by side until both are counted for the same place. So every table is brought to a lens's unit by a stated join or sum, and each lens keeps one row per unit (a test checks). Where two sources measure the same thing, one is the main measure and the other a labelled comparison; they are never added together.

questions_page.intro: The research asks five questions, from what public value the IP system creates to what interventions could achieve. Stages 1 and 2 do not answer them. They find out what the data can and cannot say about each, and which measures go together, so that the answers, when they come, rest on sound ground.
questions_page.caution: Each observation names the questions it moves closer to and says how. Those links are the analyst's guide, not findings: an observation about patents filed from overseas does not, on its own, say anything about who benefits.

data_page.intro: Every number on these pages starts in data that a public body published: IP Australia, the ABS, the ATO, the World Bank, WIPO, the OECD and others. Nothing is typed in by hand. This page follows a number from its publisher to an observation, and lists every source with its licence and where it is kept.
data_page.sources_intro: The source register (54 sources). Observation {U0} describes the corpus as profiled on 25 October 2026 (41 sources, 162 tables); the research institutions' register (ROR) was added the next day, IP Australia's own register after that, and the fee history, the Reserve Bank's rates, the national accounts, the ATO's statistics by postcode, WGEA's employers and others while filling the data gaps Stage 2 found. Open a source to see its tables, their size, where each is kept and its fingerprint.

journey.title: Published
journey.sub: A public body releases the data
journey.text: A publisher releases data on its website or an open data portal, under a licence (most here are Creative Commons, which allow reuse with credit).

journey.title: Copied as published
journey.sub: The raw file is kept unchanged
journey.text: The project downloads the file and keeps it exactly as released, with the date it was copied. Nothing is retyped.

journey.title: Tidied into tables
journey.sub: One row per record, values kept
journey.text: Code (one module per source, in the repository) reads the raw file into tidy tables. Values are not changed; where a source needed repair, the repair is in code and recorded.

journey.title: Fingerprinted and stored
journey.sub: In GitHub, or cloud storage if large
journey.text: Each table's fingerprint, rows and location go into the manifest. Small tables live in the repository; large ones in a cloud storage bucket.

journey.title: Built into a lens
journey.sub: One row per right, firm, place…
journey.text: The build code joins the tables into seven lenses, one row per unit. Every derived column is defined in one file, so anyone can check exactly how it was made. Lenses are rebuilt in minutes, never edited by hand.

journey.title: Profiled in the notebook
journey.text: A notebook runs a query on a lens, and saves its output (a table or chart) with the notebook, so it can be read on GitHub without running anything. Stage 1's notebook profiles each measure; Stage 2's relates pairs.

journey.title: Written as an observation
journey.text: The analyst writes the observation directly under the output, quoting its numbers. If a number is not on the page, it is not a finding. These pages are checked against the notebook in the same way.

limits.intro: Stages 1 and 2 are groundwork. They are honest about what they are: a careful description of each measure on its own, then of which measures go together. This page gathers what they cannot do, the assumptions they make, where the data are weakest, and the mistakes found and corrected on the way.
limits.cannot_title: What Stages 1 and 2 cannot tell you

cannot.title: Why
cannot.text: Stage 1's observations are descriptive and Stage 2's are associations. Every pair has candidate third factors, and some may run backwards (an application abandoned early may never appoint an attorney, {B6}). Stage 3 tests whether links survive other factors; causal claims need designs (such as natural experiments) after it.

cannot.title: Value
cannot.text: Counts of rights, lifetimes, reach and citations are measures of activity and private value, not of public value. The research goal treats them as indicators, never as success.

cannot.title: People from places
cannot.text: Stage 2's pairs across postal areas and countries describe the areas and countries, not the people or firms in them. Areas with more graduates file more; that does not show the graduates are the filers.

cannot.title: Small units
cannot.text: Industries (19 divisions) and OECD members (36 to 38) are few, so their intervals are wide and their pairs are leads at most.

cannot.title: Everyone
cannot.text: The firms lens holds firms that used a scheme, not all businesses. Individuals in IP RAPID are pseudonymised, so their gender cannot be estimated; only inventors' can, from names, and reliably only for inventors in Australia.

cannot.title: Small firms
cannot.text: Size and industry are known only for employers of 100 or more (WGEA). Without the ABS's BLADE (linked business data, ruled out for now), small firms' size, industry, growth and survival are out of reach (OQ20). This limits how far Questions 3 and 5 can be answered.

cannot.title: The present
cannot.text: The latest months of some records are incomplete because the register records them late (trade mark and design cessations, recent ABN links, perhaps priority claims, {B38}). Each observation says which years are safe to compare.

assumptions: Public data are taken to be what their publishers say they are. Where checks found otherwise (placeholder dates, mislabelled countries, numbers counted twice), the data were repaired and the repair recorded; elsewhere, the publisher's values stand.
A business is identified by its ABN. Related companies in a group have different ABNs and are counted apart.
A place is a postal area, reached through the postcode recorded on an application or in the business register. A registered address may be a head office or an adviser's, not where the work is done.
An industry is reached through what a right protects (its technology or goods classes), by published probabilities, because few firms in the corpus have an industry.
Gender is estimated from first names and countries, as a probability summed over many people; it says nothing about any one person, and is read only for inventors in Australia.
Money is shown as recorded (nominal) unless a page says otherwise; fees are also shown in June 2026 dollars, adjusted with the quarterly Consumer Price Index.
Where a series begins with only the survivors of an earlier system, or with partial records, those years are left out rather than estimated.

Stage 2 measures every pair on one scale from 0 to 1 and calls a pair a lead only if it reaches 0.1, survives the correction for the number of pairs, holds in a second period or sample, and is not two versions of one measure (ADR 0030).
limits.weak_intro: The binding limit on what this research can say is how well its datasets link together. These are the links the two stages found weakest.

weak.title: Firms
weak.text: Firms reach IP only through business numbers on applications, so firms' IP counts are lower bounds, and fewer recent filers carry one ({U41}, {U45}). Size and industry reach only employers of 100 or more ({U112}).

weak.title: Industries
weak.text: Industries reach patents only through a crosswalk; the recommended one leaves out services, so a second one with services sits beside it ({U75}, {U114}).

weak.title: Places
weak.text: Places reach IP only through postcodes, and half the universities' patents carry a postcode where no one lives ({U49}, {U87}).

weak.title: Institutions
weak.text: Research institutions reach their IP through a reviewed list of names and business numbers that someone in the sector has yet to check ({U81}, OQ11).

weak.title: Inventors and families
weak.text: Inventors' countries are known mostly for patents also filed abroad, gender only as an estimate that holds for Australia ({U95}, {U97}), and older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete before FY2010 ({B55}, OQ21).

limits.corrections_intro: The record corrects its own mistakes when they are found, in the notebooks and in the summaries. These are the corrections made during Stages 1 and 2 and in building these pages.

corrections.what: The policy register said the Patents Act 1990 brought in 20-year patents.
corrections.now: Its term was 16 years until 1 July 1995; the change is now the 17th policy event ({U23}).

corrections.what: Charts of trade marks before 1983 and designs before 1986 showed survivors without saying so.
corrections.now: Corrected in {U5} and {U10}; the series start where records are complete.

corrections.what: The World Bank's trade mark series was described as applications.
corrections.now: It counts classes, as WIPO's do ({U67}).

corrections.what: Five figures differed slightly between builds of the lenses, because two ties were broken arbitrarily.
corrections.now: The ties are fixed, two builds agree row for row, and the figures are corrected ({U48}, {U49}, {U52}, {U53}).

corrections.what: Three more figures depended on how ties fell (the share of people in the top tenth of areas; universities' postcodes).
corrections.now: Corrected ({U52}: 29.2% and 32.8% of people; {U87}: UNSW's 210, not 216).

corrections.what: Observation {U0} still gave the first corpus profile (152 tables from 38 sources) when the output above it gave the later one.
corrections.now: The notebook's text now follows its output (162 tables from 41 sources), found while building these pages.

corrections.what: {B11} left open whether the fall in Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia (73.02% to 40.71%) was a change in practice or in the records.
corrections.now: Mostly the records. Older Australian families' filings abroad are incomplete ({B55}), so family measures for Australian applicants are read from FY2010.

next.intro: Stages 1 and 2 prepared the ground: every measure described, then every pair related. Stage 3 looks at many measures together before the five questions are answered. Nothing below has been done yet.

stages.name: Stage 2, pairs of variables
stages.asks: Which pairs of measures move together, in what shape, how strongly, and for whom?
stages.how: Within each lens, every pair of variables was screened on one scale. A pair counted as a lead only if it was at least small, survived the correction for the number of pairs tested, and held in a second period or sample; the planned pairs were then measured in plain units, with intervals.
stages.example: Postal areas with more advantaged residents file 1.7 to 1.9 times as many standard patents per person for each step of advantage, and the gradient is not one firm's ({B29}, {B30}).
stages.adds: The first **observational** evidence: associations that bear on who benefits (Q2) and on the conditions for value (Q3), each with its candidate third factors.
stages.done: Every pair within each lens screened; each lead with its size and interval, past the correction and held in a second sample.

stages.name: Stage 3, many variables together
stages.asks: Do the signals survive once other factors are allowed for? What structure and groups exist?
stages.how: Several variables are looked at together: whether a link between two holds when a third is held steady, which variables move as a group (the gradient of advantage, education and business density across places, and of development across countries, reduced to a few components), and which kinds of firms or places form natural clusters.
stages.example: Is an area's patent rate still linked to advantage once its business mix and education are allowed for? Does the gap in grants for lone filers hold within the same route and type of applicant?
stages.adds: Separates real signals from ones explained by something else, and produces two tables: early signals (with their evidence and strength) and data gaps (with possible sources and costs).
stages.done: A table of early signals and a table of data gaps, reviewed with the owner.

stages.name: Answering the questions
stages.when: After Stage 3, with the owner's agreement
stages.how: Analyses designed for each question: descriptive where that suffices, and natural experiments or other designs wherever an additional benefit is claimed.
stages.example: Using the closure of the innovation patent, or the 2002 renewal fee rise, as a natural experiment to estimate what a policy actually changed ({B37}, {B49}).
stages.adds: Answers with evidence proportionate to each claim, as the research goal requires.
stages.done: When the owner adopts the findings.

next.leads_intro: The signals Stage 2 carried forward. Each will be tested with its candidate third factors held steady: the filer (origin and type), family reach, the route of filing, the technology field, selection at grant, firm size and industry, business density and mix, education, income, and the kind of institution.

leads.lead: Filing without an attorney against grant and renewal, within the same applicant type, origin and route
Years in force, family reach and citations by origin, within fields and among granted patents (FY2010 on for Australian applicants)
Inventions made here but owned abroad, and the patents that move overseas, by reach, field and the filing firm's age
Women's share among inventors by field and filer, with field held steady
Firms that file, and R&D claimants that never have, with size and industry for large employers
Government contracts against IP, within entity groups and with firm size where known
Area filing against advantage and remoteness, with business mix and education held steady, and the area indicators reduced to a few components
Countries' patenting against business R&D and researchers in business, with the development gradient reduced to components
Policy and fee breaks as natural experiments, each beside series it should not have moved and allowing for the cycle; renewal at each anniversary a fee changed
Patents per business against R&D across industries, reported through both crosswalks
Universities' patenting against research scale and use, and institutions' patents against licensing, by kind of institution

next.puzzles_intro: Things the analysis has found but cannot yet explain. They are kept in view, not explained away. Several are closed: IP RAPID's innovation patents in 2016 ({U67}), by the review against IP Australia; the trade mark expedite fall of November 2018 ({U34}) and the fall in filers linked to a business number ({U45}), by IP Australia's own register ({U103}, {U100}); and most of the fall in Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia ({B11}), by a gap in older records ({B55}).
puzzles: Australians' direct filing of standard patents rose to 28.3% in FY2026 ({U90}), and provisionals filed in FY2025 were followed up less often ({B38}); both could be priority claims recorded late (OQ18).
Divisional applications doubled among both Australian and overseas organisations ({B15}).
The World Bank's share of the labour force with advanced education steps up around 2010 ({U65}).
Plant breeder's rights change hands more often in recent years ({U17}).
Petty patents filed in FY1986 to FY1988 mostly have no acceptance recorded ({U32}).
next.open_intro: Some questions only the research owner, or IP Australia, can answer. They are listed so that nothing depends on an unstated guess.
owner: **When to start Stage 3.** Stage 2 is complete, and its pages are on this site.
**A sector check of the institutions link** (OQ11): a half-hour review by someone who knows the sector, which {B44} to {B46} and {B62} rest on.
**Firms' size and industry for small firms** (OQ20): known only for employers of 100 or more; small firms need a paid or requested source.
**Older Australian patent families** (OQ21): repair the links from the EPO's patent family service (free, but an account in your name), or read family measures from FY2010 only.
**Court judgments after March 2025** (OQ22) and ABS TableBuilder (OQ4, on hold).
ipa: What evidence supports IP Australia's reading that digital tools, including AI, drove the rise in provisional applications, and are the few very heavy filers part of it? (OQ5, {U8})

IP Australia's register still records "Examination expedited" for every trade mark claiming an overseas filing date, but IP RAPID stopped publishing it in November 2018. What does it mean where no one asked, and could IP RAPID publish it? (OQ6, {U34})
IP Australia's register holds a business number for most of the recent applications that have none in IP RAPID. Why does IP RAPID leave them out, and could it publish them? (OQ7, {U45})
What does IP Australia's figure of 55.6% of resident applications filed by individuals in 2022 count? (OQ12, {U13}, {U48})
IP Australia's own register, IP RAPID and WIPO agree on 2018's trade marks, about 2,000 fewer than IP Australia's report: what did the report's 2018 count include? (OQ13, {U5})
IP Australia's register holds the owner's country for most designs IP RAPID leaves without one. Could IP RAPID publish it? (OQ14, {U7})
Are inventors added to a provisional application later, or no longer recorded for some? (OQ17, {B18})
Proposed, for the owner to add: when does IP RAPID record a patent application's priority claims: when it is filed, or later? (OQ18, {B38})
next.gaps_intro: The gaps Stage 2 found were filled in October 2026, all from free sources: the fee history, the Reserve Bank's rates, the national accounts, the ATO's statistics by postcode, the Census over time, the business survey of 2024-25, WGEA's employers, the crosswalk with services, WIPO's families by origin, the NSRC and the PBS with Section 100. What remains:
gaps: Size and industry for firms under 100 employees, most IP filers (OQ20).
Older Australian patent families' filings abroad, before FY2010 (OQ21).
AusTender amendments to contracts that ended before August 2019 (coded; the nine-hour harvest has not yet run to the end).
after: Review the early signals and data gaps with the research owner.
Source the data worth adding for the gaps (free first; any cost proposed with an estimate).
Only then design the analyses that answer the five questions.

site.glossary_intro: Every technical term used on these pages, in plain English. Dotted words anywhere on the site open the same explanations.

glossary_groups.data: Data and how it is handled

corpus.name: The corpus

facts.label: sources in the profile (42 in the register today)

corpus.description: Before any lens, the project gathered public data from 42 sources into one place, its **corpus**: IP Australia's registers, business registers, R&D and procurement records, the ABS, international panels and research databases. Observation {U0} describes the corpus as a whole. Everything else is read through a lens.
limits: The number of rows a source has measures how much it records, not how much it matters to the questions.

rights.name: IP rights

facts.label: patents, trade marks, designs and plant breeder's rights
columns, after five attachments and the register's fills

rights.description:
Every patent, trade mark, design and plant breeder's right in IP Australia's open register, IP RAPID, from the first application in February 1904 to October 2026. Each row says what the right is, who filed it and who holds it now, where they are, how it reached Australia, what happened to it (examination, grant, opposition, sale, lapse) and, for patents, how widely the invention was protected abroad, how often later inventions cite it and where its inventors live.

Five **attachments** add those last groups of columns from other tables: the parties (who filed, who holds, who represents them), the events (each milestone and the right's lifetime), the links (the route into Australia), Google Patents (the worldwide family) and the inventors. IP Australia's own register fills what IP RAPID leaves out (business numbers, design owners' countries, the inventors of provisional applications), in columns beside IP RAPID's, never replacing them.

repairs.what: Where a right's applicants have no country recorded, its origin is "unknown", not "overseas".
repairs.why: Counting the unknowns as overseas had added 517,145 old patents to the overseas side.

repairs.what: Standard patents, provisional applications and second-tier (innovation and petty) patents are counted apart everywhere, and headline figures use standard patents.
repairs.why: They are different rights. A provisional is a cheap placeholder that is never granted; a second-tier patent is a cheaper, shorter right. Adding them together hides what each is doing.

repairs.what: Two placeholder dates are emptied (an end date of 1 January 1970 on 1,282 rights, and one registration before the register began).
repairs.why: 1 January 1970 is the "zero" of computer dates, standing in for an unknown date, not a real one.

repairs.what: Trade marks registered before 1986 have no "days to registration".
repairs.why: The register holds only their filing date, so their recorded time to registration is almost always zero.

repairs.what: The "technology area" is kept for patents only.
repairs.why: For every trade mark and design it simply repeated the class of goods, so it measured nothing new.

repairs.what: An attorney counts only if the agent on record is not the applicant itself.
repairs.why: The register's "agent" is the address for service, which is often the applicant's own; counting it said every trade mark had an attorney.

repairs.what: A missing Australian state is taken from the applicant's postcode.
repairs.why: The register left out the state for 34.96% of recent Australian standard patents, though the postcode was there, and postcode and state agree for over 99% of rights where both exist.

repairs.what: The business or person who **filed** a right is kept beside the one who **holds** it now.
repairs.why: "Who files, and from where" and "who holds it now" are different questions; rights are often sold.

repairs.what: Each right's milestones come only from events the register still holds as standing (not later reversed), with placeholder and impossible dates left out.
repairs.why: A lapse that was later reversed did not end the right.

repairs.what: A patent priority's office is read from the number itself, not from the register's country label.
repairs.why: The register labels 93.88% of international (PCT) numbers, and many other offices' numbers, as Australian.

repairs.what: The two tie-breaks in the build (a filer with two same-day postcodes, an agent with several names) are fixed.
repairs.why: Without them a few figures changed slightly every time the table was rebuilt.

limits: The register holds only the rights that survived until it was computerised for trade marks before 1983, designs before 1986 and provisional applications before September 1985 ({U23}).
Ownership history for patents starts with those filed in FY2003 ({U17}).
Inventors' countries are known mostly for patents also filed abroad ({U95}).

timeline.name: Australia over time
timeline.unit: One row per month, January 1904 to September 2026

facts.label: monthly series of applications and events
official fee columns, from every version of the fee regulations

timeline.description:
IP Australia's whole register month by month: applications of each type from Australian, overseas and unknown applicants; what happened to rights (grants, lapses, cessations, expiries, oppositions, sales, extensions of term) as counts of events; the Consumer Price Index each quarter; and the month each of 17 IP policy changes took effect.

Added after Stage 2: the official fees in force each month (and each change to them), the Reserve Bank's cash rate and exchange rates, GDP and each state's final demand from the national accounts, and the PBS's monthly cost with Section 100.

repairs.what: Each series starts only where its records become continuous and complete; earlier months are empty, not zero.
repairs.why: Before that, the register holds survivors, partial records or events dated in batches, so a month's count is not what happened that month. Fifteen series were started by hand for this reason.

repairs.what: The rise of the standard patent term from 16 to 20 years (1 July 1995) was added as the 17th policy change.
repairs.why: Patent expiries all but stop for four years from that month; the change was missing from the policy list.

repairs.what: Trade mark registrations are counted by the date they were entered, and each event is counted once.
repairs.why: A trade mark is registered "as from" its filing date, so counting by that date measured filings, not registrations.

limits: Months before each series' start are empty on purpose; a long series is not complete back to 1904.
Comparisons of months around a policy change do not yet allow for trends or seasons ({U28}).

firms.name: Firms

facts.label: ABNs that used one of five schemes

firms.description: Every Australian Business Number that appears in IP Australia's data, the R&D Tax Incentive, AusTender (government contracts) or the ATO's tax transparency reports, with what the business is, where it is registered, how old it is on the record, the IP it filed and holds, its R&D claims, its large-company income and its contracts. It is the businesses that used a scheme, not every business in Australia. For employers of 100 or more, WGEA's reports add a size band and an industry; smaller firms have neither.

repairs.what: Applications are credited to the business that filed them, not the one that holds them now.
repairs.why: Otherwise a firm's filing record would change whenever it bought or sold rights.

repairs.what: The ABNs that only IPLORD links to IP are flagged, and IPLORD's own counts are kept out.
repairs.why: IPLORD counts differently from IP RAPID; adding the two would mix measures.

repairs.what: Each contract counts once, at its latest value; R&D uses each firm's latest (amended) report.
repairs.why: Summing every amendment counted the same contract many times ($7,585.9 billion against $1,258.5 billion).

repairs.what: Age is "years since the earliest public registration", with a flag where the record may start late.
repairs.why: ABNs and GST began in 1999-2000, so a business first seen then may be much older.

limits: IP counts are lower bounds ({U41}), and fewer recent filers are linked to an ABN ({U45}).
No firm has an industry: the business register extract holds none.
Small firms' growth and survival are out of reach without the ABS's BLADE, which is ruled out.

regions.name: Places

facts.label: more sources in the companion table of area values

regions.description: Every Australian postal area (the ABS's version of a postcode) with its people, businesses, remoteness, socio-economic indexes, Census medians, the IP filed from it over FY2017 to FY2026, its R&D claimants and its government contracts. A long companion table holds every value of seven more area sources: the Census, Data by Region, business counts (CABEE), PHIDU's health and social atlas, the Clean Energy Regulator, the ATO's statistics by postcode and the Census time series (2011, 2016 and 2021).

repairs.what: Applications are counted at the filer's postcode, not the current holder's.
repairs.why: A right sold to a firm elsewhere should stay where it was filed.

repairs.what: A rate is shown only where 10 or more applications would be expected at the national rate.
repairs.why: A count of 10 has a 95% range of about 5 to 18 by chance alone; below that, an area's rate is mostly noise.

repairs.what: Small areas can be pooled into 335 larger ones (SA3s).
repairs.why: So that every area's filings count somewhere, even where its own rate is too uncertain to show.

repairs.what: Values published for other kinds of area are moved to postal areas by their 2021 residents.
repairs.why: A count can be split by where people live; a median or rate is averaged, weighted by the people shared.

limits: About one standard patent in eighteen comes from a postcode that is not a postal area, half of universities' patents among them ({U49}, {U87}).
An address is where a business is registered, not where it works.

national.name: Australia and other countries
national.unit: One row per country, year and indicator

facts.label: attached values (GII, OECD, WIPO and more)

national.description: Thirty indicators for every country, 1960 to 2025: IP filings, royalties, R&D, researchers, GDP and exports from the World Bank; filings by residents of each country at every office from WIPO; and the OECD's R&D intensity. A long companion table holds every value of the Global Innovation Index 2026, 24 OECD datasets, WIPO's other tables, Measuring What Matters and Closing the Gap, with supplementary values for four GII indicators blank for Australia, kept apart from the GII's own.

repairs.what: WIPO's filings by residents of former states (such as the Soviet Union) and of unknown origin are kept, with a column saying what each place is.
repairs.why: They had been dropped silently, losing 9.65% of WIPO's patent applications by origin.

repairs.what: Two sources were reprocessed (Closing the Gap's Australian Government column, Measuring What Matters' stacked tables).
repairs.why: 85 values sat in a side column, and 45 cells shared a key.

limits: Before 1995 WIPO cannot say where most applicants come from ({U64}).
Counts grow with a country's size; fair comparisons need ratios to people or GDP (Stage 2).

industries.name: Industries
industries.unit: One row per ANZSIC industry division and financial year

facts.label: patent crosswalks, without services (the main one) and with

industries.description: The 19 divisions of the Australian and New Zealand industry classification: IP applications assigned to industries through published crosswalks, businesses and their entries and exits, business R&D, wages and the creative industries' value added, value added by division from the national accounts, and three business surveys of innovation. Few firms in the corpus have an industry, so IP reaches industries only through what it protects: a patent's technology classes and a trade mark's classes of goods and services.

repairs.what: Each right is split over industries by probabilities (an "expected count"), so a division's count is a sum of shares.
repairs.why: A patent's technology can belong to several industries; the crosswalks give the chance of each.

repairs.what: 26 patent classes the crosswalk did not know (new or retired ones) are mapped to their predecessors.
repairs.why: Otherwise 12,143 class marks fell out of every count.

repairs.what: The step between two industry classifications no longer splits weight over partial links.
repairs.why: It had sent half of pharmaceuticals' patents to textile finishing and inorganic chemicals.

limits: The patent crosswalk in the corpus leaves out service industries, so patents reach only goods-producing ones ({U75}).
Business counts cover four recent years and business R&D one, so comparisons are of patterns, not models.

institutions.name: Research institutions
institutions.unit: One row per research institution and calendar year
institutions.description: Australia's research institutions, each identified by its Research Organization Registry (ROR) record: their research output and citations, the citations US patents make to their work, their ARC and NHMRC grants, the IP they file in Australia, those patents' families abroad and their government contracts. The link from an institution to its rights, grants and contracts is a reviewed list of names (including commercialisation companies) and ABNs. The National Survey of Research Commercialisation adds disclosures, licences, start-ups and licence income for 2000 to 2015.

repairs.what: Institutions are linked to rights, grants and contracts through a reviewed list of 116 extra names and 146 ABNs.
repairs.why: Universities file under former names, predecessors' names and their commercialisation companies' names.

repairs.what: An institution's works and citations are its own, never added across institutions or from a child to its parent.
repairs.why: A paper with authors at two institutions counts for both.

limits: Whether the reviewed list is complete has not yet been checked by someone in the sector (OQ11).
Research output is available only from 2010.

questions.title: What public value does the IP system create?
questions.text: The economic, social, technological and environmental outcomes that go with patents, trade marks and designs; the costs of getting, keeping and enforcing rights; the costs to consumers, competitors and later innovators; and what the evidence can say about the system's net contribution to public welfare.
sub: What economic, social, technological and environmental outcomes are associated with different forms of IP protection?
Under what circumstances do patents, trade marks and registered designs support innovation, commercialisation, investment, competition or knowledge diffusion?
What are the costs of obtaining, maintaining, licensing and enforcing rights?
What are the potential costs to consumers, competitors, follow-on innovators and the broader public?
What can existing evidence establish about the system's net contribution to public welfare?
reach: Counts of rights, lifetimes and citations measure activity and private use, not public value. The research goal treats them as indicators, never as success.
The costs to consumers and competitors are not in the data yet; fees, the most direct cost, wait for the fee history (OQ2).

questions.title: Who benefits, and who is underserved?
questions.text: Which businesses, industries, regions and groups get the most from IP protection; who faces barriers to using it; and how outcomes differ between startups, small firms, large firms and research institutions, and by gender, place and circumstance, where reliable data exist.
sub: Which businesses, industries, regions and population groups derive the greatest benefits from IP protection?
Which groups face disproportionate barriers to understanding, accessing or using the system?
Are there underserved groups with substantial unrealised innovation potential?
How do outcomes differ between startups, SMEs, established businesses, research institutions and larger enterprises?
How do outcomes vary by gender, geography, socioeconomic circumstances and other relevant characteristics?
reach: Individuals in IP RAPID are pseudonymised, so their gender cannot be estimated; only inventors' can, and reliably only for inventors in Australia ({U97}).
Without the ABS's BLADE, small firms' growth and survival cannot be followed.

questions.title: What determines whether IP protection produces value?
questions.text: The business, institutional and market conditions that let rights holders benefit from their IP: finance, skills, management, market access and collaboration; whether registering changes access to investment, licensing, procurement or overseas markets; and when alternatives such as trade secrets or open licensing work better.
sub: Which business, institutional and market conditions enable rights holders to commercialise or otherwise benefit from their IP?
How important are complementary capabilities such as finance, skills, management, market access and collaboration?
Does formal registration change access to investment, licensing, procurement, partnerships or international markets?
When do alternative approaches, such as trade secrets, open licensing, collaborative research or public funding, produce better outcomes?
What distinguishes successful use of registered IP from registration that produces little observable benefit?
reach: Firm-level outcomes (growth, survival, productivity) for small firms need BLADE, which is ruled out for now.
Alternatives to registration (trade secrets, open licensing) leave almost no trace in these data.

questions.title: Where are the greatest opportunities for intervention?
questions.text: The barriers that stop valuable innovation happening or reaching the market, which of them IP Australia could influence, and where funding, services, regulatory change, partnerships or better access to expertise could add public value; and where IP Australia should act itself, collaborate or advocate.
sub: Which barriers prevent potentially valuable innovation from occurring or reaching the market?
Which barriers could IP Australia materially influence?
Where might targeted funding, new services, regulatory changes, partnerships or improved access to expertise generate additional public value?
Which interventions could address market failures or institutional gaps that existing arrangements do not adequately address?
Where should IP Australia focus its own efforts, and where would collaboration or advocacy be more appropriate?
reach: Stage 1 can point to where use is uneven; it cannot say that changing it would add value. That needs the later stages and, for any claim of additional benefit, designs such as natural experiments.

questions.title: What outcomes could interventions produce?
questions.text: The size, spread and timing of the benefits an intervention could bring; how much would be additional to what would happen anyway; its costs; how sensitive the results are to assumptions; and what evidence would justify scaling, changing or stopping it.
sub: What is the expected magnitude, distribution and timing of the benefits?
How much would be additional to what would occur without intervention?
What are the likely financial, administrative and opportunity costs?
How sensitive are expected results to assumptions about participation, effectiveness, economic conditions and implementation?
What evidence would be needed to justify scaling, modifying or discontinuing an intervention?
reach: Additionality (what happens because of an intervention, compared with what would have happened anyway) needs causal designs that come after Stage 3. The policy changes in the timeline ({U28}) are the raw material for them.

median.title: Median
median.short: The middle value: line everything up from smallest to largest, and the median is the one halfway along. Half are below it and half above.
median.more: Unlike the average (mean), the median is not dragged up by a few very large values, so it describes the typical case when a handful of firms or places are far larger than the rest. That is why these pages use it so often.

mean.title: Mean (average)
mean.short: The ordinary average: add everything up and divide by how many there are.
mean.more: When a few values are huge, the mean is pulled towards them and stops describing a typical case. Compare it with the median.

percentile.title: Percentile
percentile.short: The value below which a given share of things fall. The 90th percentile is the value 90% of cases are below; the 99th, the value all but the top 1% are below.
percentile.more: The median is the 50th percentile. The "middle half" runs from the 25th to the 75th.

middle-half.title: Middle half (interquartile range)
middle-half.short: The range that holds the middle 50% of values, from the 25th to the 75th percentile. A quarter of cases are below it and a quarter above.

long-tail.title: Long tail (skew)
long-tail.short: A spread where most cases are small and a few are very large. The few large ones stretch out a long "tail" to the right of a chart.
long-tail.more: In a long-tailed spread, averages mislead and shares held by the top 1% or 10% are large. Skewness is a number that measures how lopsided a spread is: 0 for a symmetric one, larger for a longer right-hand tail.

log-scale.title: Log scale
log-scale.short: An axis where each step is ten times the last (1, 10, 100, 1,000) instead of adding the same amount. It lets very small and very large values be seen on one chart.
log-scale.more: On a log scale, equal distances mean equal ratios. A spread that falls in a near-straight line on two log scales is a sign of a long tail.

concentration.title: Concentration curve
concentration.short: A line that shows how much of a total the top x% hold. Line everyone up from largest to smallest; the curve rises steeply if a few hold most of it, and follows the diagonal if everyone holds the same.
concentration.more: Read it by picking a point on the horizontal axis (say, the top 1%) and reading up to the curve: that is the share of the total they hold.

lower-bound.title: Lower bound
lower-bound.short: A number the true value is at least as large as. A firm's IP count is a lower bound because some of its rights cannot be linked to it.

nominal.title: Nominal and real dollars
nominal.short: Nominal dollars are as recorded at the time. Real dollars are adjusted for inflation, so that amounts from different years can be compared fairly.
nominal.more: Money is shown as recorded unless a page says otherwise; the official fees are also shown in June 2026 dollars, adjusted with the Consumer Price Index ({U30}, {U109}).

share-of-known.title: Share among known values
share-of-known.short: A percentage worked out only over the cases where the answer is recorded, leaving out the unknowns. It is shown only where unknowns are few, or with the unknown share beside it.

survival-curve.title: Survival curve (Kaplan–Meier)
survival-curve.short: A chart of the share of rights still in force after each number of years. It counts rights that are still in force as "unfinished", rather than dropping them or treating them as ended.
survival-curve.more: Simply averaging the lifetimes of rights that have ended would leave out every right still running, which are often the longest-lived. The Kaplan–Meier method uses each right for as long as it has been observed, so recent rights still count for the years they have lived.

unfinished.title: Unfinished (censored) cases
unfinished.short: Cases whose end has not happened yet, such as a patent still in force. Their full length is unknown, but they are known to be at least as long as they have run so far.

cohort.title: Cohort
cohort.short: A group that started at the same time, such as all patents filed in the 2000s. Comparing within a cohort is fair because everyone has had the same time to change.

funnel-plot.title: Funnel plot
funnel-plot.short: A chart of each area's rate against its size, with two curved lines showing how far from the national rate an area could fall by chance alone. Small areas swing widely by chance, so the lines flare out like a funnel.
funnel-plot.more: If differences between areas were only chance, about 95% would sit inside the 95% lines. Many points outside the lines mean the areas really do differ.

chance-limits.title: 95% limits (range due to chance)
chance-limits.short: The range a count or rate would fall in 95 times out of 100 if nothing but chance were at work. A value outside it is unlikely to be chance alone.

poisson.title: Poisson model
poisson.short: A standard model of counts of rare, independent events (such as patent filings in an area). It assumes the counts vary only by chance around one rate.

negative-binomial.title: Negative binomial model
negative-binomial.short: A model of counts that allows more spread than chance alone would give. Used when areas differ far more than a Poisson model expects, as they do here ({U53}).

expected-count.title: Expected count
expected-count.short: A count made by adding up probabilities rather than whole items. If a patent is 70% likely to belong to one industry and 30% to another, it adds 0.7 and 0.3 to their counts.

correlation.title: Correlation
correlation.short: How closely two measures move together, from −1 (one rises as the other falls) through 0 (no pattern) to +1 (they rise together). Spearman's version compares ranks rather than values.
correlation.more: A correlation is a pattern, not a cause. Stage 1 uses it only to check that two sources agree; Stage 2 uses Spearman's version to measure how strongly pairs of measures go together. As a rough guide, 0.1 is small, 0.3 moderate and 0.5 or more strong.

ratio.title: Ratio (as a check)
ratio.short: One count divided by another. A ratio of 1.000 between two sources' counts of the same thing means they agree exactly; 1.05 means the first is 5% higher.

rolling-total.title: 12-month total
rolling-total.short: The sum of the last 12 months, recalculated each month. It smooths out the seasons, so a trend is easier to see.

seasonal.title: Seasonal pattern
seasonal.short: A rise or fall that comes back at the same time each year, such as fewer filings in January. Shown as each month against an ordinary month (100).

variation.title: Variation (relative)
variation.short: How much a series moves from month to month, as a share of its average. 0.08 means a typical month is within about 8% of the average; above 1 means the series is very uneven.

outlier.title: Outlier
outlier.short: A value far from the rest. Here, usually one more than one and a half times the middle half's width beyond it (the "box-plot rule"), or a month at least three times, or under a third of, the months around it.

effect-size.title: Effect size and interval
effect-size.short: How big a difference or link is (not just whether it exists), with a range showing how sure we can be. With millions of records almost everything is "significant", so size and range matter more.

multiple-testing.title: Correction for many tests
multiple-testing.short: When hundreds of pairs are tested, some will look linked by luck. A correction raises the bar so that chance findings are not mistaken for real ones.

placebo.title: Placebo date
placebo.short: A date when nothing happened, tested as if a change had. If a "change" shows up there too, the real one may be a trend or a season, not the policy.

natural-experiment.title: Natural experiment
natural-experiment.short: A real event, such as a policy change, that affects some people and not others (or at one time and not another), so that comparing them can show what the change itself did.

additionality.title: Additionality
additionality.short: The benefit that happens because of a right, policy or service, compared with what would have happened without it. The research goal puts it ahead of simple attribution.

descriptive.title: Descriptive evidence
descriptive.short: What the data show: how much, how often, for whom, since when. No claim about why. Every Stage 1 observation is descriptive.

growth-rate.title: Average yearly growth
growth-rate.short: The steady yearly rise that would take a count from its starting value to its ending value over the years between them (compound growth).

standard-patent.title: Standard patent
standard-patent.short: The usual patent: examined in full before it is granted, and lasting up to 20 years (25 for some medicines). Headline patent figures here are for standard patents.

provisional.title: Provisional application
provisional.short: A cheap placeholder that secures a filing date for 12 months while an invention is developed. It is never granted itself; the applicant must follow it with a full application.

second-tier.title: Second-tier patent
second-tier.short: A cheaper, shorter patent for smaller steps: the petty patent (1979 to 2001) and the innovation patent (2001 to 2021). They are counted apart from standard patents.
second-tier.more: An innovation patent was granted after a check of its formalities only, and examined only if "certified" later, so its grant rate and time to grant say nothing about examination. No new ones could be filed after 25 August 2021.

trade-mark.title: Trade mark
trade-mark.short: Protection for a brand (a name, logo, sound and so on) for particular goods or services. It can be renewed indefinitely, every 10 years.

design.title: Registered design
design.short: Protection for how a product looks: its shape, pattern or ornamentation. Up to 10 years.

pbr.title: Plant breeder's right
pbr.short: Protection for a new plant variety.

pct.title: PCT (international patent application)
pct.short: The Patent Cooperation Treaty lets an inventor file one international application and later enter the countries they choose (the "national phase"), usually about 30 months after first filing.

national-phase.title: National phase
national-phase.short: The step at which an international (PCT) application enters a country. In IP RAPID, a PCT application's date is when it entered Australia.

priority.title: Priority
priority.short: An earlier filing an application relies on for its date, often abroad within the past 12 months (6 for designs), or an Australian provisional.

madrid.title: Madrid system
madrid.short: The international system for trade marks: one application, through WIPO, can cover many countries. Australia joined in 2001.

divisional.title: Divisional application
divisional.short: A new application split off from an earlier one, keeping its date. It often protects a different part of the same invention.

patent-family.title: Patent family
patent-family.short: Every application for the same invention, in every country's office. How many offices a family reaches is a common sign of how much its owner expects it to be worth.

citations.title: Forward citations
citations.short: Later patents that cite a patent as earlier work. Being cited often is a common sign that later inventions build on it; it is not a measure of value on its own.

lapse.title: Lapse
lapse.short: An application that ended before it was granted or registered, for example because fees were not paid. No lapsed right was ever granted.

cease.title: Cessation
cease.short: A granted or registered right that its owner let go, usually by not renewing it.

expiry.title: Expiry
expiry.short: A patent reaching the end of its full term (20 years for a standard patent filed since 1979).

renewal.title: Renewal
renewal.short: Paying to keep a granted right in force. A patent is renewed every year from its fourth anniversary; a trade mark every 10 years; a design once, at 5 years.

grace-period.title: Grace period
grace-period.short: Extra time after a renewal fee falls due during which the owner can still pay (six months for trade marks and designs). A right ceases on the record only after its grace period, so the latest months are incomplete.

examination.title: Examination
examination.short: IP Australia's check that an application meets the law (new, inventive, distinctive and so on). Patent applicants must ask, and pay, for it.

expedited.title: Expedited examination
expedited.short: Examination brought forward at the applicant's request, for example because an invention is being copied.

acceptance.title: Acceptance
acceptance.short: The decision that an application meets the requirements. It is advertised, and others may then oppose it before grant or registration.

opposition.title: Opposition
opposition.short: A formal challenge by someone else to an application being granted or registered.

assignment.title: Assignment
assignment.short: A recorded transfer of ownership of a right, for example when it is sold.

extension-of-term.title: Extension of term
extension-of-term.short: Up to five extra years for a standard patent on a pharmaceutical substance, to make up for time lost waiting for approval to sell it.

attorney.title: Attorney (representation)
attorney.short: A professional who files and manages applications for others. Here, an agent counts as an attorney if it acts for five or more different applicants; an agent with fewer is "another agent", and no agent but the applicant is "self".

filer.title: Filer and holder
filer.short: The filer is the person or business that applied for a right (its "founding applicant"). The holder is whoever owns it now. They differ when a right is sold.

nice.title: Nice class
nice.short: One of 45 international classes of goods and services that trade marks are filed in (class 35, for example, is advertising and business services).

ipc.title: IPC and technology fields
ipc.short: The International Patent Classification sorts patents by technology. WIPO groups its classes into 35 technology fields, such as medical technology or computer technology.

raising-the-bar.title: Raising the Bar
raising-the-bar.short: Reforms that tightened Australia's patent law from 15 April 2013. Applicants rushed to file and request examination under the old rules.

grant-rate.title: Grant rate
grant-rate.short: The share of a year's applications that were eventually granted or registered. Recent years look low because many are still being examined.

lens.title: Lens
lens.short: An analysis-ready table with one row per thing being described: an IP right, a firm, a place, a country in a year, a month, an industry in a year or a research institution in a year.

corpus.title: Corpus
corpus.short: All the public data the project has gathered, from 42 sources, before it is organised into lenses.

attachment.title: Attachment
attachment.short: Extra columns or a companion table joined to a lens from another source, such as each right's events or each area's Census values.

iprapid.title: IP RAPID
iprapid.short: IP Australia's open data on every patent, trade mark, design and plant breeder's right since 1904, updated weekly.

register.title: IP Australia's register
register.short: The live records behind IP Australia's search sites, read through its trade mark, patent and design APIs. IP RAPID is a weekly copy of it, with some fields left out.
register.more: Checked against IP RAPID on 27 October 2026, the register agreed with it for nearly every record of a random sample, and held what IP RAPID leaves out: owners' business numbers, design owners' countries and its own record of fast-tracked examination. Those fill the gaps here, beside IP RAPID's own values.

filled.title: Filled (from the register)
filled.short: A value that keeps IP RAPID's where it has one and takes IP Australia's register's where IP RAPID has none. IP RAPID's own value is kept beside it.

design-shell.title: Design shell
design-shell.short: A design record with nothing in it but its number and status: no date, owner or class in IP RAPID or in IP Australia's register. 11,098 of them, numbered 1973 to 1982, are left out.

iplord.title: IPLORD
iplord.short: An older IP Australia research dataset (to 2020) that links applicants to business numbers. Used here only as a check, because it counts differently.

manifest.title: Manifest
manifest.short: The project's register of every file: its fingerprint, size, rows and where it is kept.

fingerprint.title: Fingerprint (SHA-256)
fingerprint.short: A long code worked out from a file's contents. If one character of the file changes, the code changes, so it proves a file is the one recorded.

r2.title: Cloud storage (R2)
r2.short: A private storage bucket (Cloudflare R2) for tables too large to keep in GitHub. The manifest records them like any other file.

placeholder-date.title: Placeholder date
placeholder-date.short: A false date entered where the real one is unknown, such as 1 January 1970 (the "zero" of computer dates). Such dates are found and emptied.

survivors.title: Survivors (in old records)
survivors.short: When records were computerised, only the rights still on the register were entered. Before that point the data hold the survivors, not every application, so they understate filings and failures.

batch-dates.title: Batch dating
batch-dates.short: Events recorded on a few days a year, in bulk, so that some months show none and others several months' worth.

crosswalk.title: Crosswalk (concordance)
crosswalk.short: A published table that translates one classification into another, such as patent technology classes into industries, often with a probability for each link.

pseudonymised.title: Pseudonymised
pseudonymised.short: Names replaced by codes to protect privacy. IP RAPID does this for individual applicants.

perturbation.title: Perturbation (Census)
perturbation.short: Small random changes the ABS makes to small Census counts to protect privacy, so parts need not add exactly to totals and counts of 1 or 2 are unreliable.

gender-estimate.title: Gender estimate
gender-estimate.short: A probability that a first name in a given country is a woman's, from WIPO's name dictionary. Summed over many inventors it gives an expected number of women; it says nothing about any one person.

adr.title: Decision record (ADR)
adr.short: A short, dated note of a decision and why it was made, kept in the repository (docs/adr). Every repair to the data has one.

abn.title: ABN (Australian Business Number)
abn.short: The number that identifies a business to government. It is how this project links IP to the business register, R&D claims and government contracts.

abr.title: ABR (Australian Business Register)
abr.short: The register of every ABN, with each business's type, status, state and postcode.

gst.title: GST registration
gst.short: Registration for the goods and services tax, required once turnover reaches about $75,000 a year. A rough sign of an active, trading business.

entity-group.title: Entity group
entity-group.short: The kind of business: private company, public company, trust, sole trader, partnership, government body and so on.

postal-area.title: Postal area
postal-area.short: The ABS's version of a postcode, built from small Census areas. Post office boxes and postcodes with no residents are not postal areas.

sa3.title: SA3
sa3.short: A larger ABS area (335 in Australia), used here to pool small postal areas so that every area's filings count somewhere.

remoteness.title: Remoteness
remoteness.short: The ABS's five classes of how far a place is from services, from major cities to very remote.

irsad.title: Advantage (SEIFA, IRSAD)
irsad.short: The ABS's index of relative socio-economic advantage and disadvantage. Areas are ranked and cut into tenths (deciles): 1 is the most disadvantaged tenth of areas, 10 the most advantaged.
irsad.more: A tenth of areas is not a tenth of people: small and large areas count the same.

census.title: Census
census.short: The ABS's count of every person in Australia, every five years. Here, the 2021 Census.

cabee.title: CABEE
cabee.short: The ABS's Counts of Australian Businesses, including Entries and Exits, by industry, size and area.

rdti.title: R&D Tax Incentive
rdti.short: The government's main support for business research, through tax offsets. The ATO publishes who claims and how much.

austender.title: AusTender
austender.short: The Australian Government's register of contracts it awards, with each supplier's ABN and the contract's value.

gerd.title: GERD and BERD
gerd.short: Gross and business expenditure on research and development: all R&D spending in a country, and the part spent by businesses, usually as a percentage of GDP.

oecd-median.title: OECD median
oecd-median.short: The middle value among the 38 OECD member countries: half are above and half below.

gii.title: Global Innovation Index (GII)
gii.short: WIPO's yearly ranking of economies on 79 indicators of innovation inputs and outputs. A rank reflects WIPO's choice of indicators and weights.

wipo.title: WIPO
wipo.short: The World Intellectual Property Organization, the UN agency that runs the PCT and Madrid systems and publishes IP statistics for every country.

anzsic.title: ANZSIC
anzsic.short: The Australian and New Zealand Standard Industrial Classification, with 19 broad industry divisions such as manufacturing or construction.

ror.title: ROR
ror.short: The Research Organization Registry, an open list that gives every research institution one identifier.

openalex.title: OpenAlex
openalex.short: An open database of research publications and their citations.

go8.title: Group of Eight
go8.short: Australia's eight leading research-intensive universities (Melbourne, Sydney, Monash, UNSW, Queensland, ANU, Adelaide and Western Australia).

commercialisation-company.title: Commercialisation company
commercialisation-company.short: A company a university owns to manage its inventions, such as NewSouth Innovations (UNSW) or UniQuest (Queensland). Many patents are filed in its name.

cpi.title: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
cpi.short: The ABS's measure of how prices change over time, used to adjust dollar amounts from different years for inflation.

bcs.title: Business Characteristics Survey
bcs.short: An ABS survey of businesses' innovation, barriers and finance, published by industry and size.

screen.title: Screen (of every pair)
screen.short: Stage 2's first step in each lens: every pair of measures is measured on one scale from 0 (unrelated) to 1 (perfectly related), whatever kind of measure each is, so that nothing is chosen by hand before it is looked at.
screen.more: Two numbers are compared by Spearman's rank correlation, a number and a category by a rank version of the correlation ratio, and two categories by a corrected Cramér's V. For a yes/no measure all three give the same answer, so their strengths can be set side by side (ADR 0030).

lead.title: Lead
lead.short: A pair of measures worth following up. In Stage 2 a pair is a lead only if it passes four tests: it is at least small (a strength of 0.1), survives the correction for the number of pairs tested, holds again in a second period or sample, and is not two versions of one measure.
lead.more: A lead is a pattern to explain, not an explanation. Stage 3 tests whether it survives other factors.

replication.title: Replication (a second sample)
replication.short: Checking a pattern again on different data: rights filed a decade earlier, or the other random half of the firms or places. A pattern that appears in one sample only may be chance or a quirk of that period.

interval.title: Interval (95%)
interval.short: A range around a number that shows how precisely it is known. If the study were repeated many times, ranges built this way would hold the true value 95 times in 100. A narrow interval means a precise estimate.
interval.more: Stage 2 uses intervals suited to each measure: Wilson's for a share, Newcombe's for a difference between two shares, Greenwood's for a survival curve, and the bootstrap for medians and correlations.

bootstrap.title: Bootstrap
bootstrap.short: A way to find an interval by resampling: draw the data again many times at random (with replacement), recompute the number each time, and see how much it moves. Stage 2 resamples whole patents or firms, not single records.

percentage-point.title: Percentage point
percentage-point.short: The difference between two percentages. A grant rate of 40.8% against 4.9% is a gap of 35.9 percentage points ("points"), not 35.9%.

third-factor.title: Third factor (confounder)
third-factor.short: Something else that could make two measures go together without one causing the other. Firm size could explain why firms with IP also win larger contracts. Stage 2 names the candidates; Stage 3 holds them steady.

simpsons-paradox.title: Simpson's paradox
simpsons-paradox.short: When a pattern in pooled data disappears or reverses within every group, because the groups' mix changed. Expedited patents look longer-lived overall only because more of them came from the filers who keep patents longest.

ecological.title: Between places, not people (ecological)
ecological.short: A link measured across areas or countries describes the areas, not the people or firms in them. Areas with more graduates file more, but that does not show that graduates are the ones who file.

standard-deviation.title: Standard deviation
standard-deviation.short: A measure of how spread out values are around their average. About two-thirds of areas lie within one standard deviation of the average advantage score, so "per standard deviation" means a typical step up or down.

rate-ratio.title: Rate ratio
rate-ratio.short: How many times higher one rate is than another. A rate ratio of 1.7 per step of advantage means each step goes with 1.7 times as many filings per person; 1 means no difference.

log-change.title: Change in logs
log-change.short: A way to measure proportional change: a change of 0.1 in logs is about a 10% rise, and -0.1 about a 10% fall. It makes a change of the same proportion the same size in a large series and a small one.

prediction-interval.title: Prediction interval
prediction-interval.short: The range within which a single new case (one country) would be expected to fall, given the pattern across the others. It is wider than the interval for the pattern itself, because single cases vary.

observational.title: Observational evidence
observational.short: Two things are seen to go together in data that were not designed to test a cause. Other explanations remain possible. Most of Stage 2's observations are of this kind.

official-fees.title: Official fees
official-fees.short: The fees IP Australia charges to file, examine, register and renew a right, set in regulations. They do not include attorneys' fees, which are often larger.

cash-rate.title: Cash rate
cash-rate.short: The interest rate on overnight loans between banks, which the Reserve Bank of Australia targets to steer the economy. It rises in booms and falls in downturns, so it tracks the business cycle.

gdp.title: GDP and value added
gdp.short: Gross domestic product: the value of everything produced in Australia in a period. Value added is the same measure for one industry. "Real" or "chain volume" figures remove the effect of rising prices.

wgea.title: WGEA
wgea.short: The Workplace Gender Equality Agency. Employers of 100 or more report to it each year, and it publishes each one's size band and industry by ABN: the only free source of firms' size and industry.

nsrc.title: National Survey of Research Commercialisation (NSRC)
nsrc.short: A survey of universities, research agencies and medical research institutes, 2000 to 2015: invention disclosures, patents, licences, start-ups and licence income.

asic.title: ASIC
asic.short: The Australian Securities and Investments Commission, which registers companies. Its register gives a company's registration date, one of the dates used to estimate a firm's age.

observations.statement: When the notebook was last run, the corpus held 162 tables from 41 sources, 317,792,796 rows in all. Three sources hold 69.73% of the rows: IP RAPID (31.57%), TM-Link (24.86%) and the OECD's panels (13.3%).

sources
