  Madrid applications by Australian holders. The two agree in size, though a mark is counted at its own filing and WIPO
  at the international application. Recent marks have had less time to be taken abroad.

observations.headline: Google Patents finds the worldwide family of nearly every standard patent filed since the 1980s
observations.statement: The family is found for 98.78% of standard patents filed in the 1980s, 98.99% (1990s), 94.81% (2000s), 99.23% (2010s) and 98.14% (2020s). Provisional applications, which are rarely published, are almost never found.

figures.label: of 2010s standard patents have their family found
of FY2010 to FY2019 standard patents share a family with another Australian application

points: 734 Australian application numbers fall in two families; the lower family number is taken, so every build agrees.
Sharing a family is mostly through divisionals (88.29%), so family measures repeat across those applications.
Five years of citations are complete for every family filed to FY2019, for 96.12% of FY2021's and 16.31% of FY2024's.

questions.how: Family reach and citations, the next two observations, are only usable because families are found this reliably.

prep.what: Each Australian application is matched to its Google Patents family by its Australian application number, with designs left out.
prep.why: Google converts the old numbering schemes, so one key reaches every era (ADR 0022).

prep.what: The five-year citation count is left empty where five years have not yet passed.
prep.why: A family filed recently has had less time to be cited; comparing it with older ones would mislead.

steps: Match each Australian patent application to a Google Patents family.
Work out the share found, by type and decade.
Count applications that share a family, and why.
assumptions: Google Patents' families group the same invention correctly.
limits: A family's measures are the whole family's, so divisionals share their parent's.
observations.next: Family reach and citations are compared within cohorts in Stage 2.
observations.section: 1.8.4 Google Patents: each patent's family, its reach and its citations
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U92 (descriptive). Google Patents finds the family of nearly every standard patent filed since the 1980s.**
- **Found:** standard patents 81.17% (filed in the 1970s), 98.78% (1980s), 98.99% (1990s), 94.81% (2000s), 99.23%
  (2010s) and 98.14% (2020s); second-tier patents 58.38% (1980s) to 96.68% (2020s); provisional applications, which are
  rarely published, 0% but for 11.06% of the 2000s'. The review measured 41.9% to 84.9% by decade (F06) on all patent
  numbers, provisionals and designs included.
- 734 Australian application numbers fall in two families (the lower is taken). 23.14% of standard patents filed FY2010
  to FY2019 share a family with another Australian application, 88.29% of them through a divisional: family measures
  repeat across those applications.
- **Follow-up:** five years of citations are complete for every family of a standard patent filed to FY2019, and for
  96.12% of FY2021's (3.88% empty) and 16.31% of FY2024's (83.69% empty), because a PCT application's family began about
  30 months earlier.

observations.headline: Overseas applicants' patents are filed in a median six countries' offices; Australians' in two
observations.statement: Of standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, overseas applicants' families reach a median 6 offices, 68.9% reach five or more, and 66.66% are granted in the United States. Australians' reach a median 2 offices; 45.53% are filed only in Australia, and 29.09% are granted in the United States.

figures.label: median offices reached, overseas against Australian applicants
of Australians' standard patents filed only in Australia

points: Australian individuals filed 59.91% of theirs only in Australia, organisations 40.71%.
8.28% of overseas applicants' patents were filed only in Australia.
Reach is chosen by the owner and costs money in every office, so it is a common sign of expected value.

questions.how: How widely an invention is protected is a widely used sign of its expected private value.
Australians, and individuals most, protect more narrowly, which bears on who gets value from inventing.

prep.what: Standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019 are used.
prep.why: They are nearly all decided, and five years of citations are complete for most.

steps: For each standard patent, take the number of offices its family reached and whether the US granted it.
Summarise by the applicant's origin, and for Australians by individual or organisation.
assumptions: Filing in more offices reflects higher expected value, as the literature commonly assumes.
limits: Reach also depends on markets and budgets; a small firm may value a patent it can afford to file only here.
observations.next: Stage 2 uses reach beside years in force and citations, within cohorts and technology fields.
observations.section: 1.8.4 Google Patents: each patent's family, its reach and its citations
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U93 (descriptive). Overseas applicants' patents belong to wide families; Australians' are mostly narrow.** Standard
patents filed FY2010 to FY2019:
- **Overseas applicants:** a median 6 offices; 8.28% filed only in Australia and 68.9% in five or more; 66.66% granted
  in the United States.
- **Australian applicants:** a median 2 offices; 45.53% filed only in Australia, 19.34% in five or more; 29.09% granted
  in the United States. Australian individuals filed 59.91% of theirs only in Australia, organisations 40.71%.
- Reach is chosen by the owner, and costs money in every office, so it is a common sign of expected value: a measure
  for Stage 2, alongside years in force (U36).

observations.headline: Australians' patents are cited less by later inventions than overseas applicants' patents
observations.statement: Within five years, standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019 by overseas applicants were cited by a median 6 later patent families, and 13.29% were never cited. Australians' were cited by a median 1, and 43.99% were never cited.

figures.label: median citing families in five years, overseas against Australian
of Australians' standard patents not cited within five years

points: The spread is a long tail: the 99th percentile is 136 citing families for overseas applicants' patents and 44 for Australians'.
A family filed in more offices is more often cited, so citations are compared beside family size.

questions.how: Citations are a sign that later inventions build on a patent, one route to wider public value.

prep.what: Citations are counted as distinct later families citing the family within five years of its first filing.
prep.why: A fixed window treats old and new patents alike; the count is empty where the window is not complete.

steps: For standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, take each family's five-year citation count.
Summarise by origin (median, share never cited, 99th percentile).
assumptions: A citation means the later invention builds on, or is close to, the cited one.
limits: Citations reflect family size, field and examiners' practice, not only importance.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares citations as ranks or logs, within cohorts and fields, beside family size.
observations.section: 1.8.4 Google Patents: each patent's family, its reach and its citations
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U94 (descriptive). Citations are spread unevenly, and Australians' patents are cited less.** Families citing a
standard patent's family within five years (filed FY2010 to FY2019): a median 6 for overseas applicants' (13.29% never
cited, the 99th percentile 136) and 1 for Australians' (43.99% never cited, 99th percentile 44). The spread is a long
tail (the chart's log scale), so Stage 2 compares citations as ranks or logs, within cohorts and technology fields, and
beside family size, since a family filed in more offices is more often cited.

observations.headline: Inventors' countries are missing for most patents filed only in Australia
observations.statement: An inventor's country is known for 87.57% to 97.06% of overseas filers' standard patents each decade, but for only 11.71% (1990s), 22.3% (2000s), 56.98% (2010s) and 64.27% (2020s) of Australian filers'. Of Australian filers' patents with inventors but no country, 94.33% to 99.18% were filed only in Australia, where Google's records give no inventor countries.

figures.label: of Australian filers' 2010s patents have an inventor's country
inventors named on the median standard patent

points: Inventors are named for 25.76% of rights (patents with a family that names them); standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026 name a median 3 (22.46% name one).
**So** "invented in Australia" describes Australian filers' patents that were also filed abroad, and leaves out most of those filed only here.

questions.how: Limits what can be said about who invents in Australia, and for which patents.

prep.what: Inventors come from one publication per family, the one naming the most, with countries borrowed from the rest of the family.
prep.why: Counting every publication's names nearly doubled the inventors (ADR 0008).

steps: For each patent, count its inventors and those with a known country.
Work out the share with a known country, by type, origin and decade.
For those with inventors but no country, check how many were filed only in Australia.
assumptions: An inventor's recorded country is where they lived when the invention was made.
limits: Patents filed only in Australia, half of Australians', mostly cannot be placed.
observations.next: Stage 2 reads "invented in Australia" only among patents whose inventors' countries are known.

- `inventors` is filled for 25.76% of rights (patents with a family that names inventors); standard patents filed FY2017
  to FY2026 name a median 3 (mean 3.5; 22.46% one inventor; the most 133).

observations.headline: Inventions filed from Australia are made here; very few filed from overseas are
observations.statement: Of standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026 whose inventors' countries are known, 94.47% of those filed from Australia have an inventor in Australia (16,062), against 0.85% of those filed from overseas (2,278).

figures.label: of Australian-filed patents have an inventor in Australia
of overseas-filed patents have one

points: Overseas filers' patents with an inventor in Australia numbered 28 (FY1990), 222 (FY2010), 212 (FY2020) and 222 (FY2026).

questions.how: Where inventions are made matters for where the knowledge and jobs behind them are; very little of what overseas applicants patent here is invented here.
Australian inventors working for overseas firms are a group whose benefit from the system may be indirect.

prep.what: A patent is "invented in Australia" if any inventor with a known country is in Australia.
prep.why: One Australian inventor is enough for the invention to involve work here.

steps: Take standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026 whose inventors' countries are known.
Split by whether the filer is Australian, and count those with an inventor in Australia.
Repeat by year for overseas filers.
assumptions: The inventor's country is where the inventive work was done.
limits: Most patents filed only in Australia are left out, because their inventors' countries are unknown ({U95}).
observations.next: Stage 2 relates where inventions are made to who owns them and the route they take.

observations.headline: Gender estimated from names matches WIPO's figure for Australia, but not for most other countries
observations.statement: For inventors of international applications, the share estimated to be women is 14.6% for Australia, against WIPO's published 13.8%. But the median country is 4.5 points too high, and China (34.6% against 23.4%) and Korea (37.0% against 15.7%) far too high. So estimates are read for inventors in Australia only.

figures.label: Australia, estimated against WIPO's share of women inventors
Korea's estimate above WIPO's

points: The Netherlands, Spain, New Zealand, Finland and Ireland are within 2 points.
The United States 20.0% against 15.3%; Germany 16.6% against 10.7%; Japan 16.3% against 9.0%.
For China, 49.1% of names are between 10% and 90% likely to be a woman's; in Korea only 53.3% of inventors get an estimate.
**Decision.** Estimates are read as levels for inventors in Australia only; for other countries only within one country over time; for China and Korea not at all.

questions.how: Q2 asks how outcomes vary by gender where reliable data exist; this check is what makes the Australian figure usable.

prep.what: Each inventor's chance of being a woman comes from WIPO's World Gender-Name Dictionary, by first name and country.
prep.why: Gender is not recorded anywhere; a name-based probability is the only route, and must be checked.

prep.what: WIPO's share of women among PCT inventors by country was added to the corpus for the check.
prep.why: An independent benchmark is needed before using any estimate (ADR 0022).

steps: For inventors of PCT families first filed 2015 to 2022, average their probabilities by country.
Compare with WIPO's published share for 2016 to 2023, country by country.
For Australia, compare year by year.
assumptions: Summed over many inventors, name-based probabilities give a fair count of women, where names are informative.
limits: An estimate says nothing about any individual.
Recent Australian estimates run above WIPO's (17.2% against 14.4% in 2023).
observations.next: Stage 2 compares women's estimated share among inventors in Australia by field and filer.

observations.original:
**U97 (descriptive). The gender estimates match WIPO's for Australia, but run high for most other countries, and far
too high for China and Korea.**
- **By country** (inventors of PCT families first filed 2015 to 2022, against WIPO's share of women among inventors in
  PCT applications, 2016 to 2023): Australia 14.6% against 13.8% (0.8 points); the Netherlands, Spain, New Zealand,
  Finland and Ireland are within 2 points. The median country is 4.5 points high: the United States 20.0% against
  15.3%, Germany 16.6% against 10.7%, Japan 16.3% against 9.0%.
- **China and Korea:** China 34.6% against 23.4% (11.2 points), with 49.1% of names between 10% and 90% likely to be a
  woman's; Korea 37.0% against 15.7% (21.3 points), with only 53.3% of inventors given an estimate.
- **Australia by year:** 11.8% against 13.1% (2001), 13.6% against 12.3% (2015), 14.9% against 14.6% (2021), then 17.2%
  against 14.4% (2023) and 18.4% against 17.2% (2024).
- **Decision** (ADR 0022): gender estimates are read as levels for inventors in Australia only; for other countries only
  within one country over time; for China and Korea not at all.

observations.headline: About one inventor in seven in Australia is estimated to be a woman
observations.statement: Of the inventors in Australia named on standard patents filed FY2017 to FY2026, an estimated 14.34% are women on patents filed by Australian organisations, 12.43% on those filed by Australian individuals and 12.75% on those filed from overseas.

points: It is an expected count from names, not a record of anyone's gender.

questions.how: A first, checked measure of gender among inventors in Australia, which Q2 asks about directly.

observations.headline: IP Australia's own register fills the gaps IP RAPID leaves for trade marks and designs
observations.statement: IP Australia's [[register|register]] holds what IP RAPID leaves out. Where IP RAPID has no [[abn|ABN]] for the filer, the register fills one for 134,995 trade marks and 3,097 designs. Designs of unknown origin fall from 29,628 to 4,622. And the register's own history records fast-tracked examination for 332,446 trade marks.

figures.label: trade marks given a filer's ABN by the register
designs of unknown origin, before and after

points: 73,181 of the trade marks' ABNs come through the company number (ACN) the register gives, matched to its ABN in the Australian Business Register; for designs 384.

The register was first checked against IP RAPID: IP RAPID is complete to within a week, and its fields agree with the register's for nearly every record of a random sample. So the register adds to IP RAPID; it does not correct it.
Patents are not filled: only trade marks and designs (and provisional applications' inventors) were read from the register whole.

questions.how: Who uses the system can now be counted for recent years, which IP RAPID's missing business numbers had blocked.
What IP Australia records but does not publish is itself something it can change.

prep.what: Every trade mark and design was read from IP Australia's register through its APIs on 27 October 2026.
prep.why: A sample can check accuracy, but filling gaps needs every record, so that every year is filled alike.

prep.what: A filled value keeps IP RAPID's and takes the register's only where IP RAPID has none.
prep.why: IP RAPID stays the base, and its own values can always be compared with the filled ones.

steps: Check IP RAPID against the register, field by field, on a random sample of each right.
Read every trade mark and design from the register.
Where IP RAPID has no ABN, country or expedite event, take the register's, keeping IP RAPID's beside it.
assumptions: The register's current owner is the filer while a right has not changed hands, so a filer's ABN is filled only for those rights.
limits: The register is as it stood on 27 October 2026; it can be read again with the project's code.
observations.next: Stage 2 uses the filled columns for who files and where they come from, with IP RAPID's beside them.

observations.original:
**U99 (descriptive). IP Australia's register fills IP RAPID's gaps for trade marks and designs.** It was checked
against IP RAPID first (`docs/audit-ipa-api.md`): IP RAPID is complete to within a week and its fields agree with the
register's for nearly every record of a random sample of each right, so the register adds to IP RAPID rather than correcting
it.
- **Filers' ABNs:** where IP RAPID has none, the register fills one for 134,995 trade marks (73,181 of them through
  the ACN it gives) and 3,097 designs (384 through an ACN). `filer_abn` is filled for 31.67% of rights.
- **Origin:** designs of unknown origin fall from 29,628 to 4,622; trade marks barely move (37,656 to 37,448).
- **Expedites:** the register's own history records an expedite event for 332,446 trade marks.
- Patents are not filled: the register was read whole only for trade marks and designs (and for provisionals'
  inventors, 1.8.7).

observations.headline: With the register's business numbers, the share of filers linked to an ABN does not fall after July 2024
observations.statement: In IP RAPID, Australian organisations' trade marks with the filer's [[abn|ABN]] fell from 84.1% in FY2024 to 59.9% in FY2026. [[filled|Filled]] from IP Australia's register, the share is 92.3% in FY2024, 91.4% in FY2025 and 90.9% in FY2026. The fall was in what IP RAPID publishes, not in who files.

figures.label: Australian organisations' trade marks with the filer's ABN, filled, FY2024 to FY2026
the same in IP RAPID alone

points: Designs: 88.4% against 92.3% filled (FY2024), 76.3% against 89.3% (FY2026).

The register itself records more business numbers in recent years: of the trade marks IP RAPID leaves without one, it fills 23% to 29.2% of those filed to FY2019 and 77.4% of FY2026's. So the filled share is comparable from FY2024 on, and a lower bound earlier.

questions.how: Who is newly using the system can now be followed to FY2026.
IP Australia collects the numbers but does not publish them, which it could change (OQ7).

prep.what: The share is worked out among Australian organisations only, as for U45.
prep.why: Individuals usually have no ABN, so including them would mix who files with how they are linked.

steps: For each year, take Australian organisations' trade marks and designs.
Count those with the filer's ABN in IP RAPID, and those with one once filled from the register.
assumptions: The register's ABN for a right's current owner is the filer's while the right has not changed hands.
limits: Because the register records more ABNs in recent years, the filled series is not one constant method before FY2024.
observations.next: Firm-level filing by year is compared to FY2026 with the filled columns. The question to IP Australia now asks why IP RAPID leaves the numbers out (OQ7).

observations.original:
**U100 (descriptive). With the register, the share of filers linked to an ABN does not fall after July 2024 (U45
restated).** Australian organisations' trade marks with a filer's ABN, IP RAPID's against filled: 79% against 84.9%
(FY2015), 84.1% against 92.3% (FY2024), 71.4% against 91.4% (FY2025) and 59.9% against 90.9% (FY2026); designs 88.4%
against 92.3% (FY2024) and 76.3% against 89.3% (FY2026).
- **But the register's own recording improved.** Of the trade marks IP RAPID leaves without an ABN, the register fills
  23% to 29.2% of those filed to FY2019, 44.5% to 51.9% in FY2022 to FY2024 and 69.9% and 77.4% in FY2025 and
  FY2026. So the filled share is comparable across FY2024 to FY2026, and a lower bound in earlier years, more so before
  FY2019, when the records moved between systems.
- **So** U45's fall is in what IP RAPID publishes, not in who files (OQ7, reworded).

observations.headline: Firms' entry did not fall; first-time trade mark filers rose to FY2026
observations.statement: Counted by IP RAPID's business numbers, firms filing their first trade mark fell from 11,318 in FY2024 to 7,384 in FY2026. With the register's numbers [[filled|filled]] in, they rose: 14,728 in FY2024, 15,818 in FY2025 and 19,730 in FY2026.

figures.label: firms filing their first trade mark in FY2026, filled

points: First designs: 414 against 535 filled (FY2024), 342 against 608 (FY2026).

The filled counts rise every year from FY2018 (10,143) to FY2021 (14,626), partly because the register records more business numbers from FY2019, so part of that rise is better recording, not new entry.

questions.how: How many businesses come into the IP system each year, a direct measure of its reach.

prep.what: Each firm's first trade mark and first design is dated by financial year, using the filled filer's ABN.
prep.why: The year a firm first files is its entry into the system.

steps: Credit each application to the filer's ABN, filled from the register where IP RAPID has none.
Count, for each year, the firms whose first application of a kind was filed that year.
assumptions: A firm whose earlier applications carry no ABN anywhere looks new later, which overstates entry a little in early years.
limits: The jump across FY2019 mixes new entry with better recording in the register.
observations.next: Stage 2 follows firms' entry by year to FY2026, and compares it with what IP Australia reports.

observations.headline: Designs' origin is now known for nearly all, and Australia's share is higher than IP RAPID showed
observations.statement: Of designs filed FY2017 to FY2026, 32.31% are Australian with the register's countries [[filled|filled]] in, and only 0.007% remain of unknown origin. In IP RAPID alone the share was 30.05%, with 5.062% unknown.

designs of unknown origin

points: By year: FY2025 29.83% Australian against 26.5% in IP RAPID; FY2021 35.64% against 33.46%.
So design shares by origin are no longer lower bounds once filled, as the review against IP Australia had found they were.

questions.how: How much of design protection in Australia serves Australian businesses.

prep.what: Where IP RAPID gives no applicant a country, the register's owner's country is used.
prep.why: The register holds the country for nearly every design IP RAPID leaves unknown.

steps: For each design, keep IP RAPID's origin where it has one.
Where it has none, take whether any owner the register gives is in Australia.
Work out the Australian share and the share still unknown.
assumptions: The register's current owners stand for the applicants where IP RAPID records no country.
limits: The register gives current owners, so a design that changed hands may show its later owner's country.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares design shares with the filled origin; IP Australia is asked whether IP RAPID could publish it (OQ14).

observations.headline: Trade marks claiming an overseas filing were fast-tracked in every year; the 2018 fall is in where it is recorded
observations.statement: Almost every trade mark claiming an overseas filing date ([[priority|convention priority]]) has a fast-track event: 97.82% of those filed in FY2018 and 99.55% in FY2020, taking IP RAPID and IP Australia's register together. IP RAPID records it to FY2018 and the register from FY2019, which is why IP RAPID's series fell in November 2018.

figures.label: priority-claiming trade marks with a fast-track event, FY2018 and FY2020, either record

points: IP RAPID: 97.81% (FY2018) then 0.16% (FY2020). The register: 0.06% (FY2018) then 99.53% (FY2020).
Other marks: the fast-tracks applicants ask for run 4.81% (FY2018) and 4.48% (FY2019), with no break.
The register also marks 14.95% (FY2019) to 26.69% (FY2026) of other marks 'Examination expedited', mostly without a request. What that means is a question for IP Australia (OQ6).

questions.how: Fast-tracked examination is a service IP Australia runs; it now appears to fast-track priority claims itself.

prep.what: The register's own history of each trade mark is searched for fast-track events.
prep.why: IP RAPID's events stop recording priority claims' fast-tracks at the November 2018 records move.

steps: For each trade mark, note whether IP RAPID or the register records a fast-track event.
Work out the shares by year and by whether the mark claims convention priority.
assumptions: The two records describe the same practice on either side of the records move.
limits: What the register's unrequested "Examination expedited" means is not known yet.
observations.next: Fast-track requests are compared across November 2018 with IP RAPID's events; priority-claiming marks with either record; the unrequested ones are kept apart until IP Australia explains them.

observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U103 (descriptive). Trade marks claiming convention priority were expedited in every year; the November 2018 fall
is where the record is kept (U34 restated).**
- **Claiming priority:** an expedite event in either record for 97.22% (FY2005) to 97.82% (FY2018), 98.4% (FY2019),
  99.55% (FY2020) and 99.9% (FY2026). IP RAPID records it to FY2018 (97.81%) and almost never after (0.16% in FY2020);
  the register's history records it from FY2019 (99.53% in FY2020) and almost never before (0.06% in FY2018).
- **No priority claim:** IP RAPID's events, which since the move are the expedites applicants ask for, run 8.11%
  (FY2005), 4.81% (FY2018), 4.48% (FY2019) and 3.6% (FY2026), with no break. The register also records "Examination
  expedited" for 14.95% (FY2019) to 26.69% (FY2026) of these marks, mostly without a request; what that means is OQ6.
- **Decision (revised):** trade mark expedites are compared across November 2018 as requests (IP RAPID's events), and
  priority-claiming marks with either record; the register's unrequested "Examination expedited" is kept apart until
  IP Australia explains it (ADR 0029).

observations.headline: 11,098 design records with nothing in them are left out
observations.statement: 11,098 design records numbered 1973 to 1982, all "ceased", have no date, owner or class in IP RAPID and none in IP Australia's register either. They are [[design-shell|shells]] and are dropped from the lenses, with a list of them kept.

figures.label: empty design records dropped

points: The lens now holds 257,684 designs. Yearly counts do not change, because the shells had no date.
Totals and shares across all rights change slightly.

questions.how: A record with no information cannot say anything about the system, so leaving it out loses nothing.

prep.what: A design is dropped only if neither IP RAPID nor the register gives it a date, owner or class.
prep.why: Then there is nothing to analyse; any information keeps a record in.

steps: Find designs with no date, applicant or class in IP RAPID.
Keep only those the register also gives no owner, date or class.
Drop them, and list them in the repository.
assumptions: These records were never filled in when the old registers were computerised.
limits: They may have been real designs; nothing in either record says what they were.
observations.next: The list is kept (analysis/eda/dropped/design_shells.csv), so the drop can be reversed.

observations.statement: Of 264,260 provisional application numbers asked, IP Australia's [[register|register]] holds 264,250: 264,014 that IP RAPID also has and 236 filed since IP RAPID's release. None of 300 numbers missing from IP RAPID's yearly sequences is in the register, so those numbers were never used.

missing numbers that turned out to exist

points: 10 numbers are not found in the register.

questions.how: A count of provisional applications from IP RAPID is complete, so it can be relied on.

prep.what: Every provisional is asked for by number, as the register's patent search cannot list them.
prep.why: It is the only way to read every provisional.

steps: Ask the register for every provisional number IP RAPID has, and for numbers past each recent year's last one.
Probe a random 300 of the numbers missing inside IP RAPID's yearly sequences.
assumptions: A number the register does not know was never used.
limits: The register is as it stood in October 2026.

observations.headline: Provisional applications' inventors are named from FY2003, though since FY2024 a fifth have none
observations.statement: IP Australia's register names 181,469 inventors on [[provisional|provisional applications]], which Google Patents never sees. 98.53% to 100% of those filed FY2003 to FY2023 name at least one, and none filed before FY2003 does. Since FY2024 fewer do: 78.79% (FY2024), 76.38% (FY2025) and 84.69% (FY2026).

figures.label: inventors named on provisional applications

points: A provisional names 1.18 to 1.58 inventors on average, by year: many are filed by one person.
Whether inventors are added later, or are no longer recorded for some provisionals, the data cannot say.

questions.how: Who invents, including the many inventions that are never followed by a full patent.

prep.what: The inventors are taken as the register names them on each provisional.
prep.why: Provisionals are never published, so no other source has their inventors.

steps: Count, for each year, the provisionals naming at least one inventor, and how many they name.
assumptions: The register's inventors are the provisional's inventors as filed.
limits: Coverage since FY2024 is lower, for reasons not yet known.
observations.next: The gender analysis uses provisionals from FY2003, with each year's coverage beside its figure.

observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U106 (descriptive). The register names provisionals' inventors from FY2003; since FY2024 a fifth have none.**
- 181,469 inventors are named in all. 98.53% to 100% of provisionals filed FY2003 to FY2023 name at least one, and
  none filed before FY2003 does (0.04% in FY2002).
- Since FY2024 fewer do: 78.79% (FY2024), 76.38% (FY2025) and 84.69% (FY2026). The data cannot say whether inventors
  are added later or no longer recorded for some provisionals (a lead).
- A provisional names 1.18 to 1.58 inventors on average (by year), fewer than a standard patent (U95), as many are

observations.headline: About one inventor in five on provisional applications is estimated to be a woman
observations.statement: Of the inventors named on provisional applications filed FY2017 to FY2026, an estimated 21.24% are women on those filed by Australian organisations and 15.57% on those filed by Australian individuals. By year the share rose from 19.1% (FY2003) to 24.38% (FY2012), fell to 16.83% (FY2014), recovered to 22.08% (FY2023) and was 14.56% in FY2026.

figures.label: estimated women among inventors on Australian organisations' provisionals, FY2017 to FY2026
estimated women among provisionals' inventors in FY2026

points: It is an expected count from names, not a record of anyone's gender. All but 2.97% of inventors have an estimate.
FY2026 is the year provisional filing by individuals doubled ({U8}), and individuals' provisionals have a lower share of women.
The step from FY2012 to FY2014 comes with more inventors per provisional (1.22 to 1.37); its cause is not known.

questions.how: A measure of gender among inventors that includes provisional applications, which the patent data leave out.

prep.what: Each inventor's chance of being a woman is estimated from the given name and the first applicant's country.
prep.why: The register gives no inventor's country, and the applicant's is the nearest stand-in.

steps: Estimate each named inventor's chance of being a woman with WIPO's name dictionary.
Add the chances up by year and by who filed, and divide by the inventors with an estimate.
assumptions: The applicant's country is the inventor's, which is likely for Australian filers.
limits: The method was checked against WIPO's figures only for patents, so these estimates are less tested.
observations.next: The research owner's gender analysis compares provisionals with standard patents, by field and filer.
observations.section: 1.8.7 Provisional applications' inventors, from IP Australia's register
observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**U107 (descriptive). About one inventor in five on provisional applications is estimated to be a woman, more on
organisations' than on individuals'.**
- The estimate covers all but 2.97% of inventors: 91.44% from the name and the applicant's country, 5.59% from the
  name alone.
- **By year:** 19.1% (FY2003), rising to 24.38% (FY2012), then 20.08% (FY2013) and 16.83% (FY2014), back to 22.08%
  (FY2023), and 14.56% in FY2026, the year provisional filing by individuals doubled (U8). The step in FY2013 to
  FY2014 comes with more inventors per provisional (1.22 to 1.37); its cause is not known (a lead).
- **By filer, FY2017 to FY2026:** Australian organisations 21.24% (40,437 inventors), Australian individuals 15.57%
  (23,101), overseas organisations 9.52% and overseas individuals 21.76%.
- **Compared with standard patents:** Australian organisations' standard patents have 14.34% women among inventors in
  Australia (U98). The two are not like for like: provisionals' inventors take the applicant's country, not their own,
  and the method was checked against WIPO only for patents (U97).
- **So** the gender analysis can use provisionals from FY2003, with the year's coverage beside each figure.

observations.headline: The firms table holds the businesses found in one of six sources, not every business, and its IP counts are lower bounds
observations.statement: The table has 463,279 [[abn|ABNs]]. 54.77% appear only because they filed IP in IP RAPID, 13.99% only because IP Australia's [[register|register]] links them to a trade mark or design, 11.55% only because they hold a government contract, and 10.96% only because an older IP Australia dataset ([[iplord|IPLORD]]) links them to IP. Anything measured across this table describes these firms, not Australian businesses in general.

figures.label: businesses (ABNs) in the firms table
linked to IP only by IPLORD, so their IP counts read zero
of those IPLORD-only businesses still have an active ABN

points: **Who is in it.** 253,719 ABNs are in IP RAPID alone, 64,829 linked to IP only by IP Australia's register, 53,524 in AusTender alone, 50,790 linked to IP by IPLORD alone, 7,710 in the R&D Tax Incentive alone and 3,054 in the tax transparency reports alone; the rest appear in two or more.

**Many have closed.** Active ABNs run from 47.02% of the IPLORD-only firms and 59.62% of the firms only in IP RAPID, to 91.91% of R&D claimants and 95.35% of firms in both IP RAPID and the R&D Tax Incentive.
**Filer and holder.** Where both are known, the business that filed a right is not the one that holds it now for 2.17% of standard patents, 7.11% of trade marks and 5.25% of designs.

**IPLORD's own counts are not used.** For the 152,683 ABNs with trade marks in both datasets, 81.02% have the same count, but IPLORD's total is 1.84 times IP RAPID's and its weighted total 0.42 times. They are built differently.
**Gaps.** 252 ABNs are not in the business register extract and 4,145 have no state.

questions.how: Any comparison of who uses the IP system (Q2) must say it is among firms that used a scheme, and that their IP counts are a floor, not the full picture.
The table joins IP to R&D claims, contracts and company records for the same business, which is what Q3 needs to ask what goes with IP producing value.

prep.what: One row per ABN, taken from the corpus's ABN spine, which lists every ABN found in IP RAPID, IPLORD, the R&D Tax Incentive, AusTender or the tax transparency reports.
prep.why: The ABN is the one identifier that links a business across these sources and to the business register.

prep.what: Each application is credited to the business that filed it (its first founding applicant with an ABN), not the business that holds it today.
prep.why: "Who files" should not change when a right is later sold (ADR 0016).

prep.what: A flag marks the ABNs that only IPLORD links to IP; IPLORD's own counts are kept out.
prep.why: IPLORD counts applications differently from IP RAPID, so adding the two would mix two measures.

steps: Count the ABNs in the table, and for each, the sources it appears in.
Group the ABNs by that combination of sources and count each group.
For each group, work out the share whose ABN is still active in the business register.
For rights where both the filer's and the holder's ABN are known, count how often they differ.
Compare IPLORD's trade mark counts with IP RAPID's for the ABNs that appear in both.
assumptions: An ABN stands for one business. Related companies in the same group have different ABNs and are counted separately.
A right with no ABN recorded for its filer cannot be credited to any firm; such rights are left out of firms' counts rather than guessed.
limits: The table is not a census of Australian businesses. A business that never used one of the five schemes is not in it, so rates worked out on this table are rates among scheme users.
Firms' IP counts are lower bounds, because rights with no ABN (and IPLORD-only links) add nothing to them.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares firms' IP with their R&D, contracts, age and type, always stating that the comparison is among scheme users and that IP counts are a floor.
observations.section: 2.0 Data overview and sanity checks
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**U41 (descriptive). The lens is the firms that used one of six sources, not all businesses, and its IP counts are
lower bounds.**
- **Who is in it:** 463,279 ABNs. 253,719 (54.77%) are in IP RAPID alone, 64,829 (13.99%) are linked to IP only by IP
  Australia's register (owners of trade marks or designs that IP RAPID gives no ABN, ADR 0029), 53,524 (11.55%) in
  AusTender alone, 50,790 (10.96%) linked to IP by IPLORD alone, 7,710 (1.66%) in the R&D Tax Incentive alone and
  3,054 (0.66%) in the tax transparency reports alone; the rest are in two or more.
  Rates computed on the lens are rates among these firms.
- **Active ABNs** run from 47.02% of the IPLORD-only firms, 59.62% of the IP RAPID-only firms and 76.9% of the
  register-only firms to 91.91% of the R&D claimants
  and 95.35% of firms in both IP RAPID and the R&D Tax Incentive: many firms that once filed for IP have
  since closed.
- **Filer against holder:** where both ABNs are known, they differ for 2.17% of standard patents, 7.11% of trade marks
  and 5.25% of designs; 6.04% to 7.25% of rights with a holder's ABN have no filer's ABN.
- **IPLORD-only firms** used the IP system (to FY2020) but IP RAPID gives none of their rights an ABN, so their IP
  counts are 0. IPLORD's own counts are not used: for the 152,683 ABNs with trade marks in both, 81.02% agree, but
  IPLORD's 99th percentile is 7 times IP RAPID's, its total 1.84 times and its weighted total 0.42 times. They are
  built differently.
- **Coverage:** 252 ABNs are not in the ABR extract; 4,145 have no state; `first_seen` is filled for 92.96%.

observations.headline: Private companies make up most firms in every scheme except government contracting
observations.statement: Private companies are 71.3% of all firms in the table, 82.2% of IP filers and 94.5% of R&D Tax Incentive claimants, but only 55.3% of government suppliers, where sole traders (16.2%) and trusts (12.9%) are common.

figures.label: of all firms are private companies
of R&D Tax Incentive claimants are private companies
of government suppliers are private companies

points: The R&D Tax Incentive is open to companies only, so it has no trusts, partnerships or sole traders. That is its rule, not a choice those businesses made.
**Status.** 63.5% of private companies' ABNs are still active, 71.1% of public companies' and 37.5% of partnerships'.
Of active ABNs, 78.4% of private companies and 43.5% of sole traders are registered for GST (roughly, a turnover of $75,000 or more).

questions.how: Shows which kinds of business reach each scheme, the starting point for asking who the IP system serves.

prep.what: Each ABN's entity type from the business register is grouped into eight broad groups (private company, trust, sole trader and so on).
prep.why: The register has 57 entity types; eight groups are enough to compare schemes and few enough to read.

prep.what: An "IP filer" is a firm credited with at least one IP application as a founding applicant.
prep.why: Holding a right bought from someone else is not the same as filing for one.

steps: Group every firm by its entity group.
Within all firms, IP filers, R&D claimants and government suppliers in turn, work out each group's share.
For each entity group, work out the share of ABNs that are active, and of active ones, the share registered for GST.
assumptions: The business register's entity type is taken as recorded; a business that changed form keeps its current type.
limits: Shares describe the firms that used each scheme; they do not say which kinds of business would benefit from using it.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares firms within the same entity group, so that differences between schemes are not mistaken for differences between kinds of business.
observations.section: 2.1 Entity type and status
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**U42 (descriptive). Private companies dominate every source but AusTender.** Of each group's ABNs:
- **Private companies** are 71.3% of all firms, 82.2% of IP filers, 94.5% of R&D claimants and 55.3% of government
  suppliers. The R&D Tax Incentive is open to companies only, so it has no trusts, partnerships or sole traders (by its
  rules, not by choice).
- **Government suppliers** are the most varied: sole traders 16.2% (4.1% of IP filers) and trusts 12.9% (4.1%).
- **Sole traders** are 11.3% of all firms, more than before the register was added (U41): the register links many
  sole traders' trade marks that IP RAPID does not.
- **Status:** 63.5% of private companies' ABNs are active, 71.1% of public companies' and 37.5% of partnerships'. Of
  active ABNs, 78.4% of private companies and 43.5% of sole traders are registered for GST (a turnover of $75,000 or
  more, roughly).

observations.headline: Firms are a median 12.6 years old on the public record, with a spike where ABNs began
observations.statement: Measured from a firm's earliest public registration, the [[median]] firm is 12.6 years old. The most common start date, 1 November 1999 (5,506 firms), is the day ABNs began, so many of those firms are older than the record shows.

figures.label: years, the median age on the record
firms first seen on 1 November 1999, the ABN's start
of firms dated by their ABN are possibly older than shown

points: The [[mean]] age is 15.27 years, higher than the median because of a long tail of old companies (the oldest was registered in 1817).
By the register that set the date: companies registered with ASIC are a median 13.5 years old, firms dated by GST registration 11.3 and firms dated by their ABN 13.7.
32,600 firms have no date at all.

questions.how: Age lets Stage 2 ask whether younger firms use the IP system differently from established ones.
Stage of business development is one of the conditions Q3 asks about.

prep.what: A firm's age is the years since its earliest public registration (with ASIC, for an ABN, or for GST), up to 22 October 2026, the date the corpus was built.
prep.why: The public registers give only current statuses, so the earliest registration is the best available start date. Fixing the end date stops ages changing with the day the analysis is run.

prep.what: A flag marks firms first seen when ABNs or GST began (1999 to 2000), whose real age may be greater.
prep.why: Their recorded start is the start of the register, not of the business (ADR 0010).

steps: Take each firm's earliest registration date and work out its age in years.
Summarise the ages (median, mean, spread) and find the most common start dates.
Repeat by the register that set each firm's date, and count how many are flagged as possibly older.
assumptions: A firm's earliest public registration is close to when it began. For companies this is usually true; for firms dated by their ABN or GST it may not be, which is why they are flagged.
limits: Age on the record is a lower bound on a business's real age.
observations.next: Stage 2 uses age together with its "possibly older" flag, and looks at firms first seen from 2001 separately.
observations.section: 2.2 Age
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**U43 (descriptive). Firms are a median 12.6 years old on the record, with a spike at the ABN's start.**
- Median 12.6 years, mean 15.27: a long tail of old companies (the oldest registered in 1817).
- By the register that set the date: ASIC-registered companies a median 13.5 years; firms dated by GST 11.3; by the
  ABN 13.7, of which 21.6% are truncated (first seen when ABNs began, so possibly older).
- The most common first date is 1 November 1999, the ABN's start (5,506 firms, 1.28% of those dated): the hump at
  about 27 years in the chart. 32,600 firms have no date.
- **Decision:** Stage 2 uses age with `age_truncated`, and compares firms first seen from 2001 separately.

observations.headline: A few firms file most of the patents that firms file
observations.statement: Of the 23,971 firms that filed standard patents, the top 1% filed 55.3% of them, while the typical ([[median]]) firm filed just one. Trade marks are less concentrated: the top 1% of filing firms filed 25.7%.

figures.label: of firms' standard patents were filed by the top 1% of filing firms
standard patent filed by the median filing firm
standard patents filed by the busiest single firm

points: **Standard patents.** 23,971 firms filed 183,989; the median firm filed 1 and the [[percentile|90th percentile]] firm 7.
**Trade marks.** 301,249 firms filed 1,018,160; median 1, 90th percentile 6; the top 1% filed 25.7%.
**Designs.** 14,113 firms filed 77,794, and the top 1% filed 35.6%. Provisional applications: the top 1% of 24,905 firms filed 32.0%. Second-tier patents: the top 1% of 6,077 firms filed 12.2%.
**What firms hold now.** 116,240 firms hold 430,305 rights still in force; the top 1% of them hold 28.7%.
Plotted on [[log-scale|log scales]], the number of firms filing a given number of applications falls in a near-straight line: a [[long-tail]].

questions.how: Use of the system is highly uneven, so national averages would mostly describe a handful of heavy filers. Q2's interest in distribution over averages starts here.
The contrast between the few heavy filers and the many one-off filers is a natural place to look for what distinguishes valuable use of IP.

prep.what: Each application is credited to the business that filed it (the first founding applicant with an ABN).
prep.why: Crediting today's holder would move applications to whoever bought the rights later (ADR 0016).

prep.what: Standard patents, provisional applications, second-tier patents, trade marks and designs are counted apart.
prep.why: They are different rights with different costs and purposes, and a combined count would mostly be trade marks (U4).

prep.what: Only firms with at least one application of a type are counted for that type.
prep.why: The question is how filing is spread among those who file, not how many firms never file.

steps: Start from every standard patent application whose filer has an ABN, credited to that filer.
Count each firm's applications. 23,971 firms filed 183,989 standard patents.
Line the firms up from most to fewest applications.
Take the top 1% of firms in that line and add up their applications.
Divide by all 183,989 applications. The result is 55.3%.
Repeat for each type of right, and for the rights firms hold now.
assumptions: One ABN is one firm. Companies in the same corporate group are counted separately, so concentration by corporate group would be at least as high as shown.
Applications without a filer's ABN (individuals, and some organisations) are outside this count; the shares describe firms with an ABN.
limits: A count of applications says nothing about their value. Heavy filers' patents may be worth more or less than anyone else's.
Firms' IP counts are lower bounds ({U41}), and filers after FY2024 are less often linked to an ABN ({U45}).
observations.next: Stage 2 relates firms' filing to their R&D, contracts, age and type, using medians, logs or ranks rather than averages, because averages would be pulled up by the few heaviest filers.
observations.section: 2.3 IP use
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**U44 (descriptive). Most firms file once or twice; a few file most of the patents.**
- **Standard patents:** 23,971 firms filed 183,989; the median firm filed 1, the 90th percentile 7, the most 3,811.
  The top 1% of filing firms filed 55.3% of them.
- **Trade marks:** 301,249 firms filed 1,018,160; median 1, 90th percentile 6; the top 1% filed 25.7%.
- **Designs:** 14,113 firms filed 77,794 (top 1%: 35.6%); **provisional applications:** 24,905 firms (32.0%);
  **second-tier patents:** 6,077 firms (12.2%).
- **What firms hold now:** 260,292 firms hold 1,262,125 rights; 116,240 hold 430,305 rights in force (the top 1%
  of those: 28.7%).
- Trade marks and designs are credited by the filer's ABN filled from IP Australia's register where IP RAPID has
  none (`filer_abn`, ADR 0029); standard patents, provisionals and second-tier patents are IP RAPID's alone.
- The spread is close to a straight line on log scales (the chart): a long tail, so Stage 2 uses medians, logs or
  ranks for firm counts, never means alone.

observations.headline: Recent filers are less often linked to a business number, so part of an apparent fall in new filers is in the records
observations.statement: Firms filing their first trade mark fell from 11,318 in FY2024 to 7,384 in FY2026. But over the same years the share of Australian organisations' trade marks that carry the filer's [[abn|ABN]] fell from 84.1% to 59.9%. At least part of the fall is in linking applications to businesses, not in filing.

figures.label: Australian organisations' trade marks with the filer's ABN, FY2024 to FY2026
firms filing their first trade mark, FY2024 to FY2026

points: Restated with IP Australia's register ({U100}, {U101}): it holds the business numbers IP RAPID leaves out. Filled, 92.3% of Australian organisations' trade marks have the filer's ABN in FY2024, 91.4% in FY2025 and 90.9% in FY2026, and firms filing their first trade mark number 14,728, 15,818 and 19,730.

Firms filing their first trade mark rose from 1,186 (FY1990) to 11,318 (FY2024), then fell to 8,741 (FY2025) and 7,384 (FY2026). Firms filing their first patent fell from 1,165 (FY2020) to 685 (FY2026).
The share with a filer's ABN fell for trade marks from 84.1% (FY2024) to 71.4% (FY2025) and 59.9% (FY2026); for designs from 88.4% to 76.3%; for standard patents from 88.7% to 83.9%.
ABNs may be attached to applications late, or collected less often. The data cannot say which.

questions.how: Any trend in who is newly using the system depends on this linking; until it is explained, recent years cannot be compared fairly.
Whether ABNs are collected at filing is something IP Australia controls, so the answer bears on how well it can measure its own reach.

prep.what: Each firm's first application of each type is dated by financial year.
prep.why: The year a firm first files is its entry into the system.

prep.what: The share with a filer's ABN is worked out among Australian organisations only.
prep.why: Individuals usually have no ABN, so including them would mix a change in who files with a change in linking.

steps: Count, for each financial year, the firms whose first trade mark (or patent, or design) was filed that year.
Separately, for Australian organisations' applications in each year, work out the share that carry the filer's ABN.
Compare the two over FY2024 to FY2026. The count of new filers falls while the share linked to an ABN also falls.
assumptions: Australian organisations would normally have an ABN; a falling share with one is read as a change in recording, not a change in who files.
limits: The data cannot separate late linking from less collection, or say how much of the fall in new filers is real.
observations.next: The cause is publication: IP Australia's register holds the numbers ({U100}). Firm-level filing by year is compared to FY2026 with the filled columns, and IP Australia is asked why IP RAPID leaves them out (OQ7).
observations.section: 2.3 IP use
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**U45 (descriptive). The latest years' filers are less often linked to an ABN: a lead.**
- Firms filing their first trade mark rose from 1,186 (FY1990) to 11,318 (FY2024), then fell to 8,741 (FY2025) and
  7,384 (FY2026); first patent filers fell from 1,165 (FY2020) to 685 (FY2026).
- But the share of Australian organisations' trade marks with a filer's ABN fell from 84.1% (FY2024) to 71.4%
  (FY2025) and 59.9% (FY2026); for designs from 88.4% to 76.3%, for standard patents from 88.7% to 83.9%. So at least
  part of the fall is in linking, not filing: ABNs may be attached late, or collected less.
- **Decision (to 27 October 2026):** firm-level filing by year was compared only to FY2024 until the cause was known
  (ADR 0016).
- **Restated with the register (U100, U101; ADR 0029).** The cause is publication: IP Australia's register holds an
  ABN, or an ACN that has one, for most of the marks IP RAPID leaves without. With it, 92.3% of Australian
  organisations' trade marks have a filer's ABN in FY2024, 91.4% in FY2025 and 90.9% in FY2026, and firms filing
  their first trade mark number 14,728, 15,818 and 19,730. **Decision (revised):** firm-level filing by year uses the
  filled columns (`filer_abn`, `*_first_fy_filled`) and can be compared to FY2026; IP RAPID's own columns stay, and
  the filled series' earlier years are lower bounds (U100).

observations.headline: R&D claims are spread across many firms; government contract value is concentrated in a few suppliers
observations.statement: The top 1% of R&D Tax Incentive claimants account for 28.1% of claims, but the top 1% of government suppliers hold 83.1% of contract value. The typical claimant's latest claim is $307,490; the typical supplier has 2 contracts worth $110,000.

figures.label: of R&D claims by the top 1% of claimants
of contract value held by the top 1% of suppliers
the median latest R&D claim

points: **R&D Tax Incentive.** 18,718 firms (2021-22 to 2023-24). The median latest claim is $307,490, the 90th percentile $1,996,666 and the largest $236,287,319. 195 firms claimed $0 in their latest year.
**Tax transparency reports.** 6,602 firms, with a median latest income of $201,600,950 (the reports cover entities with $100 million or more).
**AusTender.** 72,042 suppliers, a median 2 contracts and $110,000 in value; the top 1% hold 83.1% of the value and 55.9% of the contracts.

questions.how: R&D and procurement are two of the complementary activities Q3 asks about; knowing how they are spread decides how they can be compared with IP.
Government procurement is a possible lever; its concentration matters for who such a lever would reach.

prep.what: R&D uses each firm's latest report (as amended); contracts are counted once each, at their latest value.
prep.why: Summing every amendment of a contract had counted the same contract many times (ADR 0010, 0011).

prep.what: Money is shown in nominal dollars here.
prep.why: Stage 1 describes values as recorded; Stage 2 adjusts for inflation before comparing years ({U30}).

steps: For each source, take the firms with any value and summarise the spread (median, 90th percentile, largest).
Line firms up from largest to smallest and work out the share held by the top 1%.
assumptions: A contract's value is the value published in its latest notice, over its whole life.
limits: Contract values are what was agreed, not what was paid; amendments to some older contracts are missing (OQ3).
The tax reports cover only very large entities, so they say nothing about small firms' income.
observations.next: Stage 2 compares firms' IP with their R&D and contracts, in dollars adjusted for inflation.

**U46 (descriptive). R&D claims are spread; contract value is concentrated in a few suppliers.**
- **R&D Tax Incentive:** 18,718 firms (2021-22 to 2023-24); the median latest claim is $307,490, the 90th percentile
  $1,996,666 and the largest $236,287,319; the top 1% claim 28.1%. 195 firms claimed $0 in their latest year.
- **Tax transparency reports:** 6,602 firms, median latest income $201,600,950 (the reports cover $100 million or

observations.headline: IP filers and R&D claimants are more often in major cities and advantaged areas than firms in general
observations.statement: 85.3% of all firms are registered in major cities, against 87.1% of IP filers and 89.9% of R&D claimants. 33.4% of firms are in the most advantaged tenth of postcodes, against 39.3% of R&D claimants. Government suppliers are less metropolitan (78.9%).

figures.label: of R&D claimants are registered in major cities
of R&D claimants are in the most advantaged tenth of postcodes

points: **State.** New South Wales has 35.6% of firms, 36.7% of IP filers and 36.3% of R&D claimants; Victoria 26.8%, 27.6% and 27.8%. The ACT has 2.5% of firms but 9.7% of government suppliers.
**Advantage.** The three least advantaged tenths of postcodes hold 2.7%, 4.3% and 3.2% of firms.
An address here is where the business is registered, often a head office or an accountant's, not necessarily where its work is done.

questions.how: A first sign of geographic and socio-economic unevenness in who uses IP and R&D support, which Q2 asks about directly.

prep.what: Each firm is placed by the postcode of its main business address in the business register, then given that postcode's remoteness and advantage ([[irsad|IRSAD]] tenth) from the ABS.
prep.why: The register's address is the only location recorded for most firms.

prep.what: A blank state in the register is filled from the postcode where possible (165 firms).
prep.why: The register left the state blank for 3,977 ABNs (ADR 0016).

steps: Place every firm in its postcode's state, remoteness class and advantage tenth.
Work out the share of all firms, IP filers, R&D claimants and government suppliers in each class.
Compare the shares across the four groups.
assumptions: A firm's registered address stands in for where it is. For many firms that is a head office or an adviser's address.
limits: The shares say where firms are registered, not where research is done or where benefits fall.
observations.next: Stage 2 works at the level of places (the regions lens), comparing filing rates with advantage and remoteness.

observations.headline: Size and industry are now known for employers of 100 or more, few of the filers but a large share of their IP

of standard patent filers

observations.headline: The places table covers 2,641 postal areas and 25,365,506 people; individuals file a fifth of patents and two-fifths of provisionals
observations.statement: The table holds 2,641 postal areas and 25,365,506 people, with every count complete. Applications are counted where the filer was; the filer's and holder's postcodes differ for 6.05% of standard patents and 7.6% of trade marks. Individuals filed 21.53% of standard patents and 41.07% of provisional applications from Australia.

figures.label: postal areas
of standard patents filed by individuals
of provisional applications filed by individuals

points: SEIFA scores are missing for 17 areas (99.36% filled); Census medians for 1 to 34 areas (rent: 34 areas with no renters).
Individuals also filed 24.97% of trade marks, 20.71% of designs and 43.11% of second-tier patents.
A rate per business counts organisations' filings only, because the business count holds no individuals.

questions.how: Sets the ground for comparing places, and shows how large a part individuals play in Australian filing.

prep.what: Applications are counted at the postcode of the first founding applicant in Australia, over FY2017 to FY2026.
prep.why: A right sold to a firm elsewhere stays where it was filed (ADR 0017).

prep.what: Organisations' counts are kept beside the totals.
prep.why: Individuals file a fifth to two-fifths of applications, and the business count has no individuals in it.

steps: Count the postal areas and people, and check each column's completeness.
For rights filed FY2017 to FY2026 from Australia, compare filer and holder postcodes.
Work out the share filed by individuals, by type.
assumptions: The filer's postcode is where the filing happened.
limits: Some filers' postcodes are not postal areas and cannot be placed ({U49}).

observations.headline: One standard patent in eighteen comes from a postcode where no one lives, most of them universities'
observations.statement: 94.45% of standard patents' filer postcodes are postal areas. 4.14% are real postcodes with no residents, such as a university's own postcode, and 1.39% are post office box ranges. Of the twelve such codes with the most patents and provisionals, seven are universities'.

figures.label: of standard patents can be placed in a postal area
carry a real postcode with no residents

points: 2052 (NewSouth Innovations, 84.6% of its 749 patents and provisionals), 3800 (Monash University, 97.5% of 445), 2006 (the University of Sydney, 95.4% of 417), 3010 (the University of Melbourne, 87.2% of 352).
Trade marks are placed more often: 96.43% fall in postal areas, 1.7% in real codes with no residents.
So universities' patents are mostly missing from the postal-area counts; they stay in the state totals.

questions.how: Without this, places with universities would look as if they filed far less than they do.

prep.what: A filer's postcode that is not a postal area is classed by Australia Post's ranges, and checked against the business register.
prep.why: It separates post office boxes from real places with no residents (ADR 0017).

steps: Check each filer's postcode against the ABS's postal areas.
For those not found, class them by Australia Post's ranges, and check whether businesses are registered there.
Find the largest filer behind the codes with the most patents.
assumptions: A postcode in a delivery range with registered businesses but no residents is a real place, such as a campus.
limits: These patents cannot be placed in an area without a lookup of where each code is.

universities'.**

  patents and provisionals by organisations).

  provisionals, but 1.7% of trade marks. Of the twelve codes outside the postal areas with the most patents and
  provisionals, seven are universities' (by the ABR's name for the largest filer with an ABN): 2052 (NewSouth
  Innovations, 84.6% of its 749), 3800 (Monash University, 97.5% of 445), 2006 (the University of Sydney, 95.4% of
  417), 3010 (the University of Melbourne, 87.2% of 352), 2109 (Macquarie University, 91.7% of 157), 5005 (the

questions.how: Remoteness and advantage are among the characteristics Q2 asks about; this shows how to weight them fairly.

prep.why: They are the standard national measures of remoteness and advantage.

steps: Group areas by remoteness, and add up their people and businesses.
Count areas in each SEIFA tenth.
assumptions: An area's remoteness class applies to all its residents.
limits: A tenth of areas is not a tenth of people; results by tenth must be weighted by people.

observations.original:
**U51 (descriptive). Most areas are outside the cities, most people and businesses inside; SEIFA deciles are tenths of
areas, not of people.**
- **Remoteness:** major cities have 37.7% of postal areas, 72.8% of people and 77.2% of businesses; remote and very

observations.statement: Over FY2017 to FY2026, the tenth of postal areas with the most standard patents (264 areas) filed 72.5% of them, but hold 29.2% of people. For trade marks the figure is 60.8% (32.8% of people), for designs 75.4%. An area's patents are often one firm's.

of people live in those areas

In the city centres the largest filer has 5.2% to 14.6%.
**Corrected (26 October 2026):** the people shares were 29.0% and 32.9% when areas tied on their count were ordered as the file happened to hold them; ties now go by postcode.

questions.how: Filing is far more concentrated than population, and often reflects one firm, so area counts need the firms behind them before they say anything about places.

observations.original:
**U52 (descriptive). Applications are concentrated in a few areas, and an area's patents are often one firm's.**
- **Concentration:** the tenth of postal areas with the most standard patents (264) have 72.5% of them, but 29.2% of

  330 no trade mark.
- **One filer:** in 2113 (North Ryde), 76.3% of 1,708 standard patents are Aristocrat Technologies'; in 2601

- **So** a postal area's patent count is often one firm's patent count. Stage 2 reads area counts beside the firms

observations.headline: Places differ in filing far more than chance would make them
observations.statement: At the national rate (0.99 standard patents a year per 10,000 people), chance alone would put 2.5% of areas above and 2.5% below the 95% limits. Instead 6.7% are above and 68.2% below for standard patents, and 15.0% and 71.4% for trade marks. Pooled into 335 larger areas (SA3s) the pattern holds (15.5% above, 72.5% below).

figures.label: of areas below chance limits for standard patents
expected below by chance alone

points: Most areas file less than the nation, and a few file far more.
Rates are shown for 850 areas for standard patents (82.73% of people) and 2,094 for trade marks (99.46%); 324 of the 335 SA3s would expect 10 or more standard patents.
The highest rate per person is Sydney's centre, 2000 (712.6 trade marks a year per 10,000 people); for standard patents, 2113 (61.8).

questions.how: Real differences between places are the starting point for asking who is underserved; chance cannot explain them away.
Areas far below the national rate are candidates, later, for asking whether something holds them back.

prep.what: A rate is applications a year per 10,000 people over FY2017 to FY2026, shown only where 10 or more would be expected at the national rate.
prep.why: A count of 10 has a 95% chance range of about 5 to 18; below that, an area's rate is mostly chance (ADR 0017).

prep.what: Small areas are pooled into 335 SA3s as a check.
prep.why: If the pattern were small-area noise, pooling would remove it.

steps: Work out the national rate, and each area's expected count at that rate.
Draw the range chance alone would allow around the national rate, for each size of area (a funnel plot).
Count the areas above and below the range.
Repeat for SA3s.
assumptions: Each area's filings would follow a Poisson pattern if only chance were at work.
limits: The funnel shows that areas differ, not why; a single firm can lift an area ({U52}).
observations.next: Stage 2 models area counts with room for this extra spread (negative binomial models), pooled to SA3s, beside the firms behind them.
observations.section: 3.3 IP applications and rates
observations.chapter: 3. Lens: Places (one row per postal area)
observations.original:
**U53 (descriptive). Areas differ far more than chance would make them; rates are shown where they mean something.**
- **The funnels:** at the national rate (18.69 trade marks and 0.99 standard patents a year per 10,000 people), chance
  would put 2.5% of areas above and 2.5% below the 95% limits. Instead 15.0% are above and 71.4% below for trade marks,
  6.7% and 68.2% for standard patents. Most areas file less than the nation, and a few file far more.
- **Pooled into 335 SA3s** the pattern holds (15.5% above, 72.5% below for standard patents), so it is not small-area
  noise. Stage 2 models these counts with room for that spread (negative binomial, not Poisson).
- **Rates shown** (ADR 0017): standard patents per person for 850 areas (82.73% of people), trade marks for 2,094
  (99.46%), designs for 812 (81.16%); per business, 650, 2,048 and 608. 324 of the 335 SA3s would expect 10 or more standard
  patents (99.8% of people).
- **Medians and extremes:** trade marks a median 8.48 a year per 10,000 people (90th percentile 32.61) and 4.35 per
  1,000 businesses. The highest per person is 2000, Sydney's centre (712.6, with 27,940 residents and 70,543
  businesses); per business it is 26.4 there. For standard patents 2113 is highest (61.8 per 10,000 people).

observations.headline: Half of R&D claimants have never filed for IP, and claimants are rarer outside the cities
observations.statement: Of 17,627 active R&D Tax Incentive claimants placed in a postal area, 50.7% have never filed IP as a founding applicant. There are 5.6 claimants per 1,000 businesses in major cities, 2.4 in inner regional, 1.8 in outer regional, 1.3 in remote and 0.6 in very remote areas.

figures.label: of R&D claimants have never filed IP
claimants per 1,000 businesses, major cities against very remote

points: Claimants outside the cities have more often never filed IP (59.6% in outer regional areas, against 50.4% in the cities).
IP-filing firms: 49.7 per 1,000 businesses in the cities, against 19.0 to 29.3 elsewhere.
These are counts by registered address, not necessarily where the R&D is done.

questions.how: Firms doing R&D that never use the IP system ('missing filers') are an obvious group to ask about later, for barriers IP Australia could ease.
R&D without IP is one of the alternatives to registration Q3 asks about.

prep.what: Firms are placed by their business register postcode; "never filed" means never a founding applicant with this ABN.
prep.why: Filing is credited to the business that filed (ADR 0016).

steps: Count active claimants and IP-filing firms in each postal area.
Count claimants who never filed IP.
Group by remoteness and divide by businesses.
assumptions: A claimant with no IP under its own ABN has not filed; filings under a related company's ABN are missed.
limits: A lower bound on IP use: firms' IP counts are lower bounds ({U41}).
observations.next: Stage 2 studies 'missing filers' by place and industry.

observations.headline: Values split from larger areas track direct counts; CABEE counts a quarter fewer businesses than the business register
observations.statement: Data by Region's 2021 population, split from larger areas, is within 10% of the direct count for 99.34% of postal areas of 1,000 people or more. CABEE's June 2025 business count is 0.742 of the register's active GST businesses, but ranks areas almost alike (Spearman 0.988): they count different things.

CABEE counts businesses actively trading; the register counts registrations. So a CABEE count is never compared with a register count.

questions.how: Confirms the method for placing other data in postal areas, and which business count to use.

prep.what: The same quantity is taken from two routes and compared, area by area.
prep.why: Agreement shows the splitting method works; disagreement shows the measures differ.

steps: For each area, compare the Census and split population with the geography's count.
Compare CABEE's split business count with the register's.
Work out ratios of totals and rank correlations.

limits: Agreement for people does not prove agreement for every indicator.

observations.original:
**U56 (descriptive). Split values track the direct ones; CABEE counts a quarter fewer businesses than the ABR, in the
same order.**
- **People:** the Census's count (25,369,823) is the ASGS count (25,365,506) to within 0.02%, the gap being the ABS's
  perturbation. Data by Region's 2021 estimated resident population, split from SA2s, is 1.3% higher in total (it
  adds people the Census missed), and within 10% of the ASGS count for 99.34% of postal areas of 1,000 people or more
  (Spearman 0.9999).
- **Businesses:** CABEE's June 2025 count (2,713,177) is 0.742 of the ABR's active GST-registered ABNs (3,657,678);
  the median area's ratio is 0.749 and only 2.96% of areas are within 10%, but the two rank areas almost alike
  (Spearman 0.988). They count different things (businesses actively trading, against registrations), so a CABEE
  count is never compared with an ABR count. Its employment and turnover tables give the same total (ratio 1.000).
- **So** the residents-weighted split is sound for people. For businesses by postal area, the ABR (`active_gst_abns`)
  is the count; CABEE's value is its split by size and industry, which the ABR lacks.

observations.statement: Solar water heaters fell from 122,312 installations in 2009 to 18,505 in 2025. Solar panels went from 62,831 in 2009 to 360,423 in 2011, 370,287 in 2020 and 272,395 in 2025. Batteries, recorded from July 2025, numbered 339,457 in 2026 to September.

observations.headline: Thirty indicators cover 229 places from 1960, but Australia's records of R&D staff end early
observations.statement: The core table holds 30 indicators for 229 places from 1960 to 2025 (135,597 values). Australia's series are complete except for R&D: researchers end in 2010 and technicians in 2008, and the World Bank's R&D spending ends in 2021 (the OECD's runs to 2023).

points: Over 2000 to 2024 Australia has 20% of the years for R&D technicians, 24% for researchers and 40% for tertiary enrolment, against 44.2%, 81.4% and 82.8% of OECD member-years.
The World Bank supplies 113,147 values (217 countries), WIPO 19,296 and the OECD 3,154.

questions.how: International comparison is how Australia's IP system can be judged against others; gaps limit it.
Missing R&D workforce data is itself a gap worth noting for policy evidence.

prep.what: One row per country, year and indicator, from the World Bank, WIPO and the OECD.
prep.why: A country in a year is the unit of international comparison.

prep.what: The OECD's R&D series sit beside the World Bank's, never spliced.
prep.why: They differ where they overlap (2021, 1.66% against 1.86%), so they are compared, not joined (ADR 0010).

steps: For each indicator, count the countries, the years, and Australia's years.
Compare Australia's coverage over 2000 to 2024 with the OECD members'.
assumptions: The World Bank's and OECD's figures for Australia come from the ABS and are comparable across countries.
limits: Recent Australian R&D workforce figures are simply missing.
observations.next: Stage 2 uses the OECD's R&D series beside the World Bank's.

- **Australia's gaps:** researchers in R&D end in 2010 and technicians in 2008; the World Bank's R&D spending ends in

  for technicians, 24% for researchers and 40% for tertiary enrolment, against 44.2%, 81.4% and 82.8% of OECD
  member-years.
- **Across the OECD,** the least complete series are technicians in R&D (44.2% of member-years), trade mark
  applications (65.8%) and new business registrations (68.2%).

observations.statement: Of WIPO's patent applications by origin, 34.35% had an unknown origin in 1980, 29.02% in 1990 and 32.24% in 1993, then 9.0% in 1994 and 1.12% in 2024. - Of WIPO's patent applications by origin (all offices), 34.35% had an unknown origin in 1980, 29.02% in 1990 and
  32.24% in 1993, then 9.0% in 1994 and 1.12% in 2024. Former states held 22.59% in 1980 (the Soviet Union 1,729,188

observations.headline: Australia's R&D intensity peaked in 2008 and has fallen below the OECD median; manufacturing shrank twice as fast as the typical member's
observations.statement: Gross R&D spending was 1.26% of GDP in 1990, 2.24% in 2008 and 1.68% in 2023, against an OECD median of 1.85%. Business R&D was 0.91% of GDP in 2023 (median 1.18%). Manufacturing fell from 13.7% of GDP in 1990 to 5.32% in 2025, down 61%, against 30% for the median member.

figures.label: gross R&D as a share of GDP, 2008 to 2023
manufacturing's share of GDP since 1990

points: **IP royalties:** Australia pays more for others' IP than it earns from its own in every year: payments $826 million (1990) to $12.4 billion (2025), receipts $162 million to $7.4 billion (US dollars).
**Patents:** non-resident applications in Australia rose from 13,280 (1990) to 29,010 (2023) while the median member's fell.
**Two breaks to read past:** the share of the labour force with advanced education steps up to 86.33% in 2010, and net foreign investment was −3.6% of GDP in 2005, a single year.

questions.how: The national context in which the IP system works; falling R&D and a shrinking manufacturing base matter for what patents can do.
Shows where Australia sits against peers, a starting point for where intervention might matter.

prep.what: Each indicator is compared with the OECD members' median in the same year, where 10 or more report.
prep.why: The median member is a fair benchmark; with fewer reporting, it moves with who reports.

steps: Take Australia's value for each indicator and year.
Work out the OECD members' median and middle half for the same year.
Compare at chosen years.
assumptions: Indicators are measured the same way across countries, as the publishers intend.
limits: Each value is a ratio of the whole economy; it does not say why R&D fell.

  median of 0.80%, 0.95%, 0.99% and 1.18%. **Gross R&D (GERD):** 1.26%, 2.24%, 1.87% and 1.68%, against 1.42%, 1.57%,
  1.78% and 1.85%.
- **Manufacturing:** 13.7% of GDP in 1990, 5.32% in 2025 (down 61%); the median member's 18.29% to 12.79% (down 30%).
  **Exports:** 15.09% to 23.24% of GDP; the median's 26.76% to 45.37%.
- **IP royalties:** Australia pays more for others' IP than it earns from its own in every year shown: payments $826
  million (1990) to $12.4 billion (2025), receipts $162 million to $7.4 billion (current US dollars).
- **Patents:** non-resident applications in Australia rose from 13,280 (1990) to 29,010 (2023) while the median

  −3.6% of GDP in 2005, a single year.
