observations.original:
**B4 (observational). The substantive leads, and where each is followed up.** Read with their candidate third
factors (above); all hold in both decades:
- **Representation and outcome** (section 1.1): a standard patent with no attorney or agent is more often withdrawn
  (status × an agent acts 0.243; 0.217; withdrawn with no agent 28.0 times chance), as are trade marks (0.317;
  0.274), second-tier patents (0.491; 0.474) and designs filed through an agent who is not an attorney (representation
  × registered 0.323; 0.281).
- **Origin and reach** (1.3): the offices a standard patent's family is filed in vary with its route (0.431; 0.481),
  the applicant's country (0.386; 0.489: a median of 2 for Australian applicants, 9 for Italian) and the technology
  (0.328; 0.31: organic fine chemistry a median of 11).
- **Technology and inventors' gender** (1.6): the estimated share of women among a standard patent's inventors
  varies with the technology area (0.268; 0.297; biotechnology highest). Its strongest leads, with the priority
  office (0.378) and the applicant's country (0.329), are led by China, whose estimates U97 found unreliable: a
  quirk of the name dictionary, not a finding. Provisionals' inventors: organisations' have more women than
  individuals' (0.157; 0.206).
- **Place and representation:** the founding applicant's state goes with the attorney firm (0.342; 0.389; South
  Australia with Collison & Co 14.9 times chance): attorney markets are local.
- **Trade marks:** individuals go with clothing (class 25, 2.1 times chance; applicant type × class 0.207; 0.205);
  overseas applicants with medical apparatus (class 10, 1.9 times; 0.287; 0.294); attorneys file more classes per
  mark (a mean 1.958 against 1.466 for applicants filing alone; 0.163; 0.154).
- **Lifetimes:** designs' years in force vary with the Locarno class (0.288; 0.221: a median 9.41 years for class 04,
  5 for class 02, clothing); second-tier patents' with the applicant's country (0.379; 0.217: China lowest, a median
  2.54 years) and with having an ABN (0.201; 0.198: a median 6.54 years against 3.54).
- **Plant breeder's rights:** the genus goes with overseas applicants (0.513; 0.544; grapes, `vitis`, highest) and with
  the time to grant (0.336; 0.357; citrus a median 2,692 days).

observations.headline: Australian individuals file alone far more than anyone else; organisations and overseas filers almost never do, for patents
observations.statement: Of standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, Australian individuals filed 26.06% with no attorney or agent, Australian organisations 3.52%, overseas individuals 1.14% and overseas organisations 0.28%. For trade marks, Australian individuals filed 68.29% alone.

figures.label: Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone
overseas organisations' standard patents filed alone
Australian individuals' trade marks filed alone

points: In FY2000 to FY2009: Australian individuals 19.77%, Australian organisations 6.97%, overseas individuals 1.35%, overseas organisations 0.14%.
Trade marks: Australian organisations 40.23% (42.67% in the earlier decade), overseas organisations 5.37% (10.47%).

**Designs do not replicate:** Australian individuals filed 22.79% of their designs alone in FY2010 to FY2019 but 2.15% in FY2000 to FY2009, when 5,499 of their 8,144 designs went through an agent who is not an attorney. How agents were recorded seems to have changed, so designs are compared within one decade only.

questions.how: Shows who goes without professional help, the group a question about access starts from.
Sizes the group that help to file would reach.

prep.what: Representation is read from the repaired [[attorney]] columns ({U20}): an agent who is not the applicant, and whether that agent acts for five or more applicants.
prep.why: The register's own flag counted applicants as their own agents ({U2}).

steps: Split rights by origin (Australian or overseas) and applicant type (individual or organisation).
For each group, find the share filed with no attorney or agent, in each decade.
Check whether the pattern holds in both decades.
assumptions: Representation counts an agent recorded at any time during the application.
limits: The share filed alone describes who seeks help, not whether they needed it.
observations.next: {B6} asks what comes of filing alone.

observations.original:
**B5 (observational). Australian individuals file alone far more than anyone else; organisations and overseas filers
almost never do, for patents.** Share filed with no attorney or agent, FY2010 to FY2019 (FY2000 to FY2009):
- **Standard patents:** Australian individuals 26.06% (19.77%), Australian organisations 3.52% (6.97%), overseas
  individuals 1.14% (1.35%), overseas organisations 0.28% (0.14%).
- **Trade marks:** Australian individuals 68.29% (58.82%), Australian organisations 40.23% (42.67%), overseas
  organisations 5.37% (10.47%).
- **Designs do not replicate:** Australian individuals filed 22.79% of their designs alone in FY2010 to FY2019 but
  2.15% in FY2000 to FY2009, when 5,499 of their 8,144 designs went through an agent who is not an attorney.
  How agents were recorded for designs seems to have changed between the decades; design representation is compared
  within one decade only.

observations.headline: Australian individuals' patents filed alone are rarely granted, about 36 points less often, in both decades
observations.statement: Of Australian individuals' standard patents filed alone FY2010 to FY2019, 4.9% were granted, against 40.8% with an attorney: a gap of 35.9 [[percentage-point|points]] (interval 34.1 to 37.6). In FY2000 to FY2009 the gap was 36.9 points. It stays among applications whose examination was requested (34.5 points).

figures.label: Australian individuals' standard patents granted, filed alone against with an attorney
the gap, FY2010 to FY2019 (36.9 in FY2000 to FY2009)
the gap among applications that were examined

points: **Filing alone goes with not asking for examination:** 25.3% of individuals' lone applications were examined, against 75.9% with an attorney.

**Australian organisations do not replicate:** a gap of 40.0 points in FY2010 to FY2019 but -6.1 in FY2000 to FY2009, when the 1,148 organisations filing alone were granted 62.1% of the time (probably firms with their own patent staff).

**Trade marks replicate for both:** with an attorney, Australian individuals' marks are registered 24.3 points more often, organisations' 23.6 points. Designs are registered without examination, so 99.4% to 100% are, whoever files.
**Not a cause.** An application dropped early may never appoint an attorney, so the arrow can run backwards; and those who file alone differ in resources and experience.

questions.how: Individuals who file without help end with far fewer granted patents, a sign of who the system serves less well.
The lead for whether help to file would add value, the kind of intervention Q4 asks about.
Representation is a condition that goes with whether a filing becomes a right at all.

prep.what: Grant rates among standard patents whose outcome is known, by group and representation, with Wilson intervals for each rate and Newcombe intervals for the gaps.
prep.why: An [[interval]] shows how precisely each rate and gap is known.

steps: For Australian individuals, find the share of standard patents granted, filed alone and with an attorney.
Take the difference, with its interval, in each decade.
Repeat among applications whose examination was requested, to set aside those never pursued.
Repeat for Australian organisations and for trade marks.
assumptions: Patents filed long enough ago have had time to reach an outcome (the decades end in FY2019).
limits: The arrow can run backwards (abandonment before an attorney is appointed), and resources and experience differ.
Candidate [[third-factor|third factors]]: applicant type and origin, whether examination is requested, the route of filing.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3, which tests the gap with these third factors held steady. Any claim that help to file would raise grants needs a design that comes after Stage 3.

observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**B6 (observational). Standard patents filed alone are rarely granted; the gap is about 36 points for Australian
individuals in both decades, and holds among applications that were examined.**
- **Australian individuals:** 4.9% of standard patents filed alone were granted (interval 3.9% to 6.0%) against 40.8%
  with an attorney (39.3% to 42.2%), FY2010 to FY2019: a gap of 35.9 points (34.1 to 37.6). FY2000 to FY2009: 8.3%
  against 45.2%, a gap of 36.9 points (34.9 to 38.7).
- **Among those whose examination was requested,** the gap stays: 34.5 points (30.1 to 38.4) and 33.8 (29.5 to 37.7).
  Filing alone also goes with not asking for examination: 25.3% of individuals' lone applications against 75.9% with
  an attorney (FY2010 to FY2019).
- **Australian organisations do not replicate:** a gap of 40.0 points (37.5 to 42.1) in FY2010 to FY2019, but -6.1
  (-8.9 to -3.1) in FY2000 to FY2009, when the 1,148 organisations filing alone were granted 62.1% of the time. The
  earlier decade's lone organisations look like firms with their own patent staff, which the later decade's do not.
- **Trade marks** replicate for both: with an attorney, Australian individuals' marks are registered 24.3 points more
  often (23.6 to 24.9; FY2000 to FY2009: 23.2, 22.3 to 24.0), organisations' 23.6 points (23.3 to 23.9; 21.3).
  **Designs** are registered without examination, so 99.4% to 100% are, whoever files.
- **Not a cause.** Representation counts an agent on the record at any time, so an application dropped early may
  never appoint one (the arrow can run backwards), and those who file alone differ in resources and experience.
  Candidate third factors: applicant type and origin (the screen's applicant type × representation, 0.272; 0.277),
  whether examination is requested, the route of filing. Q4 asks whether help to file would add value; this is the
  lead.

observations.headline: Australian organisations' patents took longer to grant than overseas ones in one decade but not the other, so this is not a lead
observations.statement: Granted standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019 took a median 3.12 years from application for Australian organisations, against 2.65 for overseas organisations (a difference of 0.476 years). In FY2000 to FY2009 it was 3.40 against 3.32 (0.077). The gap does not hold in both decades.

figures.label: the gap in median time to grant, FY2010 to FY2019
the gap, FY2000 to FY2009

points: Counted from the examination request instead, the gap is 0.17 years in the later decade and -0.079 in the earlier.
**The route explains much of it:** an international (PCT) application's clock starts at national phase entry, about 30 months after its priority ({U6}), and overseas filers use the PCT most ({B15}).

questions.how: Checks whether Australian applicants wait longer for their rights; on this evidence, not consistently.

prep.what: Medians with bootstrap intervals that resample whole patents, from application and from the examination request.
prep.why: Medians are not pulled by the few very slow cases.

steps: Find the median years to grant for each group of filer, in each decade.
Take the difference with its interval.
Repeat from the examination request.
assumptions: Only granted patents have a time to grant; those never granted are not in the comparison.
limits: Recorded, not carried: a difference in one decade only is not a lead.
observations.next: Not carried to Stage 3.

observations.original:
**B7 (observational). Australian organisations' standard patents took longer to grant than overseas organisations' in
FY2010 to FY2019, but not in FY2000 to FY2009: not a lead.** Granted standard patents, median years from application:
Australian organisations 3.12 against 2.65 for overseas organisations (a difference of 0.476 years, interval 0.43 to
0.52; rank-biserial 0.179), but 3.40 against 3.32 in FY2000 to FY2009 (0.077, 0.044 to 0.126; 0.016). From the
examination request the difference is 0.17 years (0.153 to 0.184) in the later decade and -0.079 (-0.101 to -0.057) in
the earlier. The route is the candidate third factor: a PCT application's clock starts at national phase entry,
about 30 months after its priority (U6), and overseas filers use the PCT most (section 1.5); the screen ties time to
grant to the route (0.304; 0.237: claiming an Australian application, a median 1,617 days).

observations.headline: Australian organisations keep their standard patents longer than overseas organisations do, even within fields
observations.statement: Of granted standard patents filed FY2005 to FY2009, 78.7% of Australian organisations' were still in force after 10 years, against 72.3% of overseas organisations' and 66.4% of Australian individuals'. Within technology fields, Australian organisations keep a higher share in all but 9 of 32, by a median 4.7 points.

figures.label: Australian organisations' patents in force after 10 years (FY2005 to FY2009)
overseas organisations'
Australian organisations' median lead within the same field

points: FY2000 to FY2004 filings: Australian organisations 72.8%, overseas organisations 62.9%, Australian individuals 55.3%, overseas individuals 55.4%.
After 15 years: Australian organisations 50.3% and 42.4%; overseas organisations 43.9% and 36.8%.
Every group kept its patents longer in the later period, in line with {U36}.

**[[third-factor|Third factors]]:** selection at grant (Australians' applications are granted less often, so their granted patents may be the stronger ones, {B6}); family reach (a patent held only in Australia has one set of fees); firm size.

questions.how: Years in force is the working measure of private value the owner adopted; Australian organisations' patents score higher on it.
Whether it holds within fields says the difference is not only which fields Australians patent in.

prep.what: [[survival-curve|Survival curves]] of granted standard patents by group, with Greenwood intervals for the share in force at 10 and 15 years.
prep.why: A survival curve keeps patents still alive, rather than dropping them ({U36}).

steps: Draw each group's survival curve from grant, for two five-year cohorts.
Read the share in force at 10 and 15 years, with intervals.
Repeat within each technology field with enough patents, and compare the groups field by field.
assumptions: Keeping a patent in force (paying renewals) is a sign the owner values it, as adopted for Stage 2.
limits: Private value, not public value.
Family reach for Australian applicants before FY2010 rests partly on incomplete records ({B55}).
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 with its third factors. A sharper test is each patent's renewal when a fee changed ({B49}).

observations.chapter: 1. Lens: IP rights (one row per right)
observations.original:
**B8 (observational). Australian organisations keep their standard patents longer than overseas organisations do;
individuals, Australian or not, keep them least.** Share of granted standard patents still in force (95% interval):
- **After 10 years:** Australian organisations 78.7% (77.5% to 79.9%) for FY2005 to FY2009 filings and 72.8% (71.5% to
  74.1%) for FY2000 to FY2004; overseas organisations 72.3% (71.9% to 72.6%) and 62.9% (62.5% to 63.3%); Australian
  individuals 66.4% and 55.3%; overseas individuals 68.6% and 55.4%.
- **After 15 years:** Australian organisations 50.3% and 42.4%; overseas organisations 43.9% and 36.8%.
- **Within technology:** in 32 fields with enough patents, Australian organisations keep a higher share to 10 years
  than overseas organisations in all but 9, by a median 4.7 points (from -15.8 to 28.6): the gap is not only a
  matter of which fields Australians patent in.
- **Third factors:** selection at grant (Australians' applications are granted less often, B6, so their granted
  patents may be the stronger ones), family reach (an Australian-only patent has one set of fees, B10), and firm size.
  Every cohort lengthened its patents' lives in the later period, in line with U36.

observations.headline: Technology fields differ in how long their patents are kept, but their order is only moderately stable
observations.statement: The share of standard patents in force after 10 years (FY2005 to FY2009 filings) runs from 59.4% to 81.2% across 35 fields. The fields' order agrees between the two periods with a rank correlation of only 0.459.

figures.label: in force after 10 years, across 35 fields
agreement of the fields' order between two periods

points: A weak [[replication]]: field differences in lifetimes are kept as a lead only together with {B8}.

questions.how: Whether the field a patent is in is a condition for how long it is valued; only weakly, on this evidence.

prep.what: The same survival curves as {B8}, by technology field (WIPO's 35 fields).
prep.why: Fields are the natural unit for comparing technologies.

steps: Read each field's share in force after 10 years, in each period.
Rank the fields in each period and compare the two orders.
assumptions: WIPO's 35 fields group patents in a way that means the same in both periods.
limits: A moderate agreement means a field's position can change between periods.
observations.next: Field is a [[third-factor]] in Stage 3, not a signal on its own.

observations.original:
**B9 (descriptive). Technology areas differ in how long their patents are kept, but the order is only moderately
stable.** Share in force after 10 years, FY2005 to FY2009, from 59.4% to 81.2% across the 35 fields (chart above). The
fields' order agrees between the two periods with a Spearman rho of 0.459: a weak replication, so field differences in
lifetimes are kept as a lead only together with B8.

observations.headline: Overseas organisations renew trade marks and designs most, Australian individuals least, and Australians who file alone far less
observations.statement: Of trade marks filed FY2010 to FY2015, 56.3% of overseas organisations' were in force after 10 years, 45.9% of Australian organisations' and 26.0% of Australian individuals'. Among Australian filers, 52.0% of marks filed with an attorney were kept, against 28.6% filed alone.

figures.label: trade marks in force after 10 years, overseas organisations against Australian individuals
Australians' marks kept, with an attorney against alone
designs in force after 5 years, overseas organisations against Australian individuals

points: The earlier period (FY2003 to FY2009) gives much the same: 56.3%, 44.6% and 27.7%; with an attorney 52.1%, alone 30.2%.
Designs in force after 5 years (FY2010 to FY2019): Australian organisations 44.4%; Australians with an attorney 47.2%, alone 28.9%.
Every [[interval]] is within about 1 point, and the differences hold in both periods.

questions.how: Renewal is a sign of private value for trade marks and designs, as years in force is for patents.
Australian individuals and lone filers keep their rights least, another sign of who the system serves less.
Adds renewal to grant ({B6}) as an outcome that goes with representation.

prep.what: Survival curves of trade marks from filing and of designs from filing, by filer and by representation.
prep.why: Trade marks are renewed every ten years and designs at five, so those are the natural points to read.

steps: Read the share in force at 10 years (trade marks) and 5 years (designs) for each group, in two periods.
Repeat for Australian filers by representation.
assumptions: Renewing a mark or design is a sign its owner values it.
limits: The survival of the business behind a mark is not in these data, and individuals file alone most ({B5}).
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3, with applicant type as the main [[third-factor]].

observations.original:
**B10 (observational). Trade marks and designs: overseas organisations renew most, Australian individuals least, and
Australians who file alone renew far less.**
- **Trade marks in force after 10 years** (filed FY2010 to FY2015; FY2003 to FY2009): overseas organisations 56.3%
  (56.3%), Australian organisations 45.9% (44.6%), overseas individuals 38.0% (40.6%), Australian individuals 26.0%
  (27.7%). Among Australian filers: with an attorney 52.0% (52.1%), through another agent 34.6% (30.3%), alone 28.6%
  (30.2%).
- **Designs in force after 5 years** (filed FY2010 to FY2019; FY2005 to FY2009): overseas organisations 69.9% (62.1%),
  Australian organisations 44.4% (46.4%), Australian individuals 28.3% (27.1%); Australians with an attorney 47.2%
  (50.8%), alone 28.9% (28.8%).
- Every interval is within about 1 point. The differences hold in both periods. **Third factors:** applicant type
  (individuals file alone most, B5) and the survival of the business behind a mark, which these data do not hold.

observations.headline: Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries than overseas filers', though the gap has narrowed
observations.statement: Of standard patents filed FY2010 to FY2019, 40.71% of Australian organisations' were filed only in Australia, against 8.23% of overseas organisations'. 22.6% reached five or more offices, against 69.58%; 32.8% were granted in the United States, against 67.13%.

figures.label: Australian organisations' patents filed only in Australia (FY2010 to FY2019)
overseas organisations'
granted in the United States

points: Australian individuals: 59.91% only in Australia.
In FY2000 to FY2009: Australian organisations 73.02% only in Australia, five or more offices 13.07%, a US grant 15.79%. Most of that fall is a gap in older records, not a change in practice ({B55}).

questions.how: How far a patent family reaches is a sign of the value its owner expects; Australian organisations expect less, or protect less abroad.
Reach is the main condition behind citation differences ({B12}).

prep.what: Each standard patent's [[patent-family]] from Google Patents: the offices it was filed in, and whether it was granted in the United States ({U92}).
prep.why: A family shows where else the same invention was protected.

steps: For each group of filer, find the share of patents filed only in Australia, in five or more offices, and granted in the US.
Compare the two decades.
assumptions: Google Patents holds each family's filings abroad completely; this fails for older Australian families ({B55}).
limits: Reach is chosen and paid for by owners, so it measures expected private value.
For Australian applicants, read from FY2010 only.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 for FY2010 on.

observations.original:
**B11 (observational). Australian organisations' patents reach fewer countries than overseas filers', though the gap
has narrowed.** Standard patents, FY2010 to FY2019 (FY2000 to FY2009):
- **Filed only in Australia:** Australian organisations 40.71% (73.02%), Australian individuals 59.91% (87.31%),
  overseas organisations 8.23% (7.34%), each within about a point.
- **Five or more offices:** Australian organisations 22.6% (13.07%), overseas organisations 69.58% (72.35%).
- **Granted in the United States:** Australian organisations 32.8% (15.79%), overseas organisations 67.13% (61.93%).
- The gap holds in both decades, but Australian organisations' share filed only here fell from 73.02% to 40.71%. Whether that
  is a change in practice or in how fully Google Patents holds older Australian-only families is not shown here (a
  lead).

observations.headline: Australians' patents are cited less within their field and year, and most of the gap goes with how far they reach
observations.statement: On a scale where 50 is a typical patent of the same field and year, overseas organisations' patents score 52.3 for citations within five years, Australian organisations' 32.2 and Australian individuals' 24.1 (FY2010 to FY2019). Among patents of the same reach, the gap shrinks or reverses.

figures.label: citation percentile, overseas against Australian organisations
among patents filed in one office, Australian organisations ahead
among patents filed in five or more offices

points: In FY2000 to FY2009: 53.6, 25.0 and 20.3; among one-office patents 16.0 against 12.6; five or more offices 57.6 against 58.2.
Among patents filed in 2 to 4 offices: 39.9 against 50.7 (42.0 against 52.1).

**So reach is the main [[third-factor]]:** a narrow family is seldom cited wherever it comes from. Since owners choose and pay for reach, citations and reach are two readings of the same expected value, not independent evidence of it.

questions.how: Citations are a sign that an invention is built on by others, one route to public value; for Australians it mostly follows reach.
Reach looks like a condition for being cited.

prep.what: Each patent's citing families within five years ({U94}), turned into a [[percentile]] among patents of the same technology field and filing year.
prep.why: Fields and years are cited at very different rates, so a raw count would compare unlike with unlike.

Average the ranks for each group of filer.
Repeat within bands of family reach.
assumptions: Citations within five years are comparable across fields once ranked within them.
limits: Older Australian families' reach is incomplete in the records ({B55}), so the earlier decade is less reliable.

observations.headline: Expedited patents seem to last longer, but only because of who asks; within each kind of filer the link is mixed
observations.statement: Pooled, 76.8% of expedited standard patents (FY2010 to FY2016) were in force after 10 years, against 68.7% of others; but in FY2003 to FY2009 it was 68.7% against 71.3%. The pooled link comes from a change in who asks for [[expedited]] examination ([[simpsons-paradox|Simpson's paradox]]); only for overseas organisations does it hold in both periods.

figures.label: expedited against other patents in force after 10 years, FY2010 to FY2016
overseas organisations' examined patents that were expedited, before and from FY2010
overseas organisations, expedited against not (FY2010 to FY2016)

points: Overseas organisations: 78.5% against 71.1% in FY2003 to FY2009 too. Australian organisations: 80.2% against 77.0%, then 69.9% against 79.1%. Australian individuals: 64.6% against 70.7%, then 54.1% against 68.8% (expedited patents kept less).
As overseas organisations, who keep patents longer, became most of the expedited, the pooled figure rose.
**Expedited applications are granted more often** in every group: Australian organisations 69.75% against 57.0%, overseas organisations 82.53% against 76.18% (FY2010 on).
IP Australia's commissioned study found expedited patents kept longer (ADR 0024); here that holds for overseas organisations only.

questions.how: Expedited examination is a service IP Australia offers; whether it goes with longer-lived rights is a question about its value.
Tests a value signal (years in force) against a choice the filer makes.

prep.what: Survival curves of granted standard patents, expedited or not, pooled and by filer, in two periods.
prep.why: Splitting by filer shows whether the pooled link is real or a change in who is in each group.

steps: Compare expedited and other patents pooled, in each period.
Repeat within each group of filer.
Measure how the share of expedited patents changed in each group between the periods.
assumptions: The expedite request is recorded as made ({U34} found trade mark records changed; patents' did not).
limits: The urgency behind a request (a product on the market, a dispute) is not recorded, and could explain both.
observations.next: Recorded, not carried as a pooled signal; Stage 3 reads it by filer only.

observations.original:
**B13 (observational). Expedited standard patents last longer in the later period but not the earlier one; the
pooled link is a composition effect, and it holds only for overseas organisations.**
- **Pooled:** expedited patents in force after 10 years 76.8% (76.0% to 77.5%) against 68.7% (68.5% to 69.0%) for
  FY2010 to FY2016 filings, but 68.7% against 71.3% for FY2003 to FY2009: the association does not replicate.
- **By filer:** overseas organisations 77.4% against 68.4% (FY2010 to FY2016) and 78.5% against 71.1% (FY2003 to
  FY2009), higher in both; Australian organisations 80.2% against 77.0%, then 69.9% against 79.1%;
  Australian individuals 64.6% against 70.7%, then 54.1% against 68.8% (expedited patents kept less).
- **Who asks changed:** 0.84% of overseas organisations' examined patents were expedited in FY2003 to FY2009 and 8.0%
  from FY2010; Australian individuals 19.66% and 19.9%. As overseas organisations, who keep patents longer, became most
  of the expedited, the pooled figure rose: Simpson's paradox.
- **Expedited applications are granted more often** in every group: for example Australian organisations 69.75%
  against 57.0%, overseas organisations 82.53% against 76.18% (FY2010 on).
- IP Australia's commissioned study found expedited patents kept longer (ADR 0024); here that holds for overseas
  organisations only. Third factors: the filer (above), the urgency behind a request (a product on the market, a
  dispute), which the data do not record.

observations.headline: Most firm leads describe who is in the lens or how the registers work; a few are substantive
observations.statement: Several leads reflect how the lens was built: a government supplier has fewer trade marks (a median 0 against 1), because a firm without a contract is in the lens only if it has IP or another link. The substantive ones: larger firms claim more R&D and report more income, public companies claim far more R&D than private ones, and firms that hold patents also hold designs.

figures.label: median R&D claimed, public against proprietary companies
how much more often than chance patent holders also hold designs
R&D spend with total income, among large taxpayers who claim R&D

points: **How the lens was built:** entity type goes with rights held (0.365; 0.366) and with whether an older firm's age is cut short (0.441; 0.438), which is how ABNs began in 1999 and 2000.
R&D spend rises with contract value (0.176; 0.184), and government suppliers cluster in the ACT (a median of 1 contract against 0 in NSW).
The R&D and income pair is 0.346 in the other half: it holds, smaller.

questions.how: Separates who is in the lens from what goes with filing, so later firm findings are not artefacts of how firms were found.
Firm size and form appear as conditions tied to R&D and IP together.

prep.what: Each lead set beside how firms enter the lens (IP, R&D claims, contracts, large taxpayers' reports).
prep.why: A firm's way into the lens can make two measures go together by itself.

steps: Read each firm lead and ask whether the way the lens was built would produce it.
Set those aside, and plan proper measurements for the rest.
assumptions: The judgement of which leads are construction is the analyst's, stated so it can be checked.
limits: Firm size (employees, turnover) is not in the lens for most firms, and is the main [[third-factor]].
observations.next: The substantive leads are measured in {B22} to {B26}.

observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**B21 (observational). Most firm leads describe who is in the lens, or the registers' mechanics; a few are
substantive.**
- **How the lens was built:** a government supplier has fewer trade marks (a median 0 against 1; 0.316 in both halves),
  because a firm without a contract is in the lens only if it has IP or another link; entity type goes with rights
  held (0.365; 0.366) and with whether an older business's age is truncated (0.441; 0.438: local government 15.9 times
  chance), which is how ABNs began in 1999 and 2000.
- **Substantive, and followed up below:** larger firms both claim more R&D and report more income (average R&D spend ×
  total income, rho 0.485, interval 0.406 to 0.552, among the few firms that are both large taxpayers and claimants; 0.346
  in the other half); public
  companies claim far more R&D than proprietary ones (a median $1.381m against $0.297m; 0.225; 0.232); firms that hold
  patents also hold designs (5.5 times chance; 0.247; 0.248); R&D spend rises with contract value (0.176; 0.184); and
  government suppliers cluster in the ACT (a median of 1 contract against 0 in NSW; 0.229 in both halves).

observations.headline: Among firms that came in another way, filing IP goes with being a company, older and in a city
observations.statement: Of active R&D Tax Incentive claimants, 51.41% have filed IP; of government suppliers, 25.02%; of large taxpayers, 40.45%. Among suppliers, public companies have filed in 65.1% of cases and sole traders in 1.2%; firms in major cities 27.8% against 8.4% in very remote areas.

figures.label: R&D claimants that have filed IP
government suppliers that have filed, public companies against sole traders
suppliers that have filed, most disadvantaged to most advantaged tenth of postcodes

points: Trade marks dominate: 45.26%, 23.75% and 39.35% have filed one; standard patents 12.26%, 3.12% and 7.54%.
**Age:** claimants under 3 years old 26.9%, 20 years or more 67.4%. Age is partly time: an older firm has had longer to file.

**Advantage:** for suppliers the share rises steadily with the postcode's advantage (0.806 over the tenths; 0.782 in the other half). For R&D claimants there is no gradient (48.47% to 50.92%): once a firm does R&D, where it is registered does not go with filing.
Each figure held in the other half (for example 51.89%, 25.09% and 41.2% overall).

questions.how: Shows which firms already in contact with government (through R&D claims or contracts) have not used the IP system.
Small, young and regional firms that do business with government but have not filed are a reachable group.

prep.what: Active ABNs that entered the lens through an R&D claim, a government contract or a large taxpayer's report, with whether each has filed IP as a founding applicant.
prep.why: These firms are known to exist and be active, whether or not they have filed.

steps: For each way in, find the share of firms that have filed any IP, and each kind.
Split by entity group, age, remoteness and the advantage of the postcode.
Check every figure in the other half.
assumptions: A firm's registered postcode stands for where it is ({U47}).
limits: [[third-factor|Third factors]]: firm size (companies, older and city firms are larger), industry (not in the business register) and where a firm registers rather than works.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 with size and industry, now known for large employers only ({B50}, {B51}).
observations.section: 2.1 Who files IP, among firms that came in through another door
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**B22 (observational). Among firms that came in through another door, filing IP goes with being a company, older, and
in a city; and, for government suppliers, with an advantaged postcode.** Active ABNs, discovery half (replication):
- **Overall:** 51.41% of R&D Tax Incentive claimants have filed IP (51.89%), 25.02% of government suppliers (25.09%),
  and 40.45% of the large taxpayers (41.2%). Trade marks dominate: 45.26%, 23.75% and 39.35% have filed one; standard
  patents 12.26%, 3.12% and 7.54%.
- **Entity group (government suppliers):** public companies 65.1% (63.7%), private companies 31.4% (31.2%), trusts
  7.2% (8.0%), partnerships 6.5% (6.1%), sole traders 1.2% (1.3%). Claimants: public companies 63.8% (64.7%), private
  50.7% (51.1%).
- **Age:** claimants under 3 years old 26.9% (30.3%), 20 years or more 67.4% (66.6%); suppliers 3.2% (2.9%) and
  35.7% (35.6%). Age is partly time: an older firm has had longer to file.
- **Remoteness (suppliers):** major cities 27.8% (28.0%), inner regional 17.1% (16.4%), very remote 8.4% (8.3%).
- **Advantage of postcode:** for suppliers the share rises steadily from 20.2% in the most disadvantaged tenth of
  postcodes to 27.14% in the most advantaged (Spearman rho over the deciles 0.806; 0.782 in the other half). For R&D
  claimants there is no gradient (rho 0.236, then -0.055; 48.47% to 50.92%, then 55.38% to 52.74%): once a firm does
  R&D, where it is registered does not go with filing.
- **Third factors:** firm size (companies, older firms and city firms are larger), industry (not in the ABR), and
  where a business is registered rather than where it works (U47).

observations.headline: More R&D spend goes with patenting, but only weakly; about half of R&D claimants have never filed IP at any spend
observations.statement: Among 17,514 active R&D claimants, 9.5% of the lowest-spending tenth have filed a standard patent, rising to 24.1% of the highest-spending tenth. The rank correlation between spend and patent applications is only 0.120. 54% of the lowest spenders and 45.5% of the highest have never filed IP.

figures.label: claimants that have filed a standard patent, lowest to highest tenth of R&D spend
spend with patent applications (small)
claimants under 3 years old that have never filed (missing filers)

points: The lowest tenth spends a median $44,790 a year; the highest $3.79m.

**Missing filers** (no IP as a founding applicant) are most common among young claimants (under 3 years: 74.4%) and least among the oldest (20 years or more: 35.8%); more common in private companies (51.4%) than public ones (39.9%); somewhat more in outer regional areas (62.1%) than major cities (50.3%). They do not vary with the postcode's advantage.

**An upper bound for older firms:** IPLORD links 54.3% of the oldest missing filers to IP that IP RAPID gives no ABN, against none under 3 years old, so among young claimants the count is close to exact.
The other half agrees: 9.8% and 24.3%; spend with patents 0.128.

questions.how: Young private companies that do R&D but have never filed IP are a clear group where an intervention could add most.
R&D is only loosely tied to patenting, so R&D alone is a weak condition for IP.

prep.what: Claimants ranked into tenths by recorded R&D spend.
prep.why: Spend is very uneven; tenths show the shape without being pulled by the largest.

steps: For each tenth of spend, find the share that has filed a standard patent and the share that has never filed.
Find the share of missing filers by age, entity group, remoteness and advantage.
Check with IPLORD how many missing filers have IP that IP RAPID does not link to their ABN.
assumptions: A claimant with no IP linked by ABN has not filed, except where IPLORD finds otherwise.
limits: Industry, which the business register does not give, is the main missing [[third-factor]].
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 as a signal for Q4; among large employers, size does not explain the weak link ({B51}).
observations.section: 2.2 IP and R&D: spend, and the claimants who have never filed ('missing filers')
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**B23 (observational). More R&D spend goes with patenting, but only weakly; about half of claimants have never filed
IP at any spend.** 17,514 active claimants with a recorded spend:
- **Standard patents:** 9.5% of the lowest-spending tenth of claimants (median $44,790 a year) have filed one, rising
  to 24.1% of the highest-spending tenth (median $3.79m); 9.8% and 24.3% in the other half. Spearman's rho between
  spend and patent applications is 0.120 (0.128): small.
- **Never filed IP:** 54% of the lowest-spending tenth and 45.5% of the highest (54% and 44.4%).
- **Missing filers (no IP as a founding applicant)** are most common among young claimants (under 3 years: 74.4%;
  71.3%) and least among the oldest (20 years or more: 35.8%; 36.7%), more common among private companies (51.4%;
  51.1%) than public ones (39.9%; 39.8%), and somewhat more common in outer regional areas (62.1%; 56.8%) than in
  major cities (50.3%; 50.2%). They do not vary with the advantage of the postcode (from 45.6% to 53.3% across the
  deciles, with no order).
- **An upper bound for older firms:** IPLORD links 54.3% (56.2%) of the oldest missing filers to IP that IP RAPID
  gives no ABN, against 10.4% (9.8%) of those 3 to 10 years old and none under 3. Among young claimants the count is
  close to exact.
- **So** the claimants who do R&D but have never filed IP are mostly young private companies, wherever they are: a lead
  for Q4 (where an intervention could add most), with industry, which the ABR does not give, as the main missing third
  factor.

observations.headline: Government suppliers that have filed IP win more and larger contracts, within every kind of entity
observations.statement: Suppliers that have filed IP have a median 3 contracts against 2, and a median contract value of $273,400 against $113,800 (a difference of $159,700). Large taxpayers with IP do not report clearly more income ($214.6m against $186.8m, and not in the other half).

figures.label: median contract value, suppliers with IP against without
the difference (interval $135,700 to $185,000)
median contracts

points: The other half: $277,300 against $110,000.
Within entity groups the gap holds in both halves for private companies, public companies, government bodies and other entities; for trusts it is negligible.
Large taxpayers' other half: $204.0m against $200.2m, an interval that includes no difference: not a lead.
**Not a cause:** IP and contracts may both follow from a firm's size and capability.

questions.how: Firms with IP win more of government's business, a sign of who benefits from public purchasing.
Holding IP goes with commercial success in one measurable market, though size could explain both.

prep.what: Each supplier's contracts from AusTender, summed by ABN; large taxpayers' income from the ATO's transparency data.
prep.why: Contracts and income are the two firm outcomes the lens holds.

steps: Compare the median number and value of contracts for suppliers with and without IP, with bootstrap intervals.
Repeat within each entity group, in both halves.
Compare large taxpayers' median income with and without IP.
assumptions: Contract values are as recorded, in dollars of the day.
limits: Firm size is not in the lens for most firms and is the main [[third-factor]].
Some AusTender amendments are missing from the corpus (ADR 0034), mostly for contracts that ended before 2019.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 with firm size where known.
observations.section: 2.3 IP and government contracts, and income
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**B24 (observational). Government suppliers that have filed IP win more and larger contracts, within every kind of
entity; large taxpayers with IP do not report clearly more income.**
- **Suppliers:** a median 3 contracts against 2 (both halves) and a median contract value of $273,400 against
  $113,800 (a difference of $159,700, interval $135,700 to $185,000; rank-biserial 0.205); replication $277,300 against
  $110,000 (0.212).
- **Within entity groups** the gap holds in both halves: private companies (rank-biserial 0.114; 0.126), public
  companies (0.2; 0.214), government bodies (0.387; 0.317), other entities (0.27; 0.265); for trusts it is negligible
  (0.044; 0.065).
- **Large taxpayers:** median income $214.6m with IP against $186.8m without (rank-biserial 0.079), and $204.0m against
  $200.2m in the other half (0.04; interval -$8.3m to $19.5m, which includes no difference): not a lead.
- **Not a cause:** IP and contracts may both follow from a firm's size and capability. Firm size (employees, turnover)
  is not in the lens; it is the main candidate third factor.

observations.headline: Firms file their first trade mark early, and their first patent or design later
observations.statement: Among firms first seen in 2001 or later, the first trade mark came a median 2.03 years after the firm's first public registration, and 39.61% within the first year. The first standard patent came a median 4.62 years after, and the first design 4.72 years.

figures.label: median age at first trade mark
median age at first standard patent
first trade marks filed within the firm's first year

points: 13.39% of first standard patents came within the first year; 28.42% after 10 years or more (16.71% for trade marks).
The other half agrees: 2.06, 4.76 and 4.23 years.
Age counts from the first public registration (ABN, GST or ASIC), a [[lower-bound]] on when the business began ({U43}).

questions.how: Shows when firms first come to IP, the moment an intervention aimed at new filers would meet them.

prep.what: Firms first seen in 2001 or later, so their age is not cut short by when ABNs began.
prep.why: Older firms' registrations start in 1999 and 2000, whatever their real age ({U43}).

steps: For each firm, find its first filing of each type from FY2010.
Measure the years since its first public registration, and summarise by type.
assumptions: The first public registration is close to when a young business began.
limits: Lower bounds on age; a business may trade before it registers.
observations.next: Read beside {B26} and the missing filers ({B23}) in Stage 3.
observations.section: 2.4 How old firms are when they first file
observations.chapter: 2. Lens: Firms (one row per ABN)
observations.original:
**B25 (descriptive). Firms file their first trade mark early, their first patent or design later.** Firms first seen
in 2001 or later, first filings FY2010 to FY2026 (other half):
- **Trade marks:** a median 2.03 years after the firm's first public registration (2.06); 39.61% (39.26%) within the
  first year; 16.71% (17.05%) after 10 years or more.
- **Standard patents:** a median 4.62 years (4.76); 13.39% (13.42%) within the first year; 28.42% (28.32%) after 10
  years or more.
- **Designs:** a median 4.72 years (4.23).
- Age counts from the first public registration (ABN, GST or ASIC), a lower bound on the business's start (U43), so
  these are lower bounds on age at first filing.

observations.headline: Patents filed by the youngest firms move overseas more often, in both periods, though the numbers are small
observations.statement: Of standard patents filed from Australia by firms under 2 years old, 5.72% (33 of 577) are now held only overseas for FY2003 to FY2011 filings and 3.93% (37 of 941) for FY2012 to FY2021. Firms 2 to 5 years old: 1.93% and 2.13%.

figures.label: youngest firms' patents now held only overseas (FY2003 to FY2011)
the same, FY2012 to FY2021
firms 2 to 5 years old (FY2003 to FY2011)

points: Intervals 4.1% to 7.92% and 2.87% to 5.37%.
5 to 10 years: 4.72% and 1.34%; 10 years or more: 3.29% and 2.33%.
The youngest firms' patents are not the widest (12.31% and 20.62% filed in five or more offices, against 15.63% to 26.69% for older firms'), so reach does not explain the gap.

questions.how: Young firms' inventions are more often owned abroad later, another route by which value made here is captured elsewhere.
Points to young firms as the place where keeping value in Australia is most at stake.

prep.what: Each patent's filing firm and its age at filing, beside the patent's current holders ({B19}).
prep.why: Links the move overseas to the firm that made the invention.

steps: Group patents by the filing firm's age at filing.
Find the share now held only overseas, with intervals, in two periods.
Check whether reach explains the difference.
assumptions: A patent held only by overseas owners has been sold or transferred abroad.
limits: Small numbers. The likely [[third-factor|third factors]], the sale of young firms to overseas buyers and founders moving abroad, are not in the data.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 as a lead for Q1 that needs care.

observations.original:
**B26 (observational). Patents filed by the youngest firms move overseas more often, in both periods, though the
numbers are small.** Standard patents filed from Australia by a firm first seen in 2001 or later, now held only
overseas:
- **Firms under 2 years old when they filed:** 5.72% (33 of 577; interval 4.1% to 7.92%) for FY2003 to FY2011 filings,
  3.93% (37 of 941; 2.87% to 5.37%) for FY2012 to FY2021.
- **Firms 2 to 5 years old:** 1.93% and 2.13%; **5 to 10 years:** 4.72% and 1.34%; **10 years or more:** 3.29% and

  overseas buyers, and founders moving abroad; neither is in the data. A lead for Q1, small enough to need Stage 3's

observations.headline: Among employers of 100 or more, filing rises with size; the largest are 22 points more likely to have filed a standard patent
observations.statement: Of 7,126 firms with a WGEA report, 0.109 of those under 250 employees have filed a standard patent, against 0.328 of those with 5,000 or more: 22 points (interval 14.6 to 30.3), rising band by band. Any right: 0.701 to 0.825.

figures.label: share that has filed a standard patent, under 250 to 5,000 or more employees
the difference (14.6 to 30.3)
share that has filed any right

points: A trade mark: 0.685 to 0.81 (12.6 points).
As rank correlations with headcount the pairs are weak in both halves (0.056 to 0.093, under the screen's 0.1): the rise is steady but small beside the spread within each band.

questions.how: Size goes with using the IP system even among large employers.
Firm size is a condition for patenting, one of the third factors earlier firm leads needed.

prep.what: Each firm's size band and industry from its WGEA report ({U112}).
prep.why: WGEA is the only free source of size and industry by ABN, for employers of 100 or more.

steps: Group firms with a report by size band.
Find the share in each band that has filed a standard patent, a trade mark or any right, with intervals.
assumptions: The size band in the latest report stands for the firm's size.
limits: Employers of 100 or more only (4.05% of patent filers); small firms still have no size ([[wgea]], ADR 0032).
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 as a third factor among large employers.

observations.headline: Across postal areas the kinds of IP move together, and with education and occupation more than income
observations.statement: Postal areas that file more standard patents per person also file more provisionals (rank correlation 0.765) and trade marks (0.693). Of the four SEIFA indexes, education and occupation goes with filing most (0.665 with IP-filing firms per business, 0.455 with standard patents per person); median income goes with patents at 0.287.

figures.label: distinct leads, 75 of them about IP or R&D
education and occupation index with IP-filing firms per business
agreement between the two halves of the areas

points: Areas with more GST-registered businesses per person file more standard patents (0.513; 0.626).
IP-filing firms and R&D claimants, per business, are the strongest pair (0.884; 0.909).
**Missing filers are rarer where filing is common:** the share of R&D claimants that have never filed falls with designs (-0.259) and standard patents (-0.229) per business.
Rates are shown only where 10 or more applications are expected ({U53}), so these pairs cover the larger areas (431 areas for standard patents per person in the first half).

questions.how: Filing is concentrated in places with more educated, professional residents, a first view of which communities benefit.
Areas where R&D firms rarely file are where filing is rare generally.

prep.what: Postal areas split into two halves by a fixed rule (1,377 and 1,264 areas).
prep.why: Places have no second period in the lens, so a random half is the [[replication]] sample.

steps: Screen every pair of the lens's own columns in one half, and check it in the other.
Read which kinds of IP go together, and which area characteristics go with each.
assumptions: A filer's postcode places its filing ({U47}).
limits: Between places, not people: an area's residents and its filers need not be the same people.
observations.next: The attached indicators are screened in {B28}; advantage and remoteness are modelled in {B29}.
observations.section: 3.0 The screen: every pair of the lens's own columns
observations.chapter: 3. Lens: Places (one row per postal area)
observations.original:
**B27 (observational). The places lens: 124 distinct leads, 75 of them about IP or R&D; the IP measures move together,
and with education and occupation more than income.** Postal areas in two halves (1,377 and 1,264); 269 pairs are
leads, 16 hold in one half only, and the halves agree with a Spearman rho of 0.961.
- **The kinds of IP go together across places:** standard patents and provisionals per person (rho 0.765; 0.779 in
  the other half), standard patents and trade marks (0.693; 0.718), trade marks and designs (0.688; 0.706). Firms
  that have filed IP and R&D claimants, per business, are the strongest pair (0.884; 0.909).
- **Of the four SEIFA indexes, education and occupation (IEO) goes with filing most:** with IP-filing firms per
  business 0.665 (0.674), trade marks per person 0.64 (0.679), R&D claimants 0.568 (0.599), provisionals 0.534
  (0.579), standard patents 0.455 (0.476) and designs 0.409 (0.415). Median personal income, by comparison, goes
  with standard patents at 0.287 (0.364).
- **Business density:** areas with more GST-registered businesses per person file more standard patents (0.513;
  0.626).
- **Missing filers are rarer where filing is common:** the share of R&D claimants that have never filed IP falls with
  designs (rho -0.259; strength 0.224 in the other half, in the same direction) and standard patents (-0.229; 0.192)
  per business.
- Every rate is shown only where 10 or more applications are expected (U53), so these pairs cover the larger areas
  (431 areas for standard patents per person in the discovery half), and they are between places, not firms.

observations.headline: Most attached indicators go with filing along one broad gradient of advantage, education and business density
observations.statement: 6,406 area indicators from five sources were set against six filing rates: 24,792 pairs are leads in both halves. Standard patents per person go most with finance, professional and large businesses per resident, and least with single mothers receiving Parenting Payment; trade marks most with professional businesses and Year 12 completion.

figures.label: indicators screened against filing
leads in both halves
professional, scientific and technical businesses per resident with trade marks per person

points: Standard patents per person: businesses with a turnover of $2m or more (0.593), financial and insurance businesses (0.575); most negative, single mothers receiving Parenting Payment (-0.482) and children whose mothers have low educational attainment (-0.477).
Trade marks per person: Year 12 completion (0.697), bachelor degrees (0.685), house prices (0.689); most negative, Year 9 as the highest year of school (-0.598) and land area (-0.594).

observations.headline: Filing rises steeply with advantage and falls with remoteness; both hold when read together
observations.statement: For each [[standard-deviation]] of advantage (the IRSAD score), a postal area files 1.717 times as many standard patents per person (1.857 in the other half; 1.884 pooled into SA3s). Inner regional areas file at 0.259 of major cities' rate. With both in one model, advantage's ratio is 1.442 and inner regional areas still file at 0.382.

figures.label: standard patents, the rate ratio per standard deviation of advantage
inner regional areas' rate against major cities'
the advantage ratio with remoteness allowed for

points: Trade marks 1.648 (1.707; 1.477), designs 1.504, provisionals 1.582. Very remote areas file standard patents at 0.173 of the cities' rate.

**The shape is not a straight line:** standard patents run 0.33 to 0.75 a year per 10,000 people across deciles 1 to 8, then 1.51 to 1.62 in deciles 9 and 10. Most of the gradient is in the most advantaged fifth of areas; trade marks rise more steadily (7.63 to 29.24).
A few city-centre postcodes with many filers and few residents (Sydney's 2000) make the top decile fragile (1.62 against 3.37 between halves); the model's ratio is the steadier reading.
The spread between areas is large (alpha 1.354 and 1.65 for standard patents), as {U53} found, which is why a [[negative-binomial]] model is used.

questions.how: Advantaged and city areas file far more, a measure of whose communities take part in the IP system.
Regional and disadvantaged areas are where filing is lowest, if access is the question.

prep.what: Area counts of applications modelled with the area's people as the exposure, in a negative binomial model that allows for extra spread.
prep.why: Counts in small areas vary far more than chance alone would make them ({U53}).

steps: Model each type's count on the area's IRSAD score, then on remoteness, then on both.
Repeat in the other half and pooled into SA3s.
Compare pooled rates by decile of advantage to see the shape.
assumptions: Applications are counted at the filer's postcode, and people from the Census.
limits: [[third-factor|Third factors]]: business density and mix ({B31}), education ({B28}), and where firms register ({U47}).
Between places, not people.

observations.original:
**B29 (observational). Filing rises steeply with advantage and falls with remoteness; both hold when read together,
in both halves and pooled into SA3s.** Negative binomial rate ratios, per standard deviation of the IRSAD score
(discovery; replication; SA3s):
- **Standard patents:** 1.717 (1.597 to 1.845); 1.857 (1.717 to 2.008); 1.884 (1.728 to 2.055). **Trade marks:** 1.648;
  1.707; 1.477. **Designs:** 1.504; 1.639; 1.672. **Provisionals:** 1.582; 1.823; 1.771.
- **Remoteness, against major cities** (standard patents): inner regional areas file at 0.259 (0.252) of the cities'
  rate, very remote areas at 0.173 (0.06); trade marks 0.369 (0.338) and 0.201 (0.158).
- **Together:** with remoteness in the model, the IRSAD ratio for standard patents falls to 1.442 (1.326 to 1.567) and
  1.49 (1.357 to 1.635), and inner regional areas still file at 0.382 (0.38) of the cities' rate at the same
  advantage; trade marks 1.392 and 1.406, designs 1.199 and 1.266. Each accounts for part of the other, and both stay.
- **The shape is not a straight line:** pooled rates of standard patents are 0.33 to 0.75 a year per 10,000 people
  across deciles 1 to 8 (0.37 to 0.93 in the other half), then 1.51 to 1.62 in deciles 9 and 10 (1.48 to 3.37). Most
  of the gradient is in the most advantaged fifth of areas; trade marks rise more steadily (7.63 to 29.24; 6.62 to
  52.18). The top decile differs most between the halves (1.62 against 3.37 for standard patents) because a few
  city-centre postcodes with many filers and few residents (Sydney's 2000, U53) fall in one half: pooled rates there
  are fragile, and the model's ratio is the steadier reading.
- The spread is large (alpha 1.354 and 1.65 for standard patents), as U53 found, which is why a negative binomial is
  used. Candidate third factors: business density and mix (3.4), education (B28), and where firms register (U47).

observations.headline: Areas that gained graduates or income over the decade to 2021 did not gain filing
observations.statement: The median area's share of people with a bachelor degree or higher rose 5.9 points from 2011 to 2021, and its residents' standard patents per person fell. Gaining graduates goes with the change in filing at -0.086 (patents) and -0.124 (trade marks); gaining income at -0.079 and -0.008. All small, all the same sign in both halves.

**So** levels go together ({B29}, {B58}), changes do not: the advantage gradient is a standing difference between places, not one that moves with them.

observations.headline: Across countries, IP filing moves with R&D, research and income as one development gradient, and holds over a decade
observations.statement: Across 160 countries of a million people or more (2016 to 2020), residents' patent applications per million people go with business R&D as a share of GDP (rank correlation 0.844), researchers per million (0.837) and GDP per person (0.769). Residents' trade marks go with GDP per person (0.797) and tertiary enrolment (0.804), and much less with R&D: trade marks follow commerce, patents follow research.

figures.label: residents' patents per million with business R&D share of GDP
residents' trade marks per million with GDP per person
distinct leads, 134 involving IP or royalties

points: Each held in 2006 to 2010 (for example 0.827 and 0.868).

Patents also go with journal articles (0.817), royalty receipts per person (0.782) and high-technology exports per person (0.755). Manufacturing's share of GDP goes only weakly with residents' patenting (0.201).
**Nothing about IP is unrelated to development**, which is why these are leads for Stage 3's components, not drivers.

questions.how: Sets Australia's IP in the pattern every country follows, the baseline for judging whether it does well or badly.
R&D and income are the broad conditions for patenting across countries.

prep.what: Each indicator as a ratio to people or GDP, averaged over 2016 to 2020 and 2006 to 2010, for countries of a million people or more.
prep.why: Ratios make countries of different size comparable, and two periods give a [[replication]].

steps: Screen every pair of indicators across countries in the later period, and check each in the earlier one.
Read which indicators go with residents' patents and trade marks.
assumptions: Each source's indicator means the same thing in every country.
limits: Between countries, not firms or people; business R&D is measured for OECD members only.

are leads (188 distinct, 134 of them involving an IP measure or royalties), 22 hold in one period only.
- **Residents' patent applications per million people** go with business R&D as a share of GDP (rho 0.844; 0.827 in
  2006 to 2010), researchers per million people (0.837; 0.896), journal articles (0.817; 0.798), royalty receipts per
  person (0.782; 0.811), GDP per person (0.769; 0.747) and high-technology exports per person (0.755; 0.758).
- **Residents' trade marks per million people** go with GDP per person (0.797; 0.868), tertiary enrolment (0.804;
  0.788) and new business density (0.621; 0.734), and much less with R&D (business R&D 0.373; 0.292, marked not
  replicated: business R&D is measured for OECD members only, and with so few countries 0.292 does not pass the
  correction): trade marks follow commerce, patents follow research.

observations.headline: Across OECD members patenting rises with business R&D almost one for one, but changes in R&D barely go with changes in patenting
observations.statement: Across 36 members, residents' patents per person rise with business R&D (rank correlation 0.853; a slope of 1.151 on log scales). Australia filed 103.3 applications per million people in 2016 to 2020, about what its R&D predicts (98.46). But across members the change in patenting over the decade goes with the change in business R&D at only 0.165.

figures.label: business R&D with residents' patents, across members
Australia's patenting against what its R&D predicts (2016 to 2020)
change in R&D with change in patenting

points: In 2006 to 2010 Australia filed 125 against 226.3 predicted (55.22%). The [[prediction-interval|prediction intervals]] are wide (17 to 580), so Australia is within the members' range in both periods: its change in position came from falling R&D, not rising patenting.
23 members' residents filed less over the decade. Australia's patenting fell (a log change of -0.083) as its business R&D fell by 0.34 points of GDP.
**So** the strong link is between countries' levels, which share a long history; within a decade the two do not move together.

questions.how: Raising R&D would not, on this evidence, raise patenting quickly.
Tempers projections that tie patenting outcomes to R&D spending within a policy horizon.

prep.what: A line fitted across members on log scales, of patents per person on business R&D as a share of GDP.
prep.why: On log scales, the slope says how patenting scales with R&D.

steps: Fit the line across members in each period, and predict Australia's patenting from its R&D.
Relate members' changes in R&D to their changes in patenting.
assumptions: Residents' patent applications count invention in the same way across members.
limits: Wide intervals with 34 to 36 members; between countries, not firms.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3; {B61} adds the share of researchers in business.
observations.section: 4.2 Invention against R&D: does Australia patent what its business R&D would suggest?
observations.chapter: 4. Lens: Australia and other countries (one row per country, year and indicator)
observations.original:
**B34 (observational). Across OECD members, residents' patenting rises with business R&D almost one for one; Australia
filed about what its R&D predicts in 2016 to 2020, about half in 2006 to 2010; but changes in R&D barely go with
changes in patenting.**
- **The levels:** Spearman rho 0.853 over 36 members (0.795 over 34 earlier); on log scales the slope is 1.151 (1.106),
  so a member with twice the business R&D share files a little more than twice the patents per person.
- **Australia:** 103.3 patent applications per million people in 2016 to 2020, against 98.46 predicted from its
  business R&D (104.9% of predicted; 95% prediction interval 17 to 580); 125 against 226.3 in 2006 to 2010 (55.22%;
  41 to 1,262). The prediction intervals are wide, so Australia is within the members' range in both periods: its
  change in position came from falling R&D (B33), not rising patenting.
- **The changes:** across 34 members, the change in patenting from 2006-2010 to 2016-2020 goes with the change in
  business R&D at a Spearman rho of only 0.165; 23 members' residents filed less. Australia's patenting fell (a log
  change of -0.083) as its business R&D fell by 0.34 points of GDP.
- **So** the strong link is between countries' levels, which share a long history; within a decade the two do not
  move together. A lead for Q4: raising R&D would not, on this evidence, raise patenting quickly.

Women's share of researchers goes the other way (-0.647), as does the higher-education sector's share of researchers.
