Where research is done more in business, patenting is higher, and business research employs fewer women: a [[third-factor]] pattern to test, not a gender finding.

questions.how: Business research, venture capital and knowledge-intensive jobs are the conditions that go with patenting across countries.

prep.what: Each indicator of the companion table (`national_indicators`) against residents' patenting only.
prep.why: As for places, indicator-to-indicator pairs would serve no question.

steps: Measure each indicator against residents' patents per person, in two halves of the economies.
Keep those past the threshold and correction in both.
assumptions: The GII's and OECD's indicators are comparable across members, as published.
limits: The same development gradient runs through most of them.
observations.next: Stage 3's components, as for {B32}.
observations.section: 4.3 The attachments: every cross-country indicator against residents' patenting
observations.chapter: 4. Lens: Australia and other countries (one row per country, year and indicator)
observations.original:
**B35 (observational). Of the cross-country attachments, about half go with residents' patenting, again along
development: research workforce, knowledge-intensive jobs and business-funded R&D lead, and women's share of
researchers goes the other way.** 485 indicators measured (8 of them counts of patents, not screened); 225 leads: 64 of
79 GII indicator values, 83 of 145 OECD R&D statistics, 66 of 231 well-being indicators, 6 of 8 venture capital
series and 6 of 22 industry and innovation goals.
- **GII 2026** (halves of the economies): researchers per million people 0.856 (0.871), knowledge-intensive employment
  0.814 (0.864), business-performed R&D 0.785 (0.874); the youth share of the population -0.743 (-0.79).
- **OECD R&D statistics:** GERD financed by business, as a share of GDP, 0.841 (0.81); business R&D in the computer,
  electronic and optical industry 0.806 (0.755). Women's share of researchers -0.647 (-0.65), and the higher-education
  sector's share of researchers -0.616 (-0.536): where research is done more in business, patenting is higher, and
  business research employs fewer women, so this is a third-factor pattern to test, not a gender finding.
- **Venture capital:** later-stage venture investment 0.642 (0.673), start-up and early stage 0.61 (0.699).
- **Well-being:** household disposable income 0.695 (0.566); difficulty making ends meet -0.748 (-0.764).

observations.headline: Across OECD members, business-financed R&D and business researchers go with patenting; Australia finances R&D like a middling member but patents like a low one
observations.statement: Across 36 or 37 members, patents per unit of GDP go with GERD financed by business (rank correlation 0.78) and with the share of researchers in business (0.67). With its supplementary values, Australia ranks 17th of 38 on business financing but 28th on patents per GDP, and 31st of 37 on researchers in business.

figures.label: business-financed R&D with patents per GDP
Australia on business financing against patents per GDP
Australia on the share of researchers in business

points: Researchers per million people with patents per GDP: 0.723. Australia ranks 23rd on researchers.
{B34}'s gap holds with the supplementary values; the low share of researchers working in business is a candidate reason, beside industry mix.

questions.how: Where researchers work (business or university) may be a condition for how much research becomes patents.
Points to researchers in business, not R&D funding alone, as the place to look.

prep.what: Four of the six GII indicators blank for Australia filled from Australia's own statistics ({U120}), kept apart from the GII's own rows.
prep.why: Australia's blanks would otherwise drop it from these comparisons.

steps: Relate each GII research measure to patents by origin per GDP across members, with intervals.
Rank Australia on each, with its supplementary values.
assumptions: The supplementary values are close to how the GII would measure them; each differs as {U120} records.
limits: Never used to recalculate a GII score or rank.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 with industry mix.
observations.section: 4.4 The supplementary values against patenting (added after Stage 2, gap B7)
observations.chapter: 4. Lens: Australia and other countries (one row per country, year and indicator)
observations.original:
**B61 (observational). Across OECD members, business-financed R&D and business researchers go with patenting; with its
supplementary values, Australia finances R&D like a middling member but patents like a low one.** Over 36 or 37
members (the GII's latest data years), patents by origin per billion PPP$ GDP (6.1.1) against GERD financed by business:
rho 0.78 (strength interval 0.59 to 0.89); against the share of researchers in business 0.67 (0.41 to 0.85); against
researchers per million people 0.723 (0.51 to 0.87). Australia ranks 17th of 38 on business financing but 28th on
patents per GDP; 31st of 37 on researchers in business, 23rd on researchers.
- **For Stage 3:** B34's gap (Australia patents less than its business R&D suggests) holds with the supplementary
  values; the low share of researchers working in business is a candidate reason, beside industry mix.

observations.headline: As changes, the monthly series hardly move together; the one pair that holds is the trade mark process itself
observations.statement: Every pair of monthly series was screened as quarterly year-on-year changes, in two periods. Only one pair is a lead: trade mark registrations and trade mark oppositions (rank correlation 0.658; 0.588), because more marks reaching the end of examination means more to register and more to oppose.

figures.label: lead among the monthly series
trade mark registrations with oppositions
pairs that are negligible

points: 68 quarters in the first period and 72 in the second; 198 pairs below the correction, 28 measured in too few quarters.
Australians' and overseas applicants' filings do not move together; nor do filings and the CPI, nor filings and the events that follow them a year or more later.
Each series' changes are driven by its own events (rushes, pauses, rule changes), not a common cycle, which is why policy changes are read one by one ({B37}).

questions.how: Shows there is no common cycle to strip out, so each policy change can be read against its own series.

prep.what: Each monthly series turned into year-on-year changes by quarter.
prep.why: Levels of almost any two growing series go together; changes do not unless they are linked.

steps: Screen every pair of series' changes in each period.
Keep pairs past the threshold and correction in both.
assumptions: Quarterly changes smooth the monthly noise without hiding real links.
limits: A link that takes longer than a year to show would be missed.
observations.next: The policy changes are tested one by one in {B37}.
observations.section: 5.0 The screen: every pair of series, as changes
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B36 (observational). As changes, the monthly series hardly move together: one pair holds in both periods, and it is
the trade mark process itself.** 68 quarters in the discovery period and 72 in the replication: 1 lead, 1 pair
that holds in one period only, 178 negligible, 198 below the correction, 28 measured in too few quarters.
- **The one lead:** trade mark registrations and trade mark oppositions (rho 0.658, interval 0.498 to 0.786; 0.588):
  more marks reaching the end of examination means more to oppose and more to register in the same quarters.
- **What does not move together:** Australians' and overseas applicants' filings, as changes (5.3); filings and the
  CPI; filings and the events that follow them a year or more later. Each series' changes are driven by its own
  events (rushes, pauses, rule changes), not a common cycle, which is why Stage 1's 17 policy changes are read one by
  one (5.1).

observations.headline: The two rushes, three of four steps and both 1995 pauses are far outside anything seen at placebo dates
observations.statement: For each policy change, the size of the spike or step in filing was compared with the same measure at up to 72 [[placebo]] months. The rush before Raising the Bar (a spike of 1.476 in logs for Australians' standard patents), the innovation patent's closure (1.459), the 20-year term, the extension of term regime and the Trade Marks Act 1995 were all larger than every placebo month (0%).

figures.label: of placebo months as large as the two rushes
Australians' usual month, in the rush before Raising the Bar
of placebo months as large as the 1991 pause's step (ordinary)

points: **Steps:** the 20-year term (July 1995), patent expiries -3.937; extension of term (January 1999) 2.419; the innovation patent's introduction (May 2001), second-tier applications 0.531; the Designs Act 2003, overseas applicants' designs 0.292. All 0% of placebos.
**Not beyond the ordinary:** Australians' designs after the Designs Act (0.063, 29.17%) and the Patents Act 1990 (April 1991), whose pause came two months after commencement.
**Pauses:** the Trade Marks Act 1995 (January 1996), registrations -7.205 and Australians' applications -0.712, both 0%.

questions.how: These six changes give clean breaks for the natural experiments Q5 needs, each beside series it should not have moved.
Shows which kinds of policy change visibly move filing.

prep.what: For each change, the spike (the change month against the year before) and the step (the year after against the year before), in logs.
prep.why: Logs make a change of the same proportion the same size in a large and a small series.

steps: Measure each change's spike and step in the series it should move.
Repeat at up to 72 placebo months from five years either side.
Report the share of placebo months with a change at least as large.
assumptions: Placebo months show how large an ordinary month-to-month change can be.
limits: A placebo test shows a break is unusual, not what caused it; other events in the same window can contribute.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 and the question designs as the starting points for [[natural-experiment|natural experiments]].
observations.section: 5.1 Before and after each policy change, against placebo dates
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B37 (observational). The two rushes, three of the four steps and both of the 1995 pauses are far outside anything
seen at placebo dates; the Designs Act's effect on Australians and the 1991 pause are not.** For each change, the
share of placebo months (up to 72, from five years either side) with a spike or step at least as large:
- **Rushes:** Raising the Bar (April 2013), Australians' standard patents a spike of 1.476 in logs (4.39 times
  the usual month, U28) and overseas applicants' 0.977, with 0% of placebo months as large; Australians' step after it
  -0.413 (0%), overseas -0.079 (15.28%). The innovation patent's closure (August 2021): a spike of 1.459 and a step of
  -3.17, both 0%.
- **Steps:** the 20-year term (July 1995), patent expiries -3.937 (0% of 36); the extension of term regime (January
  1999) 2.419 (0%); the innovation patent's introduction (May 2001), second-tier applications 0.531 (0%); the Designs
  Act 2003, overseas applicants' designs 0.292 (0%). Australians' designs (0.063, 29.17%) and design registrations
  (0.218, 38.89%) did not step beyond the ordinary.
- **Pauses:** the Trade Marks Act 1995 (January 1996): registrations a spike of -7.205 and Australians' applications
  -0.712, both 0%. The Patents Act 1990 (April 1991): patent grants 0.19 (33.33%), a step of 0.046 (93.06%): the pause
  U28 saw came in June 1991, two months after commencement, so the commencement month itself is ordinary.
- **For Q5:** these six changes give clean breaks for the natural experiments the research goal asks for after Stage
  3, each beside series it should not have moved. The fee changes, IP Australia's most direct lever, are still not in
  the data (R3, OQ2).

observations.headline: Provisionals filed in FY2025 were followed up less often, individuals' by about half, but late recording cannot be ruled out
observations.statement: 6.66% of Australian individuals' provisionals filed in FY2025 were followed by an Australian complete application within 12 months, against 12.24% to 18.76% in FY2018 to FY2024; organisations' 9.49%. But Australian filers' standard patents claiming an Australian application also fell, to 40.48% in FY2026, so if claims are recorded late, both would fall whatever applicants did.

figures.label: individuals' FY2025 provisionals followed up within 12 months
the same, FY2018 to FY2024
Australians' standard patents claiming an Australian application, FY2018 to FY2026

points: Organisations: 9.49% in FY2025, against 10.63% to 20.68% before.
Claims were 55.31% to 60.61% in FY2018 to FY2023, then 53.53%, 49.15% and 40.48%, the same pattern {U90} read as a rise in direct filing.
The individuals' fall is the larger (12.25% to 6.66%, against 12.05% to 9.49%), which fits the surge in individuals' provisionals ({U8}) being ones not pursued; but this is a lead, not a finding.
It adds a question for IP Australia (OQ18): whether priority claims are recorded when an application is filed or only later.

questions.how: If real, many recent provisionals lead nowhere, a possible point for guidance to new filers.
Individuals' provisionals are followed up least.

prep.what: Each provisional linked to any later complete application claiming it, from IP RAPID's links.
prep.why: A provisional lapses after 12 months unless a complete application claims it.

steps: For each year's provisionals, find the share claimed by an Australian complete application within 12 months, with intervals.
Check the share of standard patents claiming an Australian application in the same years.
assumptions: The links record every claim; for the latest years this may not hold.
limits: Late recording would produce the same fall; OQ18 asks IP Australia.
observations.next: Read as a lead only for FY2024 on, until IP Australia answers.
observations.section: 5.2 The provisional rise: how often provisionals are followed up
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B38 (observational). Provisionals filed in FY2025 were followed up less often within 12 months, individuals' by
about half; but priority claims in general are falling in the latest years, so late recording cannot be ruled out.**
- **Followed by an Australian complete application within 12 months:** Australian individuals' provisionals 6.66%
  in FY2025 (interval 5.62% to 7.88%, 1,891 provisionals), against 12.24% to 18.76% in FY2018 to FY2024;
  organisations' 9.49% (8.46% to 10.63%), against 10.63% to 20.68%.
- **But the claims themselves are thinning:** Australian filers' standard patents that claim an Australian
  application were 55.31% to 60.61% in FY2018 to FY2023, then 53.53% (FY2024), 49.15% (FY2025) and 40.48% (FY2026),
  the same pattern U90 read as a rise in direct filing.
- **Reading:** if claims are recorded late, both measures fall for the latest years whatever applicants did. The
  individuals' fall is the larger (from 12.25% in FY2024 to 6.66%, against 12.05% to 9.49% for organisations), which
  fits the surge of U8 being concentrated in individuals' provisionals that are not pursued, but this is a lead, not a
  finding. **It adds a question for IP Australia:** whether priority claims and associated provisionals are recorded
  in IP RAPID when an application is filed or only later (beside OQ5 and U90's lead).

observations.headline: Australians' and overseas applicants' filings do not move together, and no Australia-only annual series moves with Australians' filing
observations.statement: As quarterly changes, Australians' and overseas applicants' trade marks go together only weakly (0.332, then 0.137), and designs and standard patents not at all. Of 568 pairs of an Australia-only annual series with Australians' filing, only 4 pass the correction, and all four are other counts of the same filings.

figures.label: pairs with Australia-only annual series that pass the correction
the World Bank's residents' patent applications with IP RAPID's, over 44 years

points: 336 series with 8 or more years of changes. 54 pairs reach 0.5 or more, but on short series (9 to 14 years), which the correction does not let through.
Overseas filings follow the PCT's 30-month delay and foreign cycles ({U6}).
**So** the Australia-only sources add context, not year-to-year signals about filing.

questions.how: Australia-only economic series are for the context of Stage 3's designs, not for pairing with filing.

prep.what: Each annual series for Australia alone (Measuring What Matters, BCARR and others) as year-on-year changes.
prep.why: Annual series need changes, as the monthly ones do.

steps: Relate Australians' and overseas applicants' changes, in two periods.
Relate each annual series' changes to Australians' filing, with the correction for 568 pairs.
assumptions: Eight years of changes is the least that can show a link.
limits: Short series cannot show any but very strong links.
observations.next: Not carried as pairs; used as context in Stage 3.
observations.section: 5.3 Australian against overseas applicants, and the annual series for Australia alone
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B39 (observational). Australians' and overseas applicants' filings do not move together from quarter to quarter, and
no annual series for Australia alone moves with Australians' filing once the number of series is allowed for.**
- **Australian against overseas, quarterly changes:** trade marks rho 0.332 then 0.137 (below the correction in the
  second period), designs 0.059 and 0.041, standard patents -0.038 then 0.45. Their drivers differ (overseas filings
  follow the PCT's 30-month delay and foreign cycles, U6).
- **Annual series for Australia alone:** 336 series with 8 or more years of changes, 568 pairs with Australians'
  standard patent or trade mark applications. Only 4 pass the correction, and all four are other counts of the same
  filings (the World Bank's residents' patent applications, rho 0.636 over 44 years; residents' and non-residents'
  trade marks, 0.734 to 0.785 over 20 years). 54 pairs reach a rho of 0.5 or more, but on short series (the
  strongest shown have 9 to 14 years), which the correction does not let through.
- **So** the Australian-only sources add context (what Measuring What Matters or BCARR say about the economy), not
  year-to-year signals about filing; their use is in Stage 3's designs, not in pairs.

observations.headline: Changes in the fees to obtain a right rarely moved filing beyond what placebo months show; the clear breaks are new Acts
observations.statement: 18 fee changes of 10% or more (12 rises, 6 cuts) were tested against placebo months: 34 pairs of change and filing series. Filing rushed beyond 95% of its placebo months 4 times and stepped 3 times, against about 1.7 of each expected by chance. The clearest breaks came with the Trade Marks Act 1995 and the Designs Act 2003.

figures.label: pairs of a fee change and a filing series
rushes and steps beyond 95% of placebos
of each expected by chance

points: The Trade Marks Act 1995 (January 1996, the cost of a trade mark up 36.59%): Australians' applications -0.315 in logs (2.778% of placebos as large), the pause of {B37}.
The Designs Act 2003 (June 2004, a design's filing fee up 122.2%): overseas applicants' designs rose (a rush of 0.369, 0%).

Breaks the way a price would point: overseas applicants' standard patents after the 15.31% cut of January 1998, and their trade marks after the 40.48% cut of October 2016 (a step of 0.175, 2.778%); Australians' trade marks did not move then (-0.035, 63.89%).
Windows can hold other changes: July 2012's patent step includes the rush before Raising the Bar.

questions.how: At the national level, official fees have been a weak lever on filing, IP Australia's most direct lever.
Fee changes are candidate natural experiments, but most are small and some are confounded with Acts.

prep.what: The cost of obtaining each right in each month, read from every version of the fee regulations ({U108}).
prep.why: A change in the fee is dated by the regulation that made it.

steps: Take each month in which the cost of obtaining a right changed by 10% or more.
Measure the rush and step in filing around it, as {B37} does for policy changes.
Compare each with up to 72 placebo months, and count those beyond 95% of them.
assumptions: Filers respond to the official fee, not the attorney's fee (not recorded), which is often larger.
limits: Several changes coincide with new Acts, so a break cannot be put down to the price alone.
observations.next: {B48} relates the size of each change to the size of the step; {B49} tests renewal fees.
observations.section: 5.4 Official fee changes against placebo dates (added after Stage 2; ADR 0031)
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B47 (observational). Changes in the fees to obtain a right rarely moved filing beyond what placebo months show;
the clearest breaks are new Acts, not prices.**
- 22 months with a fee change have a filing series around them (70 pairs of change and series). 18 changed the fees
  to obtain a right by 10% or more (12 rises, 6 cuts; 34 pairs).
- Of those 34, filing rushed beyond 95% of its placebo months 4 times (3 of 22 pairs after rises, 1 of 12 after
  cuts) and stepped 3 times (2 and 1), against about 1.7 of each expected by chance at that threshold.
- The breaks are new Acts: the Trade Marks Act 1995 (January 1996, the cost of a trade mark up 36.59%), Australians'
  applications -0.315 in logs (2.778% of placebos as large) and overseas applicants' -0.229 (1.389%), the pause of
  B37; the Designs Act 2003 (June 2004, a design's filing fee up 122.2%), overseas applicants' designs rose (a rush of
  0.369 and a step of 0.317, 0%).
- The breaks that point the way a price would: overseas applicants' standard patents after the 15.31% cut of January
  1998 (a rush of 0.147, 2.778%; a step of 0.096, 5.556%), and their trade marks after the 40.48% cut of October 2016
  (a step of 0.175, 2.778%); Australians' trade marks did not move then (-0.035, 63.89%).
- Windows can hold other changes: July 2012's patent step for Australians (0.26, 0%) includes the rush before Raising
  the Bar (April 2013, B37), and October 2020's (0.178, 1.429%), with no change to the fees to obtain a patent,
  the rush before the innovation patent closed (August 2021).

observations.headline: Bigger fee rises go with smaller steps in filing, but the interval includes no link
observations.statement: Across the 34 pairs, the change in the fees to obtain a right and the step in filing that follows have a rank correlation of -0.306 (95% interval -0.646 to 0.080). The direction is a price's, but the size cannot be told from no association with 18 changes, several confounded with Acts.

figures.label: fee change with the step in filing
the 95% interval, which includes no link

points: A bootstrap interval, resampling the pairs.

questions.how: Too few fee changes to estimate how filing responds to price; a sharper test is needed.

prep.what: The 34 pairs of {B47}, each with the size of its fee change and its step.
prep.why: Relates the size of a price change to the size of the response.

steps: Rank the fee changes and the steps, and correlate them.
Bootstrap the pairs for an interval.
assumptions: Each pair is an independent test (several share a change).
limits: 18 changes; Acts confound some.
observations.next: Not a lead; the right-level test in Stage 3 is sharper.
observations.section: 5.4 Official fee changes against placebo dates (added after Stage 2; ADR 0031)
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B48 (observational). Across the larger changes, bigger rises go with smaller steps in filing, but the interval
includes none.** Spearman's rho between the change in the fees to obtain a right and the step that follows: -0.306
over 34 pairs (95% bootstrap interval -0.646 to 0.080). The direction is a price's; the size cannot be told from no
association with 18 changes, several of them confounded with Acts.

observations.headline: Patent cessations rose beyond every placebo month after the 2002 renewal rise; no other change to renewal fees did
observations.statement: After renewal fees for the full term rose 16.17% in September 2002, patent cessations in months 7 to 18 rose 0.353 in logs, more than at any of 72 placebo months. No other renewal change moved cessations beyond the ordinary, including October 2020's rise of 42.82% (0.114, 31.25% of placebos as large).

figures.label: rise in patent cessations after September 2002, in logs
of placebo months as large
October 2020's renewal rise, with no unusual move

points: Trade marks: the 40% cut of November 1998 and the 33.33% rise of November 2016 show nothing beyond the ordinary.
Designs: no change beyond the ordinary, including July 2004 ($55 to $275, when the 2003 Act's renewal replaced the first extension).
**For Q4 and Q5:** at the national level fee changes have been a weak lever on how many rights are kept, apart from 2002; the sharper test is each right's renewal at the anniversary a fee changed.

questions.how: Renewal fees have rarely changed how many rights are kept, nationally.
The 2002 rise is a candidate natural experiment for the effect of renewal fees on keeping patents.

prep.what: The cost of keeping each right for its full term ({U109}), and monthly cessations.
prep.why: Owners decide at each renewal whether to keep paying.

steps: Take each change in renewal fees.
Measure the change in cessations 7 to 18 months later, against placebo months.
assumptions: Owners respond within a year and a half, when renewals at the new fee fall due.
limits: National counts mix rights of every age; the right-level test is sharper.
observations.next: Carried to Stage 3 as the right-level test of renewal at each anniversary a fee changed.
observations.section: 5.4 Official fee changes against placebo dates (added after Stage 2; ADR 0031)
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B49 (observational). Patent cessations rose beyond every placebo month after the September 2002 rise in renewal
fees; no other change in the fees to keep a right, up or down, moved cessations beyond the ordinary.**
- Patents: September 2002 (the full term's renewals up 16.17%), cessations in months 7 to 18 up 0.353 in logs (0% of
  72 placebos as large). The others did not, including October 2020's rise of 42.82% (0.114, 31.25%) and July
  2012's of 15.12% (0.069, 66.67%); August 2010's rise of 10.97% came before a fall (-0.236, 6.944%).
- Trade marks: the 40% cut of November 1998 (0.068, 58.33%) and the 33.33% rise of November 2016 (0.113, 44.44%)
  show nothing beyond the ordinary. July 1992 and July 1993 (rises of 4.255% and 2.041%) did (0.148 and 0.283, 0%),
  while cessations were climbing in the series' first years (it starts in 1987).
- Designs: no change beyond the ordinary (36.11% to 66.67% of placebos as large), including July 2004, when the
  2003 Act's renewal replaced the first extension (a different step: $55 to $275).
- **For Q4 and Q5:** at the national level, fee changes have been a weak lever on how many rights are filed or kept,
  apart from the 2002 renewal rise; the sharper test is each right's renewal at the anniversary a fee changed
  (the rights lens, B8 and B10), for Stage 3.

observations.headline: The dollar's value does not go consistently with filing from overseas; interest rates and overseas filing rise together in booms
observations.statement: As yearly changes by quarter, the dollar against overseas applicants' standard patents is -0.213 before 2008 and 0.259 after: the sign flips. The cash rate rises with overseas applicants' trade marks (0.416 and 0.201) and designs (0.194 and 0.342). Australians' filing barely moves with either.

figures.label: the dollar with overseas standard patents, before and after 2008
the cash rate with overseas trade marks

points: A dearer dollar goes with more overseas designs, not fewer (0.187 and 0.198): a shared cycle, not a price.
Australians' filing: -0.165 to 0.231 over the ten pairs.
**For Stage 3:** the business cycle, here in the [[cash-rate]], is a [[third-factor]] for any before-and-after comparison; the exchange rate is not a usable price signal at this resolution.

questions.how: Identifies the cycle that before-and-after comparisons of policy must allow for.

prep.what: The RBA's cash rate and exchange rates ({U113}) as yearly changes by quarter.
prep.why: Matches the timeline screen's form.

steps: Relate each RBA series to each filing series, before and after mid-2008.
assumptions: Monthly averages (cash rate) and month-end values (dollar) stand for the quarter.
limits: Two periods of 68 and 72 quarters; the cycle may differ again.
observations.next: The cycle is a third factor in Stage 3.
observations.section: 5.5 The dollar and the cash rate against filing (RBA; added after Stage 2, gap B1)
observations.chapter: 5. Lens: Australia over time (one row per month)
observations.original:
**B52 (observational). The dollar's value does not go consistently with filing from overseas; Australian interest
rates and overseas filing rise together in booms.** Year-on-year changes by quarter, 68 quarters (1991Q3 to 2008Q2)
and 72 (2008Q3 on):
- The dollar in US dollars against overseas applicants' standard patents: -0.213, then 0.259: the sign flips between
  periods. Against overseas designs it is positive in both (0.187 and 0.198): a dearer dollar goes with more, not
  fewer, which is a shared cycle, not a price.
- The cash rate against overseas applicants' trade marks: 0.416 and 0.201; against their designs 0.194 and 0.342.
- Australians' filing barely moves with either (-0.165 to 0.231 over the ten pairs).
- **For Stage 3:** the business cycle, here in the cash rate, is a third factor for any before-and-after comparison
  (B37, B47); the exchange rate is not a usable price signal at this resolution.

observations.headline: Real GDP goes with overseas applicants' patenting, more strongly since 2008; the states' demand does not track Australians' filing
observations.statement: As yearly changes by quarter, real GDP goes with overseas applicants' standard patents at 0.159 to mid-2008 and 0.373 after; with Australians' standard patents at -0.075 and 0.194. Of 16 pairs of a state's final demand with Australians' filing, two keep their sign at 0.1 or more in both periods, about what chance gives.

figures.label: real GDP with overseas applicants' standard patents
state demand pairs that hold their sign

points: Overseas applicants' trade marks and designs: 0.05 to 0.227. Australians' trade marks 0.207 and -0.202.
The two that hold are the Northern Territory's (patents 0.168 and 0.164, trade marks -0.189 and -0.3).
**So** the cycle ({B52}) and real growth go with filing from overseas, not from here.

audit.title: Checked against IP Australia
audit.eyebrow: Review · Stage 1 against the publisher's own figures
audit.lead: IP Australia publishes its own figures on the IP system every year, in its Australian IP Reports, and its own research. This review checks Stage 1's observations against them: where IP Australia has published the same thing, do the two agree? Where it has drawn a conclusion, what does Stage 1's evidence add?
audit.banner: **This review leaves every observation as it was written.** The observation pages, and the notebook they quote, are unchanged at this stage. Where the review qualifies an observation, it says so here; revising the observation itself is the research owner's decision.

stats.label: figures IP Australia published, recounted from Stage 1's data

in_brief: **Stage 1's counts hold up.** IP Australia's own yearly figures are reproduced from Stage 1's data for every kind of right. Standard patent applications agree in all 12 years from 2014 to 2025, within 0.34%; provisional applications within 0.25%; standard patents granted within 0.03%.

**No observation is contradicted.** 23 are corroborated, 9 are consistent with what IP Australia says, 1 is disputed in part, and 66 cannot be tested because IP Australia publishes nothing comparable.
**Four things do not agree** (below). Three change how an observation should be read; none overturns one.

**Two questions close or narrow.** The jump in innovation patents in 2016 ({U67}) was a real rise that IP Australia reported itself. The fall in first-time trade mark filers ({U45}) is a fall in linking filers to their ABNs, not in filing.

method.title: Find what IP Australia has published
method.text: Its twelve Australian IP Reports (2015 to 2026), its research papers and its analytic notes, as the project's companion repository holds them, page by page. The IP Report 2026 was read in full; the others were searched topic by topic, and every passage that bears on an observation was read in context.

method.title: Count the same thing the same way
method.text: IP Australia counts calendar years, and counts an application as Australian if one of its filers gave an Australian origin. Stage 1's data were recounted the same way. This reproduces IP Australia's count of Australian standard patent applications exactly in 2022 and 2025 (2,494 and 2,810).

method.title: Allow for small differences
method.text: A count agrees if it is within 2% of IP Australia's, a share if it is within 1 percentage point. IP Australia revises its figures between editions, so the latest edition to give a year is used.

method.title: Give each observation a verdict
method.text: Each observation is marked by how it stands against IP Australia's evidence, from corroborated to not testable. A match says Stage 1 reads the register as IP Australia does; it says nothing about why.

method.title: Keep it checkable
method.text: The 195 figures, each with its report and page, and the code that recounts them, are kept in the repository. A test fails if they fall out of step with the data.

verdict_words.corroborated: IP Australia publishes the same figure, and Stage 1's data reproduce it once both count it the same way.
verdict_words.consistent: IP Australia publishes a related figure or finding that points the same way, but not the same figure.
verdict_words.qualified: IP Australia's figures agree, but show a caveat the observation does not state.
verdict_words.disputed: IP Australia gives a figure for what reads as the same thing, and Stage 1's data cannot reproduce it.
verdict_words.contradicted: IP Australia's figure disagrees, and no difference in how it was counted explains it.
verdict_words.not testable: IP Australia has published nothing that can be compared.

audit.measures_intro: Each row is a kind of figure IP Australia publishes year by year. "Agree" counts the years within the tolerance. Most of the figures outside it differ only because IP Australia counted them another way; the four that do not are set out below. By state, for example, IP Australia counts an application in the state of each of its Australian applicants and Stage 1's data in the first filer's, so the counts differ while each state's share agrees within 0.2 points.
audit.closeness_intro: Each dot is one figure IP Australia published, placed by its value (across) and by the same figure recounted from Stage 1's data (up). On the line, the two are equal. Both scales are logarithmic, so a small count and a large one can be read on the same chart.
audit.untestable_intro: IP Australia does not publish these things, so they stand on Stage 1's own checks. Most are about the data's structure and the repairs made to it, the register's fine detail, or sources other than IP Australia's.
audit.conclusions_intro: What IP Australia concludes, how strongly it says it, and what Stage 1's evidence adds. None of IP Australia's conclusions is adopted here: that is the research owner's decision.

conclusions.claim: The rise in provisional applications reflects digital tools, including AI, lowering the cost of a first filing.
conclusions.strength: "Consistent with"; "an important focus for ongoing analysis".
conclusions.adds: {U8}: the rise is broad (single-filing individuals 1,538 to 2,507) and concentrated (54 individuals filed 1,528). Both fit; neither proves it.

conclusions.claim: A firm's first patent or trade mark coincides with lasting gains in income and productivity.
conclusions.adds: Nothing to test. Stage 1 has no data on firms' performance.

conclusions.claim: Patents whose examination is sped up are renewed, used in products and built on more.
conclusions.strength: Research commissioned by IP Australia; an association.
conclusions.adds: {U34} (expedited requests, 1.87% to 10.31%) and {U36} (years in force) are the same two measures: a pair for Stage 2 that would repeat the finding with open data. Stage 2 found it holds for overseas organisations only; pooled, it is a change in who asks ({B13}).

conclusions.claim: The innovation patent did not meet its goal of serving small businesses.
conclusions.strength: IP Australia's and the Productivity Commission's research.
conclusions.adds: {U7}: Australians' share of second-tier patents fell from 79.2% to 87.4% (FY1990 to FY2010) to 16.1% in FY2021.

conclusions.claim: Raising the Bar increased competition and follow-on invention, unevenly across fields.
conclusions.adds: {U28} and {U33} show the rush and the early examination requests that any evaluation must allow for.

conclusions.claim: Clutter on the trade mark register is not an immediate concern, though falling renewals are a possible source.
conclusions.adds: {U36} confirms the fall in renewals; Stage 1 cannot measure whether marks are used.

conclusions.claim: IP rights do not significantly raise market concentration.
conclusions.adds: Not testable here. Stage 1's concentration is of filing ({U44}, {U52}), a different thing.

conclusions.claim: The 2021 rise in Australians' patent applications was brought forward by the innovation patent's closure.
Chinese patent filings in Australia stalled in 2021 and fell 8.2% in 2022, after China stopped paying for filings abroad.
conclusions.adds: Not in an observation; Stage 2's comparisons by origin ({U13}, {U70}) should allow for it.

conclusions.claim: The rise in direct patent filing in 2025 partly reflects which countries file.
conclusions.adds: {U90}: Australians' own direct filing rose, which a change in countries cannot explain.

conclusions.claim: Women are under-represented among Australian inventors, below the world average.
Collaboration between universities and industry is "not a crisis"; Australia is 13th of 35 OECD countries.
conclusions.strength: IP Australia's analysis of jointly filed IP.
conclusions.adds: {U84}'s joint filing is the same kind of measure; Stage 2 can bring it up to date.

audit.changes_intro: What the review changes for Stages 2 and 3. The observations themselves are not changed (see the note at the top).
changes: Design shares among designs of known origin are read as lower bounds (D1).
Innovation patent counts include standard patents converted into innovation patents, as IP Australia's later reports do ({U67}).
Stage 2's look at the innovation patent's closure includes Australians' standard patents in 2021 and 2022 ({U28}).
From FY2025, first-time filers are counted by applicant as well as by ABN ({U45}).
A new pair for Stage 2: expedited examination against how long patents are kept (C3). Done: it holds for overseas organisations only ({B13}).
Any comparison with IP Australia's figures counts calendar years, and Australian applications the way IP Australia does.
audit.questions_intro: Three questions the review raised, added to the research owner's request to IP Australia on 27 October 2026.

questions.text: What does IP Australia's "55.6% of resident applications were filed by individuals" (2022) count? (D3)
What did IP Australia's report count for 2018's trade marks, about 2,000 more than IP RAPID, WIPO and IP Australia's own register? (D2; reworded after the register check)
IP Australia's register holds the owner's country for most designs IP RAPID leaves unknown; could IP RAPID publish it? (D1; reworded after the register check)

limits.title: Not independent
limits.text: IP Australia's reports come from its own register, as IP RAPID does. Agreement shows Stage 1 reads the register as IP Australia does, not that the register is right. The independent checks are WIPO's and the World Bank's, and they agree too.

limits.title: Two reports are scanned
limits.text: The 2018 and 2021 reports have no text layer, so their text was read by OCR. Every figure used from them agrees or is explained, which checks both.

limits.title: Searched, not read in full
limits.text: Beyond the 2026 report, the documents were searched topic by topic, so a statement in words the searches did not reach may be missed.

limits.title: Much cannot be tested this way
limits.text: 66 observations concern things IP Australia does not publish. They stand on Stage 1's own checks.

findings.title: Most designs with no recorded origin are Australian
findings.text: IP Australia counts 2,595 Australian design applications in 2021, 2,652 in 2023 and 3,078 in 2025. Stage 1's data find 2,331, 2,358 and 2,653 with an Australian filer, while the totals agree. The difference is the designs IP RAPID publishes with no applicant country: IP Australia counts about three in four of them as Australian.
findings.means: A share of designs among those of known origin understates Australians, by about 2 to 3 points in recent years. It is a [[lower-bound]].

findings.title: Trade marks filed in 2018 are short in IP RAPID
findings.text: IP Australia reported 79,490 trade mark applications in 2018; Stage 1's data hold 77,496, or 1,994 fewer. Every other year from 2015 to 2025 agrees within 0.05%. The missing ones are [[madrid|Madrid]] applications: IP Australia reported them rising by around 13 per cent that year, while IP RAPID's stay level. Why is not known.
findings.means: Stage 2 flags 2018 in any trade mark series, and reads Madrid counts across it with care.

findings.title: One IP Australia figure cannot be reproduced
findings.text: IP Australia's IP Report 2023 says that in 2022, 55.6% of resident applications were filed by individuals rather than organisations. Stage 1's data give 20.65% of Australians' standard patent applications with an individual as the first filer, and 26.76% of their applicants. No other way of counting comes near 55.6%.
findings.means: {U13} and {U48} stand on Stage 1's evidence. IP Australia has been asked what the 55.6% counts (OQ12).

findings.title: Trade marks in force in 2005, for context only
findings.text: IP Australia counts 391,450 trade marks in force in 2005 and 635,355 in 2017. Stage 1's data give 367,344 and 645,872: 2017 agrees, and 2005 is 6% lower, which fits the register's incomplete records of older rights.
findings.means: No observation quotes a count of marks in force, so nothing changes.

verdicts.label: Corroborated; an explanation offered
verdicts.evidence: IP Australia: 4,343 (2024) to 6,867 (2025), "one of the clearest structural shifts"; individuals "close to half", up from "around one-third"; 'new filers' 63% (42% in 2021 to 2024); self-filers 52% (19% to 27%); "consistent with reduced entry costs and faster drafting and search enabled by digital tools, including artificial intelligence" (ipr-2026 p21). Lens: 6,874; individuals 48.25% and 34.08%; new filers by applicant 68.85% (2025) against 56.02% to 60.07% (2021 to 2024), a jump in the same year (the lens's level is higher: an applicant counted by party id)

It reads the rise as consistent with digital tools, including AI, making a first filing cheaper and easier. That is IP Australia's interpretation, not a finding here, and the few very heavy filers this observation found are not in IP Australia's account.

verdicts.note: IP Australia's yearly counts of standard patents granted match exactly, in all 10 years it published. It does not publish grant rates by year of application, so those are not tested.

One IP Australia figure cannot be reproduced: that 55.6% of residents' applications in 2022 were filed by individuals. Stage 1's data give 20.65% (D3).

verdicts.note: Each state's share of Australians' standard patent applications agrees with IP Australia's within 0.2 points, in 2021, 2023 and 2025.

verdicts.evidence: Annual counts (section 3); the 2009 fall "following the events of the Global Financial Crisis" (ipr-2017 p6); trade marks −11.2% in 2022 (ipr-2023 p6; U25: −11.2%); design records in 2024 and 2025 with non-residents 70.1% (ipr-2026 p57, p58); IP Australia's 2.5% average growth of standard patents in 2010 to 2019 (ipr-2020 p7) against U25's 2.0% a year (a compound rate; IP Australia does not say how it averaged)
verdicts.follows: Rates spanning 2018 for trade marks: D2

verdicts.label: Corroborated; wording clarified
verdicts.evidence: Standard grants match exactly (section 3), peaking at 23,743 in 2016 among the years IP Australia published (2014 to 2025); 2024's 24% rise "due largely to productivity improvements in examination" (ipr-2025 p4). U27's 25,687 counts all patents granted (the timeline's series includes second-tier patents); standard patents alone are 23,744
verdicts.follows: Quote standard grants from `rights`, all patents from `timeline`, and say which

verdicts.label: Corroborated and extended
verdicts.evidence: Raising the Bar: residents' applications fell 35% in 2014 (ipr-2015 p9; lens 3,122 to 2,028, −35.0%). The innovation closure: 7,844 applications in 2021, +71%, non-residents 78% of the growth (ipr-2022 p16; lens 7,833). And a response U28 does not list: residents' standard patents grew 24.8% in 2021 because applicants "bring forward standard patent applications" to keep the option of converting them into innovation patents (ipr-2023 p13); the lens's resident standard patents rise 2,403 to 2,998, +24.8%
verdicts.follows: Stage 2's closure window includes Australians' standard patents in 2021 and 2022
verdicts.note: IP Australia reports the same responses to Raising the Bar (Australians' applications fell 35% in 2014) and to the innovation patent's closure. It adds one this observation does not list: Australians' standard patents rose 24.8% in 2021, filed early so they could still be turned into innovation patents. Stage 1's data show the same 24.8%.

verdicts.label: Corroborated; the direct-filing lead supported
verdicts.evidence: PCT share 73.4% (2022), 69.6% (2024) and 66.7% (2025) (ipr-2023 p11, ipr-2026 p26), within 0.34 points; "provisional patents and direct filings have expanded, particularly among domestic innovators" (ipr-2026 p19). Madrid: 56% of overseas trade marks in 2020 (ipr-2021 p12; U90's 57.2% in FY2020); Australians lodged 3 of 14,451 Madrid applications in 2015 (ipr-2016 p14), as U90's 97.9% to 99.1% direct shows
verdicts.follows: IP Australia explains the overall shift partly by country mix (fewer US filings, more Australian and Chinese); U90's rise is among Australians, so the mix does not explain it, and IP Australia reads it as a real change. "Priority claims recorded late" is not excluded
verdicts.note: IP Australia reports the same shift away from the PCT (66.7% of standard applications in 2025) and says direct filings have expanded, particularly among domestic innovators, which supports this observation's lead.

verdicts.label: Consistent
verdicts.evidence: "The share of Australian classes filed abroad through the Madrid system has increased, from 45.0% in 2019 to 56.6% in 2024" (ipr-2026 p54); 53% of Australians' trade mark applications abroad went through Madrid in 2021 (ipr-2022 p23). U91 counts marks taken abroad, a different unit
verdicts.note: IP Australia reports Australians using the Madrid system more to take their trade marks abroad, measured another way.

verdicts.label: Corroborated
verdicts.evidence: "In 2022, women constituted 14.6% of Australian inventors, the same level as in 2021", a participation rate "2 percentage points lower than the international average" (ipr-2023 p66, p67). Its 14.6% for 2021 is the WIPO figure U97 checked its estimate (14.9%) against, so IP Australia reads WIPO's data as U97 does. About 12% of unique Australian inventors on applications in Australia in 2016 (ipr-2022 p17), beside U97's 13.6% estimate for 2015
verdicts.note: IP Australia gives women as 14.6% of Australian inventors in 2021 and 2022: the WIPO figure this observation checked its estimate against.

verdicts.label: Consistent
verdicts.evidence: As U97: IP Australia's 14.6% (PCT, 2022) and about 12% (2016), beside U98's 14.34%, 12.43% and 12.75%
verdicts.note: IP Australia's figures (14.6% on international applications in 2022, about 12% in 2016) are in line with about one inventor in seven.
